name: Fior di Latte Gelato Base
tagline: The plain-milk base every other gelato in the case starts from.
story: Fior di latte is the mother base of the gelato case: clean dairy flavour, dense and slow-melting, built without egg yolk so it never masks whatever's churned into it next. Boris scales this one recipe up and turns it into pistachio, hazelnut, and stracciatella by addition rather than starting each flavour from scratch. Get the balance of sugars and non-fat solids right here and every derivative flavour inherits it.
method:
1. Combine milk, milk powder, and half the sugar in a pot; sweat over medium heat to 40°C, whisking to dissolve the powder fully.
2. Add cream, glucose syrup, remaining sugar, and salt. Bring to 65°C, whisking constantly.
3. Sprinkle stabilizer over the surface while whisking to disperse it without clumping (if using).
4. Heat to 85°C for pasteurization, holding at temperature for 2 minutes. Do not let it catch on the bottom.
5. Chill immediately over an ice bath to below 4°C, then rest covered in the fridge a minimum of 4 hours, overnight preferred, so the fats and stabilizer fully hydrate.
6. Churn in the gelato machine following the manufacturer's cycle, until it holds a soft, glossy ribbon and reads around -6 to -8°C off the machine.
7. Transfer to storage tubs, level, and blast or hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 2 weeks in the display cabinet at -12/-14°C; up to 6 weeks in a -18°C freezer, well sealed against ice crystals.

**Chef's notes:** under-pasteurizing or rushing the 4-hour rest is the single most common cause of an icy, thin-bodied gelato — the stabilizer needs that time to bind water. Never re-melt and re-churn a batch that has fully hardened.

name: Vanilla Custard Ice Cream
tagline: Egg-rich crème anglaise base, churned cold, for the vanilla anchor of the case.
story: Where fior di latte stays lean, this is the rich end of the spectrum: a proper crème anglaise churned cold, carrying real vanilla bean and enough yolk to hold a dense, custardy set. It's the base Boris reaches for whenever a dessert needs an ice cream that tastes of something on its own, not just texture. Steady heat and a thermometer are non-negotiable; scrambled yolk cannot be fixed.
method:
1. Split vanilla pods, scrape the seeds; warm the milk, half the cream, and the pods and seeds to 70°C. Cover and infuse off heat for 15 minutes.
2. Whisk yolks and sugar together until pale, about 1 minute — do not let sugar sit on raw yolk unmixed, it will lump.
3. Temper: pour a third of the hot milk onto the yolks whisking constantly, then return everything to the pot.
4. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring in a figure-eight with a spatula, to 82–84°C, until the custard coats the back of the spoon and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line. Do not exceed 85°C.
5. Strain immediately through a fine sieve into the remaining cold cream to arrest cooking.
6. Chill over ice to below 4°C, then rest covered a minimum of 4 hours, ideally overnight.
7. Churn to a soft-serve consistency (-6 to -8°C), then transfer to tubs and hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 2 weeks in cabinet; 6 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** the custard is done by feel and thermometer together — past 85°C the yolk proteins seize and the base grains. If it curdles, blitz immediately with a stick blender and pass through a fine chinois before it goes further.

name: Pistachio Gelato
tagline: Fior di latte finished with raw, unsweetened pistachio paste — no green colouring.
story: Pistachio gelato lives or dies on the paste, not the base — Boris only uses unsweetened, unsalted 100% pistachio paste and lets its natural colour show, a duller khaki than the fluorescent green most guests expect. It sits alongside fior di latte and stracciatella as one of three gelati that never leave the case. The nut has to be tasted before it's sweet.
method:
1. Prepare the fior di latte base through pasteurization (see Fior di Latte Gelato Base): heat milk, milk powder, sugar, cream, glucose, and salt to 85°C.
2. Off heat, whisk in the pistachio paste until fully smooth with no streaks.
3. Chill over ice to below 4°C, cover, and rest a minimum of 4 hours.
4. Churn until it holds a dense, matte ribbon, around -6 to -8°C.
5. Fold through the chopped roasted pistachio if using, working quickly so it doesn't melt the batch.
6. Transfer to tubs, level, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 2 weeks in cabinet; 6 weeks frozen and sealed, covered well as pistachio oils oxidize faster than dairy fat.

**Chef's notes:** cheap pistachio paste is often cut with almond and coloured — taste it raw off the spoon before committing a batch; it should taste bitter-green and slightly resinous, not sweet.

name: Hazelnut Gelato
tagline: Pure roasted hazelnut paste, not sweetened gianduia — the other nut base in the case.
story: Hazelnut gelato is the other pure-nut base, made with 100% roasted hazelnut paste rather than the sweetened gianduia paste most suppliers push, which lets the roast character carry instead of cocoa and sugar. Keep it on separate scoops and spades from pistachio to avoid cross-flavour on the line.
method:
1. Prepare the fior di latte base through pasteurization: heat milk, milk powder, sugar, cream, glucose, and salt to 85°C.
2. Off heat, whisk in the roasted hazelnut paste until fully smooth.
3. Chill over ice to below 4°C, cover, and rest a minimum of 4 hours.
4. Churn until it holds a dense, matte ribbon, around -6 to -8°C.
5. Fold through chopped toasted hazelnuts if using, working quickly.
6. Transfer to tubs, level, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 2 weeks in cabinet; 6 weeks frozen and sealed, well covered against oxidation.

**Chef's notes:** taste the hazelnut paste raw before committing a batch — a stale or low-fat paste tastes flat and cardboard-like once frozen, and freezing will not hide it.

name: Stracciatella Gelato
tagline: Fior di latte, shattered with a thin stream of melted dark chocolate mid-churn.
story: Stracciatella is fior di latte finished at the very last moment: a thin stream of melted dark chocolate poured into the machine while it's still turning, which shatters into fine, brittle shards instead of clumping into chips. It only works if the base is properly churned and the chocolate is thin enough to snap, not chew.
method:
1. Churn the fior di latte base to a soft-serve consistency, -6 to -8°C.
2. Melt dark chocolate with a little neutral oil or cocoa butter to 45°C so it stays fluid and thin enough to shatter — about 10% oil by weight of chocolate.
3. With the machine still running, drizzle the chocolate in a thin, steady stream directly onto the moving gelato. It will seize into shards within seconds — stop as soon as it's evenly distributed; over-mixing turns shards into streaks.
4. Transfer immediately to tubs, level, and hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 10 days in cabinet — the chocolate shards soften and lose crunch faster than a straight gelato holds; 4 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** chocolate poured in too thick, or off too cold a stream, clumps into chunks instead of shards — thin it with oil and pour slowly.

name: Olive Oil Ice Cream
tagline: Fruity extra virgin olive oil, streamed in cold, finished with a pinch of flaky salt.
story: A savoury-leaning ice cream built around a fruity, peppery extra virgin olive oil, finished with a pinch of flaky salt — the oil is folded in cold, after churning starts, so its aromatics survive the machine instead of cooking off in the custard. Boris pairs it with citrus and stone fruit desserts on the Taller tasting menu, where a plain vanilla would be too sweet.
method:
1. Warm the milk and half the cream with sugar to 70°C.
2. Whisk yolks with the remaining sugar; temper with the hot milk, then return to the pot and cook to 82°C, stirring constantly, until it coats a spoon.
3. Strain into the remaining cold cream, chill to below 4°C, and rest a minimum of 4 hours.
4. Begin churning; once it reaches soft-serve consistency, stream in the olive oil in a thin trickle with the machine running so it emulsifies rather than pools.
5. Add a pinch of fine salt in the last 30 seconds of churning.
6. Transfer to tubs, level, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 10 days in cabinet — best within 2 weeks, as the oil can taste flat past that; 4 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** adding the oil to a hot base splits it and dulls the flavour — it must go in cold, into an already-churning machine, in a thin stream.

name: Brown Butter Ice Cream
tagline: Butter cooked to a deep hazelnut brown before it goes into the custard.
story: Butter cooked to a deep hazelnut-brown before it goes into the custard, so the ice cream carries that toasted, nutty depth rather than plain dairy fat. It reads as an autumn flavour on the Bistro Mondo dessert board, next to poached fruit or a bare tuile, and needs nothing else added to taste finished.
method:
1. Cook butter over medium heat, swirling, until the milk solids turn deep amber-brown and it smells toasted, about 6-8 minutes. Strain through a fine sieve, reserving the browned solids and the clarified butter separately.
2. Warm milk and cream with half the sugar and the reserved browned milk solids to 70°C; steep 10 minutes, then strain out the solids.
3. Whisk yolks with remaining sugar; temper with the hot dairy, return to heat, and cook to 82-84°C, stirring, until it coats a spoon.
4. Off heat, whisk in the brown butter itself until fully emulsified.
5. Strain, chill over ice to below 4°C, rest a minimum of 4 hours.
6. Churn to soft-serve consistency, transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 2 weeks in cabinet; 6 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** if the brown butter is added to a base that's too hot or too cold it separates on freezing into a grainy, oily texture — it needs to be warm and fully emulsified with a whisk or stick blender before chilling.

name: Frozen Yogurt
tagline: Tart, low-sugar strained yogurt, churned to cut through rich desserts.
story: A tart, low-sugar frozen yogurt built to cut through rich desserts rather than compete with them — mostly strained Greek-style yogurt with just enough cream and glucose to keep it scoopable. It's the palate-cleanser register on both menus, served plain with olive oil and citrus, or under stone fruit.
method:
1. Warm a third of the yogurt with the sugar, glucose syrup, and milk powder to 45°C, whisking to dissolve fully — do not overheat or the yogurt will split.
2. Off heat, whisk in the remaining cold yogurt and cream until smooth.
3. Add lemon juice and salt, taste — it should read tart before sweet.
4. Chill to below 4°C if not already cold, rest 2 hours (yogurt bases need less resting than custard).
5. Churn until it holds a soft, glossy set (-6 to -8°C) — it will be looser than a custard ice cream, which is correct.
6. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 10 days in cabinet; 3 weeks frozen — it loses tang faster than a custard base.

**Chef's notes:** heating the yogurt above 50°C, or heating all of it at once, causes it to split into curds and whey — only warm a portion, gently, to carry the sugars.

name: Coconut Sorbet
tagline: Dairy-free coconut cream sorbet, sharpened with lime.
story: A dairy-free sorbet built on coconut cream and water rather than milk, so it stays clean and pourable instead of waxy — useful for guests avoiding dairy and as a base for tropical composed desserts. A little lime keeps it from tasting flat.
method:
1. Combine coconut cream, water, sugar, glucose syrup, and stabilizer in a pot.
2. Heat to 85°C, whisking, holding for 2 minutes to pasteurize and hydrate the stabilizer.
3. Chill over ice to below 4°C, rest covered a minimum of 4 hours.
4. Add lime juice and a pinch of salt to sharpen the flavour, tasting for balance — it should taste distinctly of coconut, not just sweet.
5. Churn to a soft, glossy set (-5 to -7°C; sorbets churn slightly softer than ice creams).
6. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 10 days in cabinet; 4 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** coconut cream separates on standing — whisk or blend it smooth before measuring, or the fat will pool unevenly through the batch.

name: Mango Sorbet
tagline: Ripe mango purée and stock syrup, balanced to taste rather than fixed ratio.
story: Made from ripe mango purée and a light stock syrup, balanced with lime to keep the sweetness from going flat — mango varies enormously in sugar and acid batch to batch, so the syrup ratio is a starting point that gets tasted and adjusted every time, not a fixed formula.
method:
1. Make a syrup: heat water, sugar, and glucose syrup to 85°C, whisking to dissolve; cool completely.
2. Purée ripe mango flesh until completely smooth, pass through a coarse sieve to remove fibre.
3. Combine mango purée with the cooled syrup and lime juice; taste and adjust — riper, sweeter mango needs more lime and less syrup, and vice versa. The mix should taste slightly sweeter than you want the final sorbet, as freezing mutes sweetness.
4. Chill to below 4°C, rest 2 hours.
5. Churn to a soft, glossy set (-5 to -7°C).
6. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 5 days in cabinet — fresh fruit sorbets oxidize and lose brightness fastest of the case; 3 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** never add the syrup hot to raw purée — it cooks the fruit's edges and dulls the colour and flavour; always cool the syrup fully first.

name: Raspberry Sorbet
tagline: Straight raspberry purée, seeded out, no filler fruit.
story: Straight raspberry purée seived against seeds, syrup, and a touch of lemon — no filler fruit added, so the colour and the sourness are both real. It's the sharpest sorbet on the pass and the one Boris uses to reset a palate between rich courses at Taller.
method:
1. Purée raspberries, then pass firmly through a fine sieve to remove all seeds — work it with a ladle in a circular motion; this takes a few minutes and cannot be rushed without leaving fruit behind.
2. Make a syrup: heat water, sugar, and glucose to 85°C; cool completely.
3. Combine raspberry purée, cooled syrup, and lemon juice; taste and balance — it should taste tart enough to sting slightly before freezing mutes it.
4. Chill to below 4°C, rest 2 hours.
5. Churn to a soft, glossy set (-5 to -7°C).
6. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 5 days in cabinet; 3 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** frozen raspberries work as well as fresh and are more consistent in acidity — thaw fully before puréeing so no ice dilutes the mix.

name: Blood Orange Sorbet
tagline: Juiced to order in season, syrup ratio adjusted to the fruit's swing in acidity.
story: Juiced to order in season for the colour as much as the flavour — the depth of red varies fruit to fruit, and Boris tastes the juice raw before setting the syrup ratio, since blood orange swings between sweet and quite tart within the same box. A little zest in the syrup keeps the aroma from going flat once frozen.
method:
1. Zest two of the oranges into the sugar for the syrup and let sit 10 minutes to release the oils.
2. Juice all the blood oranges, strain out pulp and seeds.
3. Make the syrup: heat water, the zested sugar, and glucose to 85°C, whisking; strain out the zest, cool completely.
4. Combine juice, cooled syrup, and a squeeze of lemon; taste and adjust the ratio for the batch's natural sweetness.
5. Chill to below 4°C, rest 2 hours.
6. Churn to a soft, glossy set (-5 to -7°C).
7. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 4 days in cabinet — citrus sorbets fade fastest of all; 3 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** juice loses aromatic top notes within a day even refrigerated — juice as close to churning as the schedule allows.

name: Chocolate Sorbet
tagline: Dairy-free, water-based chocolate sorbet — darker and denser than any ice cream version.
story: An intense, dairy-free chocolate sorbet made with water rather than milk or cream, so the cocoa reads darker and more bitter than any ice cream version could — dense, almost fudgy, and holding its shape well past the melt point of a dairy base. Runs on the Taller dessert list for guests who can't take dairy.
method:
1. Combine water, sugar, glucose syrup, and cocoa powder in a pot, whisking to break up lumps before heat.
2. Bring to a simmer, whisking constantly, and cook 3-4 minutes to fully hydrate the cocoa and cook out its raw edge.
3. Remove from heat, add chopped dark chocolate, and whisk until fully melted and smooth.
4. Pass through a fine sieve to remove any grit, chill over ice to below 4°C, rest covered a minimum of 4 hours.
5. Churn to a soft, glossy set (-5 to -7°C) — it will look denser and darker than a dairy ice cream, which is correct.
6. Transfer to tubs, hard-freeze to -18°C.

Holding: 10 days in cabinet; 4 weeks frozen and sealed.

**Chef's notes:** cocoa powder needs real cook time in liquid or it tastes chalky and raw — don't skip the simmer stage.

name: Granita di Caffè
tagline: Strong sweetened coffee, frozen and raked by hand into loose crystals.
story: The simplest thing in the freezer and one of the most exact — strong sweetened coffee frozen in a shallow tray and raked with a fork every half hour so it sets as loose, glassy crystals rather than a solid block. Served with unsweetened whipped cream on the side, never folded in, so the guest controls the richness.
method:
1. Brew strong coffee (or pull concentrated espresso) and sweeten while still hot, stirring until the sugar fully dissolves. Taste — it should be a touch sweeter than a coffee you'd drink, since freezing mutes sweetness.
2. Cool completely, then pour into a shallow metal tray no more than 3cm deep.
3. Freeze uncovered. After 45 minutes, once ice crystals form at the edges, rake through with a fork, dragging the frozen edges into the liquid centre.
4. Repeat every 30-45 minutes for 3-4 hours, until the entire tray is a mass of loose, separate ice crystals with no liquid remaining and no solid block.
5. Cover once fully set; keep at -18°C.
6. To serve, rake again with a fork to loosen the crystals before scooping into a chilled glass.

Holding: best within 3 days — granita re-freezes into a denser block the longer it sits, losing its loose crystal texture; 2 weeks frozen is the outside limit, raking harder each time.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the raking schedule is the only way to fail this — an unattended tray just becomes a coffee ice block.

ingredients.name: water
ingredients.notes: to dilute to volume, adjust to taste

name: Granita de Almendra
tagline: Raw almond milk, lightly sweetened and frozen the same way as the coffee version.
story: A Spanish almond-milk granita: raw almonds soaked and blitzed with water, strained, lightly sweetened, and frozen the same way as the coffee version. It shows up on the Taller menu as a savoury-adjacent palate cleanser, sometimes with a few drops of good olive oil or sherry vinegar on top rather than fruit.
method:
1. Soak raw almonds in cold water a minimum of 8 hours or overnight, refrigerated.
2. Drain, then blitz the almonds with fresh water until completely smooth, about 2 minutes on high speed.
3. Strain through a fine cloth or nut bag, squeezing firmly to extract all the milk; discard the pulp (or reserve for another use).
4. Warm a portion of the almond milk with the sugar until fully dissolved, then combine with the rest, cold. Add a pinch of salt and a few drops of lemon juice to lift it.
5. Chill to below 4°C, pour into a shallow tray no more than 3cm deep.
6. Freeze uncovered, raking with a fork every 30-45 minutes for 3-4 hours until it's a mass of loose ice crystals.
7. Cover once set; keep at -18°C.

Holding: best within 3 days for texture, 2 weeks frozen as the outside limit.

**Chef's notes:** don't over-blend or over-heat the almond milk — it can split and turn grainy; keep the warming step gentle and brief.

name: Chili Crisp
tagline: Slow-fried shallot, garlic and chili flake in oil, crackling with numbing spice.
story: A spoon of this replaces three seasonings at once — heat, crunch and savoury depth over rice, noodles, eggs or grilled fish. Built like a Sichuan condiment but kept in constant rotation across both kitchens because it holds for weeks and never tastes tired. The point is textural contrast: shattering fried alliums suspended in a lightly numbing, star-anise-scented oil.
method:
1. Slice 150 g shallot and 100 g garlic as thinly and evenly as possible; uneven slices burn unevenly.
2. In a heavy pot, heat 1000 g neutral oil to 140°C with 2 star anise, 1 cinnamon stick and 15 g Sichuan peppercorn. Hold at 140°C for 8 minutes to infuse, then strain out the whole spices and discard.
3. Return oil to 130°C. Fry the shallot first, stirring constantly, until deep gold, 8-10 minutes. Lift out with a spider onto paper.
4. Fry the garlic the same way at 120°C until gold, 4-5 minutes — it colours faster than shallot and turns bitter past golden. Lift out.
5. Let oil drop to 100°C. Place 120 g coarse chili flake and 30 g soy sauce in a heatproof bowl. Pour the hot oil over in three additions, stirring between each — one pour at full heat would scorch the flake instantly.
6. Stir in the fried shallot, fried garlic, 20 g sugar and 20 g toasted sesame oil. Salt to taste.
7. Cool fully before jarring; the oil sets slightly cloudy when cold, that is normal.
Holding: airtight jar, fridge, 6 weeks; always use a dry spoon.
**Chef's notes:** the failure point is oil temperature at the chili-flake pour — too hot and the flake turns acrid and black instead of deep red; a thermometer is not optional here.

name: Garlic Confit Oil
tagline: Whole garlic cloves cooked low in oil until sweet, strained to a clean garlic oil.
story: Confiting the garlic first and using the cooking oil as the finished product gives a rounder, sweeter garlic flavour than a raw-infused oil, with none of the raw bite or the risk of harshness. The confit cloves themselves are kept separately and mashed into dressings, spreads or mash — nothing here is wasted.
method:
1. Peel 250 g garlic cloves, keeping them whole.
2. Place in a small, heavy pot and cover with 1000 g olive oil — the cloves should be fully submerged.
3. Bring to a bare simmer over low heat until the oil reaches 90°C, then hold between 85-90°C, never letting it bubble hard; a hard boil scorches the garlic and turns the oil bitter.
4. Cook 35-40 minutes, until the cloves are pale gold and yield to no pressure from a knife tip.
5. Remove from heat and cool the garlic in the oil to room temperature — this is where most of the flavour transfers.
6. Strain the oil through a fine sieve into a clean jar; reserve the confit cloves in a separate covered container.
Holding: oil keeps refrigerated 3 weeks; confit cloves under their own oil, refrigerated, 2 weeks. Bring oil to room temperature before use as it clouds and thickens cold.
**Chef's notes:** temperature control is everything — above 100°C the garlic browns and turns acrid rather than sweet; use a thermometer until you know the pot.

name: Chive Oil
tagline: Blanched chive blended to a vivid green, herbaceous oil for plating.
story: A blender oil for finishing plates cleanly — a bright green line under fish, a dot on a soup, a wash under a canapé. Blanching before blending fixes the colour so the oil stays a true, saturated green instead of fading to khaki within a day.
method:
1. Bring a pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil; have an ice bath ready.
2. Blanch 200 g chive for 15 seconds only, then plunge immediately into the ice bath. Drain and squeeze dry in a clean cloth — any residual water dilutes the oil and shortens its life.
3. Blend the chive with 500 g grapeseed or other neutral oil on high speed for 2 minutes, until the jug feels warm to the touch (roughly 45-50°C from friction) and the mix is uniformly bright green.
4. Pour into a container and refrigerate 2 hours to fully chill and let solids settle.
5. Strain through a coffee filter or muslin-lined sieve, undisturbed, for at least 2 hours or overnight in the fridge — do not press the solids or the oil turns cloudy.
Holding: refrigerated in an airtight container away from light, 4-5 days; colour fades gradually after that, so make in small batches.
**Chef's notes:** blending too long overheats the chive and dulls the colour to olive-green — stop as soon as it is uniformly green and warm, not hot.

name: Basil Oil
tagline: Blanched basil blitzed with oil into a clean, bright-green finishing oil.
story: The same blanch-and-blend method as chive oil, tuned for basil's more delicate leaf and higher water content. It is the workhorse green oil of the pass — over tomato dishes, under burrata, around a bowl of minestrone — because it reads purely as basil, not as bruised, oxidised herb.
method:
1. Pick 200 g basil leaves from the stem; discard stems or reserve for stock.
2. Blanch in boiling salted water for 10 seconds, then shock in an ice bath immediately. Drain and press dry thoroughly in a clean cloth.
3. Blend with 500 g grapeseed oil on high speed for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until the jug is warm from friction (about 45°C) and the colour is fully broken down and even.
4. Chill the blended mixture in the fridge for 2 hours to let it settle and firm slightly.
5. Strain through a fine muslin-lined sieve or coffee filter over 2+ hours in the fridge, without pressing.
Holding: airtight, refrigerated, out of light, 4-5 days for best colour; flavour holds a little longer but greys.
**Chef's notes:** basil oxidises and blackens faster than chive if any leaf goes into the blender unblanched or under-dried — dry the leaves thoroughly, this is the single biggest cause of a dull, brownish oil.

name: Dill Oil
tagline: Blanched dill blended into a fine green oil for fish and cured dishes.
story: Dill's aniseed lift makes this the natural partner to cured or raw fish, potato and cucumber across the Nordic-leaning tasting menu — a few drops carry more than a whole sprig laid on top, and without the wilted-herb look on the plate.
method:
1. Pick 200 g dill fronds, keeping only tender growth, no thick stems.
2. Blanch 10 seconds in boiling salted water, shock in ice water, drain and press dry in a clean cloth until no moisture remains.
3. Blend with 500 g grapeseed oil at high speed for 90 seconds, until warm to the touch and uniformly green.
4. Chill 2 hours, then strain through muslin or a coffee filter over a bowl in the fridge for 2+ hours, unforced.
5. Decant into a squeeze bottle or jar.
Holding: airtight, refrigerated, away from light, 4-5 days.
**Chef's notes:** dill is more delicate than basil or chive and scorches in flavour if the oil is left in a warm blender jug too long — blend in short bursts if the jug is heating up fast, and dry the fronds thoroughly before blending or the oil separates. Taste a drop on a spoon before bottling: it should read clean and green, with no bitterness from over-blending or residual water.

name: Smoked Paprika Oil
tagline: Pimentón bloomed gently in warm oil, strained to a deep red-orange oil.
story: A single bottle carries most of the smoke and colour Boris needs across both menus — a swirl into a romesco, a finish over grilled octopus, a line around a bowl of chickpeas. Bought smoked pimentón already does the work fire would otherwise need to do, so the technique here is just about not burning it.
method:
1. Warm 500 g olive oil in a small pot to 70°C — no hotter.
2. Off the heat, whisk in 60 g sweet smoked pimentón (pimentón de la Vera) and 10 g hot smoked pimentón until fully dispersed, no lumps.
3. Return to the lowest possible heat and hold at 60-65°C for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, to let the paprika bloom and colour the oil deep red-orange without scorching — paprika burns above roughly 80°C and turns bitter and dull brown.
4. Remove from heat, cool to room temperature, then let stand overnight in the fridge for the sediment to settle.
5. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin into a clean bottle; discard the sediment.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, away from light, 3 weeks; oil solidifies cold, bring to room temperature to pour cleanly.
**Chef's notes:** the failure point is heat — paprika added to hot oil scorches within seconds and the oil turns muddy brown instead of clear red; always bloom it off the heat first.

name: Rosemary Oil
tagline: Rosemary gently warmed in oil for a resinous finishing oil, no bitterness.
story: Brushed over sourdough as it comes out of the wood oven, or over roasted lamb and root vegetables — this is the fastest route from garden to plate in the Bistro Mondo kitchen, and warming rather than frying the rosemary keeps it fragrant instead of harsh.
method:
1. Strip 60 g rosemary needles from the woody stems.
2. Warm 500 g olive oil in a small pot to 60°C.
3. Add the rosemary, remove from the heat immediately, and let steep off-heat, covered, for 30 minutes as the oil cools — this is a gentle infusion, not a fry.
4. Blitz briefly with a stick blender for 10 seconds to release more oil from the needles, then let stand a further 30 minutes.
5. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing lightly to extract the oil, then pass again through muslin for clarity if using for plating rather than the pass.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 2-3 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** rosemary left steeping in hot oil past 70°C turns resinous and soapy rather than fragrant — keep the infusion gentle and always off direct heat once the herb goes in. Made fresh every two weeks rather than in a single large batch, since the aroma is at its best in the first ten days.

name: Anchovy Oil
tagline: Salted anchovy melted into warm olive oil for a savoury, umami finishing oil.
story: Melting anchovy into oil rather than mincing it into a dish gives seasoning without visible fish — used to dress bitter leaves, brush over grilled bread, or finish a bagna cauda-style vegetable plate. A little goes a long way; it should read as depth, not as anchovy.
method:
1. Warm 500 g olive oil in a small pot over low heat to 60°C.
2. Add 100 g salted anchovy fillets and 2 crushed garlic cloves.
3. Cook gently at 55-60°C, stirring and breaking up the fillets with a wooden spoon, until they have fully dissolved into the oil, 8-10 minutes — the oil should never simmer or the anchovy turns gritty and bitter rather than melting smooth.
4. Remove from heat, cool to room temperature.
5. Strain through a fine sieve to remove bones and garlic solids; discard solids.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 2 weeks; oil clouds and thickens cold, warm gently or bring to room temperature to use.
**Chef's notes:** the anchovy must dissolve, not fry — any colour on the fillets or a visible simmer in the oil means it has gone too hot and will taste burnt and fishy rather than round and savoury. A small jar by the pass is enough for a service; there is rarely a reason to hold more than two weeks of stock at a time.

name: Brown Butter Oil
tagline: Butter cooked to noisette and cut with neutral oil, for a pourable brown-butter finish.
story: Straight beurre noisette solidifies cold and cannot be drizzled from a bottle; cutting it with a neutral oil while still liquid keeps the nutty, toasted-milk-solids flavour but gives a finishing oil that stays pourable at fridge temperature — used over pasta, fish and roasted vegetables where a clean stream matters more than a solid dollop.
method:
1. Melt 500 g unsalted butter in a wide, pale-bottomed pot over medium heat — a pale pot lets you judge the colour of the solids accurately.
2. Cook, swirling the pot often, as the butter foams and the milk solids begin to brown; watch and smell closely from the 5-minute mark.
3. Remove from heat the moment the solids turn hazelnut-brown and the butter smells toasted and nutty, 6-9 minutes total — it goes from perfect to burnt within 20-30 seconds, so stay at the stove.
4. Immediately whisk in 200 g neutral oil off the heat to arrest the cooking and thin the fat.
5. Pour through a fine sieve to remove the darkest solids if a completely smooth oil is wanted, or leave the fine solids in for more texture and flavour.
6. Cool to room temperature before bottling.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 2 weeks; the oil will firm slightly cold but stays pourable, unlike pure butter.
**Chef's notes:** the failure point is walking away in the last minute — brown butter turns to black, bitter butter almost without warning; pull it a shade lighter than you want, since residual heat keeps darkening it after it is off the stove.

name: Scallion Oil
tagline: Scallion slow-fried in oil until crisp and sweet, strained to a fragrant green-gold oil.
story: A classic Cantonese technique — the scallion is cooked slowly enough to caramelise rather than burn, giving an oil that is sweet, savoury and deeply aromatic with none of the acridity of a quick, hot fry. Used over steamed fish, rice or noodles wherever a single spoon needs to do all the seasoning work.
method:
1. Trim and roughly chop 250 g scallion, white and green parts separately.
2. Place 500 g neutral oil and the scallion whites in a cold pot; set over low heat.
3. Cook gently, stirring occasionally, as the oil slowly heats and the whites begin to soften and turn gold, about 8 minutes — starting from cold oil prevents scorching before the alliums have released their moisture.
4. Add the scallion greens and continue cooking at a gentle simmer, around 110-120°C, until all the scallion is deep golden-brown and crisp at the edges, a further 6-8 minutes.
5. Remove from heat as soon as the colour turns, since carryover heat continues to darken it.
6. Cool slightly, then strain, reserving the crisp scallion bits separately as a garnish and the oil for use.
Holding: oil refrigerated, airtight, 2 weeks; crisp scallion bits in a sealed container at room temperature, 3-4 days, or fridge for longer.
**Chef's notes:** starting in cold oil and heating slowly is what prevents bitterness — scallion dropped into oil already hot burns on the outside before it has softened through.

name: Raspberry Vinegar
tagline: Fresh raspberries macerated and infused into white wine vinegar, strained bright pink.
story: A fruit vinegar for cutting through rich, fatty dishes — foie gras, duck, roasted beetroot — where a squeeze of lemon would be too sharp and flat. The colour alone signals what it is before it is tasted, which matters on a tasting menu built around single, clear ideas per course.
method:
1. Lightly crush 400 g fresh raspberries in a non-reactive bowl.
2. Pour over 750 g white wine vinegar, cover, and macerate at room temperature for 24 hours, stirring once or twice.
3. Transfer to a pot and warm gently to 60°C — just enough to help extraction, never to a simmer, which cooks the fruit flavour flat.
4. Hold at 60°C for 10 minutes, then remove from heat and let cool fully in the liquid.
5. Strain through a muslin-lined sieve, letting it drip undisturbed for at least 2 hours; do not press hard or the vinegar turns cloudy and overly tannic from the seeds.
6. Taste and adjust with a little sugar if the batch of berries was tart; dissolve any sugar into the warm vinegar before the final strain.
Holding: bottled and refrigerated, 2 months; the colour will mellow slightly over time.
**Chef's notes:** heat is the main risk — vinegar taken above 65-70°C during infusion loses its fresh fruit top-note and tastes cooked rather than bright.

name: Fig-Leaf Vinegar
tagline: Fig leaves infused into white wine vinegar for a coconut-and-almond edged acidity.
story: Fig leaf carries a strange, almost coconut-and-marzipan quality that fig fruit alone does not have, and it grows freely around the finca — an ingredient cost of almost nothing for a flavour Boris cannot buy. Used to dress stone fruit, soft cheese or a simple leaf salad in late summer.
method:
1. Rinse 8-10 fresh fig leaves (about 150 g) and tear roughly to expose more surface area.
2. Toast the leaves lightly in a dry pan over medium heat for 1-2 minutes per side, until fragrant and just beginning to wilt — this coaxes out the coconut-almond aromatics that raw leaf does not give.
3. Place the warm leaves in a non-reactive container and pour over 750 g white wine vinegar.
4. Cover and infuse at room temperature for 48 hours, or in the fridge for up to 5 days for a gentler flavour.
5. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the leaves lightly to extract the last of the infused liquid.
6. Taste; if the flavour is faint, re-infuse with a fresh batch of toasted leaves for another 24 hours.
Holding: bottled and refrigerated, 2 months.
**Chef's notes:** over-toasting the leaves before infusing tips the flavour from coconut-almond to simply bitter and grassy — a light toast just to fragrance is enough, do not let them brown.

name: Herb Vinegar
tagline: A house green-herb vinegar — tarragon, chervil, parsley stems — for everyday vinaigrettes.
story: The catch-all vinegar for trim and stems that would otherwise go to the compost: parsley and chervil stalks, tarragon offcuts, chive ends. Made on a rolling basis rather than to a fixed recipe, but always built the same way, so any cook on either pass can put one together without asking.
method:
1. Gather 100 g mixed soft-herb trim — parsley stems, chervil, tarragon, chive — bruising it lightly with the back of a knife to release oils.
2. Warm 750 g white wine vinegar to 50°C in a non-reactive pot; do not let it simmer.
3. Pour the warm vinegar over the herbs in a jar, seal and infuse at room temperature for 24 hours, then move to the fridge for a further 24 hours.
4. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, pressing gently.
5. Taste for strength; a faint batch can be re-infused with fresh trim for another day.
Holding: bottled and refrigerated, 6-8 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** vinegar poured on fully boiling kills the bright top notes of soft herbs and gives a flat, cooked-green flavour — keep the pour under 50°C and let time, not heat, do the extraction. Label the jar with the date it was started, since batches vary slightly and a running house style is easier to hold than a fixed formula.

name: Quick Apple Cider Shrub
tagline: Apple, sugar and cider vinegar cooked together fast for a drinking vinegar syrup.
story: A same-day shrub rather than the traditional two-week macerated version — built for the bar, where a sharp, fruity syrup is needed to lengthen a spritz or sharpen a non-alcoholic pour, not sat waiting on a shelf. Also useful in the kitchen as a quick glaze base or a dressing sweetener with built-in acidity.
method:
1. Coarsely grate or fine-dice 300 g apple, skin on.
2. Combine the apple with 250 g sugar in a non-reactive pot and macerate for 15 minutes at room temperature, stirring once, until visibly juicy.
3. Set over low-medium heat and warm to 70°C, stirring until the sugar fully dissolves into a light syrup, about 5 minutes — do not boil, which cooks the apple to mush and mutes the fresh top note.
4. Remove from heat, stir in 300 g cider vinegar, and let stand off-heat for 10 minutes to marry.
5. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the apple lightly to extract the juice; discard the solids.
6. Cool fully before bottling.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 3-4 weeks. Shake before use as some settling is normal.
**Chef's notes:** the shortcut here trades some depth for speed — if time allows, letting the strained shrub rest a further 24 hours in the fridge before use rounds out the sharp edges considerably.

name: Harissa
tagline: Roasted red pepper and dried chili pounded with garlic, cumin and caraway.
story: The backbone chili paste of the kitchen — stirred into stews, thinned into a marinade, or spooned raw onto flatbread. Built from rehydrated dried chilies rather than fresh for a rounder, less watery heat, and finished with raw olive oil so the spice stays vivid instead of cooking flat.
method:
1. Stem and deseed 60 g dried guajillo or ñora chili and 20 g dried chile de árbol; soak in hot water for 20 minutes until pliable, then drain, reserving 50 g of the soaking liquid.
2. Char 300 g red bell pepper directly over a flame or under a hot grill until the skin is fully blackened, then steam in a covered bowl for 10 minutes and peel; discard skin and seeds.
3. Toast 15 g cumin seed and 10 g caraway seed in a dry pan over medium heat until fragrant, about 90 seconds, then grind fine.
4. In a food processor, combine the soaked chilies, charred pepper, toasted spices, 40 g garlic, 10 g smoked paprika and the reserved soaking liquid. Blend to a coarse paste.
5. With the motor running, stream in 150 g olive oil until glossy and just holding together — it should be a paste, not an emulsion.
6. Season with salt and 15 g lemon juice to taste; adjust chili heat with more soaking liquid if too thick.
Holding: pack into a jar, cover the surface with a film of olive oil, refrigerate, 3 weeks; freezes well in small portions, 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** blending too fine turns harissa into a smooth sauce rather than a paste with texture — pulse the last additions rather than running continuously.

name: Zhug
tagline: Raw green chili and coriander paste, sharp with garlic and cardamom.
story: A raw counterpart to harissa's cooked depth — all green heat and fresh herb, used to cut through fatty grilled meat and fish or stirred through yoghurt for a quick sauce. Made fresh in small batches because the colour and punch fade fast once blended.
method:
1. Roughly chop 150 g fresh green chili (jalapeño or serrano, seeds in for more heat, out for less), 100 g garlic and a large bunch each of coriander and parsley, about 150 g total.
2. Toast 6 g cumin seed and 6 green cardamom pods in a dry pan for 1 minute until fragrant; grind fine, discarding the cardamom husks.
3. Combine chili, garlic, herbs and ground spice in a food processor with 5 g salt.
4. Pulse, scraping down the sides, while streaming in 150 g olive oil, until the mixture forms a coarse, spoonable paste — it should keep visible flecks of herb, not turn to a smooth purée.
5. Finish with 15 g lemon juice and adjust salt to taste.
Holding: refrigerated, surface covered with a film of oil, 5-6 days — colour dulls after that even though flavour holds a little longer; not recommended for freezing as the herb breaks down on thawing.
**Chef's notes:** over-processing heats the blade and the herb, turning bright green to a drab khaki within minutes — pulse rather than run continuously, and use a chilled bowl in hot weather.

name: Gochujang Glaze
tagline: Gochujang reduced with soy, rice vinegar and honey to a glossy brushing glaze.
story: A finishing glaze for the grill — brushed on in the last minute over charcoal so the sugars catch and lacquer rather than burn to bitterness. Sweet-savoury-hot in balance, built to sit under grilled short rib, pork belly or roasted aubergine.
method:
1. Combine 300 g gochujang, 80 g soy sauce, 60 g rice vinegar, 100 g honey, 40 g brown sugar and 30 g grated garlic and 15 g grated ginger in a pot.
2. Whisk over medium heat until fully combined and just beginning to bubble at the edges.
3. Reduce heat to low and simmer gently for 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until it coats the back of a spoon and has reduced by roughly a fifth — it will thicken further as it cools, so stop slightly looser than the final target.
4. Off heat, whisk in 15 g toasted sesame oil and 10 g toasted sesame seed.
5. Cool to room temperature before storing.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 3-4 weeks. Warm gently before brushing as it stiffens cold.
**Chef's notes:** the sugar content means this scorches fast on a hot grill — brush on in the final 60-90 seconds of cooking only, in two thin coats rather than one heavy one.

name: Sriracha-Style Sauce
tagline: Fresh red chili fermented briefly then cooked down with garlic and vinegar.
story: A house hot sauce built for consistency once the bottled version runs out mid-service — a short salt ferment gives it the same rounded tang as the commercial original, rather than the flatter, straight-vinegar heat of an unfermented quick version.
method:
1. Roughly chop 500 g fresh red chili (a mix of cayenne and jalapeño works well) and 60 g garlic.
2. Combine in a non-reactive container with 20 g salt and 30 g sugar, cover and leave at room temperature for 48-72 hours, stirring daily, until visibly bubbling and smelling pleasantly sour rather than sharp and raw.
3. Blend the ferment with 150 g rice vinegar until smooth.
4. Transfer to a pot and simmer gently at a low bubble for 12-15 minutes, until slightly thickened and the raw ferment smell has cooked off.
5. Pass through a fine sieve for a smooth, pourable sauce; adjust salt and a touch more vinegar to taste once cooled, since flavours mute slightly warm.
Holding: bottled, refrigerated, 6-8 weeks; the ferment continues very slowly in the fridge, deepening flavour over the first two weeks.
**Chef's notes:** if the ferment smells of alcohol, ammonia or anything sharply unpleasant rather than pleasantly sour, discard and restart — that is spoilage, not fermentation, and usually means too little salt or a contaminated container.

name: Black Garlic Purée
tagline: Bought black garlic blended smooth with a little oil and vinegar into a dark, tarry purée.
story: Built from bought fermented black garlic rather than made in-house, since a true black garlic ferment takes three to four weeks under controlled humidity — not something worth the shelf space here. Its molasses-sweet, umami depth underlines a beurre blanc, a jus or a raw bar dish without adding acidity or heat.
method:
1. Peel 250 g black garlic cloves.
2. Blend in a small food processor with 30 g neutral oil and 15 g sherry vinegar, scraping down the sides often, until completely smooth — black garlic is sticky and clumps easily, so patience matters more than speed here.
3. If the purée is still grainy after 2 minutes of blending, pass it through a fine sieve or tamis, pressing with a spatula.
4. Season with a pinch of salt to taste; it needs very little, as black garlic is already deeply savoury.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 3-4 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** cheap black garlic can taste flat or acrid — taste the cloves raw before committing a batch; a good one should taste like fig, molasses and balsamic, with no harsh raw-garlic edge at all. Keep a small dedicated jar for this rather than reusing an oil-and-vinegar bottle, since the colour stains and is hard to fully clean out.

name: Miso Butter
tagline: Softened butter beaten with white miso and a touch of mirin for a savoury compound butter.
story: Finishes grilled corn, roasted vegetables or a piece of fish straight off the grill, melting into an instant, salty-sweet sauce with no further reduction needed. White (shiro) miso keeps it mellow enough not to overpower delicate fish.
method:
1. Bring 500 g unsalted butter fully to room temperature, soft enough to beat by hand.
2. Beat the butter in a stand mixer with the paddle, or by hand, until smooth and slightly aerated, about 2 minutes.
3. Add 100 g white miso paste and 20 g mirin, and beat until fully incorporated and streak-free, scraping down the bowl once.
4. Taste — miso brands vary in salt, so add table salt only if needed.
5. Transfer to a piece of parchment or plastic film, roll into a log, twist the ends, and chill until firm.
Holding: refrigerated log, 2-3 weeks; freezes well pre-portioned into discs, 3 months — slice frozen discs straight onto hot food.
**Chef's notes:** overbeating warms the butter and it can split slightly — if this happens, chill the bowl 10 minutes and beat again briefly to bring it back together. Slice discs straight from the freezer onto hot corn or fish so the butter melts evenly rather than sliding off in one greasy pool.

name: Anchovy Butter
tagline: Softened butter beaten with pounded anchovy and lemon, classic maître d'hôtel style.
story: Melted onto a grilled steak or a piece of turbot at the pass, this is the fastest sauce in the kitchen — no reduction, no emulsion to break, just cold butter that becomes a glossy anchovy sauce the moment it hits hot food.
method:
1. Pound 60 g salted anchovy fillets to a smooth paste with a mortar and pestle, or mince very finely with a knife.
2. Bring 500 g unsalted butter to room temperature and beat until smooth.
3. Beat in the anchovy paste, 10 g lemon zest and 15 g lemon juice, and a good grind of black pepper, until fully combined and uniform in colour.
4. Taste before adding any salt — anchovy is already salty; adjust only if needed.
5. Roll into a log in parchment, twist the ends, and chill until firm.
Holding: refrigerated, 2-3 weeks; freezes well as pre-cut discs, 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** unpounded anchovy leaves visible fibrous strands through the butter — take the extra two minutes to get it to a true paste before beating it in. Keep a log ready in the freezer at all times; it is one of the fastest ways to finish a piece of grilled fish under time pressure.

name: Café de Paris Butter
tagline: The classic steak-house compound butter — a dozen aromatics folded into softened butter.
story: The definitive butter for a grilled steak, built to the long, fussy classic formula rather than a shortcut version, because the layered aromatics — anchovy, capers, shallot, herbs, curry, cognac — are exactly what makes it recognisable. Made in one large batch a few times a year and frozen in portions, since assembling the full ingredient list is not a daily task.
method:
1. Finely mince 40 g shallot, 15 g garlic, 20 g capers, 20 g cornichon and 15 g flat parsley; pound 20 g salted anchovy fillets to a paste.
2. Bring 500 g unsalted butter to full room temperature and beat until smooth and slightly aerated.
3. Beat in the minced aromatics and anchovy paste along with 10 g Dijon mustard, 15 g cognac, 10 g Worcestershire sauce, 5 g curry powder, 5 g sweet paprika, 8 g lemon zest, 20 g lemon juice, a pinch of cayenne and a good grind of black pepper.
4. Mix until fully and evenly combined — the finished butter should show flecks of every ingredient, not stripes.
5. Taste and adjust salt carefully given the anchovy, capers and Worcestershire.
6. Roll into a log in parchment or plastic film, twist tightly, and chill until firm.
Holding: refrigerated, 2 weeks; freezes very well as pre-cut discs, 3 months, and is best made ahead — the flavours marry further after a day in the fridge.
**Chef's notes:** the classic recipe carries roughly fifteen ingredients and a day of resting time for the flavours to settle — rushing straight to service the same day gives a butter where the curry and anchovy dominate before the shallot and herb have caught up.

name: 'Nduja Butter
tagline: Softened butter beaten with spreadable 'nduja for a spicy, smoky compound butter.
story: Melts into a instant spicy sauce over grilled bread, shellfish or roasted cauliflower — the 'nduja does all the seasoning work, so the butter needs almost nothing added beyond a touch of acid to balance the fat.
method:
1. Bring 500 g unsalted butter to room temperature and beat until smooth.
2. Add 200 g 'nduja and beat until fully streaked through and even in colour — small flecks of chili are fine, but no unblended lumps of paste should remain.
3. Beat in 10 g lemon juice to brighten the fat content.
4. Taste; 'nduja varies significantly in salt and heat between producers, so adjust nothing further unless clearly needed.
5. Roll into a log in parchment, twist the ends, and chill until firm.
Holding: refrigerated, 2-3 weeks; freezes well pre-portioned, 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** 'nduja softens faster than butter at room temperature and can start to separate if the batch sits out too long while beating — work quickly, or beat in a chilled bowl in warm kitchens. Keep a log in the freezer alongside the anchovy and café de Paris butters so the grill station always has a fast finishing option to hand.

name: Tahini Sauce
tagline: Raw tahini loosened with lemon, garlic and iced water into a pourable, silky sauce.
story: The base sauce for falafel, grilled vegetables and roasted lamb across the Levantine-leaning dishes — the trick is entirely in the order of additions, since tahini seizes into a stiff paste before it loosens back out into a sauce, and cooks unfamiliar with that step often panic and add too much liquid too fast.
method:
1. Whisk 250 g raw tahini with 10 g crushed garlic and 60 g lemon juice in a bowl — it will immediately seize and thicken into a stiff, clumped paste; this is expected.
2. Continue whisking while adding iced water a little at a time, about 120-150 g total, until the mixture loosens and turns pale, smooth and pourable — it passes through a thick, broken stage before it comes together, so keep whisking through that point rather than adding all the water at once.
3. Season with salt to taste and a little more lemon juice if needed for brightness.
4. Check consistency: it should ribbon off a spoon and hold a trail for a second before settling.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 5-6 days; it thickens in the fridge, so loosen with a little more iced water before serving.
**Chef's notes:** adding water too fast, all at once, before the paste has fully seized can leave the sauce grainy and never fully smooth — always let it clump first, then loosen gradually.

name: Muhammara
tagline: Roasted red pepper and walnut, sharpened with pomegranate molasses and chili.
story: A dip built for texture as much as flavour — the walnut should stay coarse enough to bite, never blended to a smooth purée, which is the most common way this gets ruined. Sweet-sour-hot in the same bite, it needs nothing more than warm flatbread alongside it.
method:
1. Char 400 g red bell pepper over a flame or under a hot grill until fully blackened; steam in a covered bowl 10 minutes, then peel, deseed and roughly chop.
2. Toast 200 g walnut in a 160°C oven for 8-10 minutes, until fragrant and lightly coloured; cool, then pulse in a food processor to a coarse rubble — not a fine meal.
3. Toast 40 g fresh breadcrumb in a dry pan until golden, to help bind and add body.
4. In the food processor, pulse the pepper, half the walnut rubble, the breadcrumb, 30 g pomegranate molasses, 15 g Aleppo pepper or chili flake, 20 g olive oil and 15 g lemon juice until it comes together into a rough, spoonable paste.
5. Fold in the reserved walnut rubble by hand for texture.
6. Season with salt and adjust the molasses-to-chili balance to taste — it should be clearly sweet-sour before it is hot.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week.
**Chef's notes:** processing all the walnut into the base blend gives a flat, sandy dip — always reserve and fold in a portion at the end for bite.

name: Baba Ganoush
tagline: Fire-charred aubergine, smoked through and through, mashed with tahini, garlic and lemon.
story: The smoke has to go all the way through the aubergine, not just blacken the skin, which means genuinely charring it over open flame or very hot coals rather than roasting it in the oven — a shortcut that produces a merely cooked, not smoked, dip that misses the entire point of the dish.
method:
1. Prick 800 g whole aubergine a few times with a knife tip.
2. Char directly over an open flame — gas ring, wood-oven embers or a grill — turning regularly, until the skin is fully blackened and blistered on all sides and the flesh feels completely collapsed and soft, 15-20 minutes; the outside will look ruined, that is correct.
3. Transfer to a colander set over a bowl and let drain and cool for 15 minutes — this removes bitter, smoky liquid that would otherwise water down the dip.
4. Split the aubergine, scoop the flesh away from the charred skin, discarding any large seed pockets and all skin, and roughly chop.
5. In a bowl, combine the flesh with 15 g crushed garlic, 60 g tahini, 30 g lemon juice and 20 g olive oil. Mash by hand with a fork for a rustic texture, or pulse briefly in a processor for a smoother finish — do not over-process into a purée.
6. Season with salt to taste.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 3-4 days; flavour is best within the first 24 hours.
**Chef's notes:** skipping the draining step is the most common mistake — undrained aubergine carries bitter, smoky juice that makes the whole dip taste acrid rather than smoky-sweet.

name: Labneh
tagline: Salted full-fat yoghurt strained overnight into a thick, tangy fresh cheese.
story: The technique is nothing more than time and gravity, but the result — a spreadable, tangy cheese somewhere between yoghurt and cream cheese — underpins a dozen small plates, from a base for roasted vegetables to a plinth under grilled fish. Straining time controls the final texture, so it is made to order for how it will be used, not to a single fixed recipe.
method:
1. Whisk 1000 g full-fat plain yoghurt with 12 g salt until fully dissolved.
2. Line a sieve with a double layer of muslin or a clean cloth, set over a deep bowl or container, leaving room for the whey to drip without touching the sieve base.
3. Pour in the salted yoghurt, gather the cloth over the top loosely, and refrigerate.
4. Strain 4-6 hours for a soft, spoonable labneh; 24 hours for a thick, spreadable one; 48 hours for a firm cheese that can be rolled into balls.
5. Discard or reserve the drained whey — it is useful in bread doughs or as a light acidic addition to soups.
6. Transfer the strained labneh to a clean container; finish with a drizzle of olive oil if serving directly.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week; if rolled into balls and covered in oil, up to 3 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** using low-fat yoghurt gives a thin, chalky result no matter how long it strains — full-fat, minimally processed yoghurt (no stabilisers) is essential for a rich, clean-tasting labneh.

name: Whipped Feta
tagline: Feta whipped with cream and oil into a light, spreadable base for vegetables.
story: A single technique that turns a crumbly, salty cheese into a soft, mousse-like base for roasted or grilled vegetables — the aeration from whipping cuts feta's sharpness without diluting its flavour with too much dairy fat, so it reads as feta, just lighter.
method:
1. Crumble 400 g feta and place in a food processor with 100 g cream cheese and 60 g heavy cream.
2. Blend on high for 1-2 minutes, scraping down the sides once, until completely smooth with no visible feta granules.
3. With the motor running, stream in 40 g olive oil to loosen and add sheen.
4. Taste — feta is salty enough on its own for most uses; add black pepper or a little lemon zest rather than salt if more seasoning is wanted.
5. Transfer to a piping bag or container and chill at least 30 minutes to firm slightly before use.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 5 days.
**Chef's notes:** cheap or pre-crumbled feta often carries anti-caking starch that keeps it grainy no matter how long it blends — use a block feta packed in brine for a truly smooth result. Spread it thick on the plate before setting roasted vegetables on top, rather than dolloping it, so the base actually holds the food in place.

name: Tapenade
tagline: Black olive, caper and anchovy pounded to a coarse Provençal paste.
story: Kept coarse rather than smooth so it reads as chopped olives rather than olive paste — spread thin on grilled bread, folded through pasta, or used as a savoury base under roasted tomato. A true Provençal condiment with almost no cooking involved.
method:
1. Pit 300 g good black olives (Niçoise or Kalamata) if not already pitted.
2. Combine the olives with 30 g capers, 20 g salted anchovy fillets and 15 g garlic in a food processor.
3. Pulse — do not run continuously — until coarsely chopped and just holding together, 8-10 short pulses; stop well before it becomes a smooth paste.
4. Add 15 g fresh thyme or a mix of Provençal herbs and pulse twice more to combine.
5. Transfer to a bowl and stir in 60 g olive oil and 10 g lemon juice by hand, along with a small amount of black pepper.
6. Taste before adding any salt — olives, capers and anchovy already carry plenty.
Holding: refrigerated, surface covered with a film of oil, 2 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** running the processor continuously turns this into a smooth olive purée with none of the classic rustic texture — pulse in short bursts and check often.

name: Olive Salt
tagline: Dehydrated black olive ground into coarse salt for a savoury, briny finishing seasoning.
story: A way to carry the flavour of good olives into dishes where whole olives would not belong — dusted over a fried egg, a piece of raw fish or a bowl of chips. The olive is dried, not cooked, so it keeps its dark, fruity edge rather than turning bitter.
method:
1. Pit 300 g good black olives and pat thoroughly dry with paper towel.
2. Spread in a single layer on a tray lined with a silicone mat or parchment.
3. Dehydrate in an oven set to its lowest temperature, ideally 60-70°C, with the door propped slightly ajar, for 3-4 hours, or use a dehydrator at 60°C for 6-8 hours, until fully brittle and shattering when snapped — any residual chew means moisture remains that will clump the salt.
4. Cool fully, then blitz in a spice grinder with 200 g coarse sea salt until it reaches an even, coarse, dark crumb — not a fine powder.
5. Sieve out any larger unground fragments and re-grind if needed.
Holding: airtight container away from moisture and light, 2 months; discard if any clumping or off smell develops, a sign of residual moisture.
**Chef's notes:** any olive left even slightly moist will mould inside a sealed jar within days — when in doubt, dehydrate longer, since over-drying only makes it easier to grind.

name: Smoked Salt
tagline: Coarse sea salt cold-smoked over wood chips for a house smoke seasoning.
story: House-smoked using the same beech and oak offcuts as the wood oven, so the flavour lines up with everything else that comes out of it — a pinch finishes a dish that needs the memory of smoke without the time or heat of actually cooking over fire.
method:
1. Spread 300 g coarse sea salt in a thin, even layer on a perforated tray or a mesh screen.
2. Set up a stovetop smoker or a smoking box with a handful of beech or oak wood chips over low heat, or use a covered grill banked to one side with a smoke packet on unlit coals.
3. Keep the smoke source at a gentle smoulder, not an open flame, and hold the salt in the smoke chamber at under 30°C — cold smoke, not hot — for 45-60 minutes, stirring the salt every 15 minutes to expose fresh surface.
4. Check colour and aroma: the salt should look faintly toasted and smell clearly of wood smoke, without any bitter or acrid note.
5. If a stronger flavour is wanted, repeat the smoking cycle with fresh wood chips a second time.
6. Spread out to fully cool and dry before storing.
Holding: airtight, indefinitely at room temperature — flavour mellows slowly over months, so use within 3-4 months for full intensity.
**Chef's notes:** smoke that gets too hot or too dense turns bitter and acrid on the salt rather than sweetly smoky — thin white-blue smoke at low heat, not thick black smoke, is the target throughout.

name: Dukkah
tagline: Toasted hazelnut, sesame and cumin-coriander, crushed to a crunchy dry blend.
story: Meant to be eaten with bread dipped first in olive oil, then in this — but equally useful scattered over roasted vegetables, labneh or a piece of grilled fish for texture. Kept coarse; a food processor run too long turns it into a nut butter rather than a crumb.
method:
1. Toast 150 g hazelnut in a 160°C oven for 10 minutes, until the skins crack and the nut is golden inside; rub in a cloth to remove most of the skins, then cool.
2. Toast 60 g sesame seed in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until light gold, 2-3 minutes; cool.
3. Toast 30 g cumin seed and 30 g coriander seed together in the same pan for 90 seconds until fragrant; cool, then grind coarsely.
4. Pulse the cooled hazelnut in a food processor 4-5 times, until roughly crushed into pea-sized and smaller pieces — do not run continuously, or the oil in the nuts releases and turns the mix into a paste.
5. Combine the crushed hazelnut, toasted sesame, ground cumin-coriander, and salt to taste in a bowl; mix by hand.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place, 3-4 weeks; the sesame oil eventually turns the mix slightly stale past that.
**Chef's notes:** the moment the mixture starts to look damp or clumped rather than dry and crumbly, the nuts have released their oil — pulse in shorter bursts to avoid this.

name: Furikake
tagline: Toasted nori, bonito and sesame seasoned with sugar and soy, dried to a crisp topping.
story: A rice and vegetable seasoning built from the same dashi pantry as the tasting menu's Japanese-leaning dishes — nothing here is difficult, but drying it fully is what keeps it crisp in a jar rather than turning soft and clumping within a day.
method:
1. Toast 15 g nori sheet, torn into pieces, in a dry pan over low heat for 1 minute until crisp and fragrant; crumble by hand or pulse briefly in a processor into small flakes, not powder.
2. Toast 30 g white and 10 g black sesame seed together in a dry pan over medium heat until the white seeds are lightly golden, 2-3 minutes; cool.
3. In the same pan, toss 20 g bonito flake (katsuobushi) with 10 g soy sauce and 8 g sugar over low heat, stirring constantly, until the liquid has fully evaporated and the flakes are dry and slightly crisp again, about 4-5 minutes — this step must go to full dryness or the finished furikake goes soft in storage.
4. Combine the nori, sesame and seasoned bonito flake in a bowl with 3 g salt; mix gently to avoid crushing the nori to dust.
5. Spread on a tray and let air-dry, uncovered, for 15 minutes before jarring, to release any last moisture.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place, 3-4 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** any residual moisture in the bonito step is the single cause of furikake clumping and going stale early — do not jar it until it feels bone-dry and separate to the touch.

name: Za'atar
tagline: Dried thyme, toasted sesame, sumac and salt in the classic Levantine ratio.
story: Used constantly and simply: mixed with olive oil for flatbread, scattered over labneh, or dusted straight onto roasted vegetables. Sumac's tartness is what sets this apart from a plain thyme-salt blend, so buying good, deep-red sumac rather than a faded, brownish one matters more than any other single ingredient.
method:
1. Toast 40 g sesame seed in a dry pan over medium heat, stirring constantly, until light gold, 2-3 minutes; cool fully before mixing, as warm seeds sweat and clump the blend.
2. If using fresh thyme rather than dried, dry 60 g thyme sprigs in a low oven (60-70°C) for 1-1.5 hours until fully brittle, then strip the leaves and discard stems; if using dried thyme, use 30 g directly.
3. Combine the dried thyme with 40 g sumac and 8 g salt in a bowl.
4. Add the cooled toasted sesame and mix thoroughly by hand, breaking up any clumps of thyme.
5. Taste on a piece of bread with olive oil to check the balance before finishing a full batch — it should taste tart first, then herbal, with sesame as texture rather than a dominant flavour.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 2-3 months; sesame oil eventually turns the mix stale, so make in batches sized to a few weeks' use.
**Chef's notes:** mixing warm sesame straight from the pan into the blend causes clumping and uneven distribution — always cool the seeds fully first.

name: Ras el Hanout
tagline: A whole-spice blend of cumin, coriander, cinnamon and rose, toasted and ground fresh.
story: Ras el hanout translates loosely as "top of the shop" — every spice merchant's own signature mix, so this is Bistro Mondo's version rather than a definitive one, built for a warm, rounded North African flavour under roasted lamb, carrots or a tagine-style braise. Grinding whole spices fresh rather than buying it pre-mixed is what keeps it from tasting dusty.
method:
1. Toast whole spices separately in a dry pan over medium heat, since they colour at different rates: 20 g cumin seed and 20 g coriander seed together for 90 seconds; 10 g whole black peppercorn and 6 green cardamom pods for 60 seconds; set each aside to cool as it finishes.
2. Break 2 whole cinnamon sticks into pieces and toast 30 seconds until fragrant.
3. Grind all the toasted whole spices together in a spice grinder to a fine powder, discarding the cardamom husks after cracking them first if the seeds do not release fully.
4. Combine the ground mix with 10 g ground ginger, 8 g ground turmeric, 5 g ground allspice, 3 g ground cloves, 3 g cayenne pepper and 5 g dried rose petal, crushed fine.
5. Sieve the whole blend to remove any coarse fragments, re-grinding them if needed.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 2-3 months; grind in batches no larger than 3 months' use for full aromatic strength.
**Chef's notes:** toasting all the whole spices together in one go burns the faster-colouring ones (pepper, cardamom) before the slower ones (cumin, coriander) are ready — always toast in the batches given, by how fast each spice colours.

name: Garam Masala
tagline: Warm whole spices toasted and ground fresh — the finishing spice of North Indian cooking.
story: Used as a finishing dust rather than a base seasoning — stirred in at the very end of cooking or dusted over just before serving, since its aromatics are volatile and fade fast under sustained heat. Fresh-ground, it should smell noticeably more fragrant than any jar bought pre-mixed.
method:
1. In a dry pan over medium heat, toast 20 g cumin seed and 20 g coriander seed together for 90 seconds until fragrant and a shade darker.
2. Add 10 g black peppercorn, 8 green cardamom pods and 4 black cardamom pods, and toast a further 60 seconds.
3. Add 2 whole cinnamon sticks (broken), 6 whole cloves and 2 bay leaves, and toast 30 seconds more, until the whole mix smells intensely aromatic — pull it the moment it does, before any spice starts to smoke.
4. Cool completely, then grind fine in a spice grinder, discarding the bay leaves and any tough cardamom husks that do not grind down.
5. Stir in 8 g grated nutmeg.
6. Sieve for a fine, even powder, re-grinding any coarse residue.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 6-8 weeks — this blend loses potency faster than most due to the volume of whole spices freshly ground; make small batches often rather than one large batch.
**Chef's notes:** grinding while the spices are still warm from toasting causes the oils to gum up the grinder and clump the powder — always cool fully first.

name: Shichimi Togarashi
tagline: Seven-spice Japanese blend — chili, citrus peel, sesame, seaweed and Sichuan pepper.
story: The house version of the classic seven-flavour blend, kept in a shaker by the pass for noodles, grilled fish and soup — built with dried mandarin peel rather than the traditional yuzu peel, which is harder to source reliably, but kept close to the original ratio of heat, citrus and nuttiness.
method:
1. Dry 20 g mandarin or orange zest, peeled in strips, in a low oven at 60-70°C for 45-60 minutes until fully brittle; grind to a coarse powder.
2. Toast 15 g white sesame seed and 10 g black sesame seed in a dry pan over medium heat until the white seeds are lightly golden, 2 minutes; cool.
3. Toast 5 g Sichuan peppercorn for 30 seconds until fragrant; grind coarsely.
4. Toast a sheet of nori (about 3 g) briefly until crisp; crumble to small flakes.
5. Combine 20 g coarse dried chili flake, the ground citrus peel, toasted sesame, ground Sichuan pepper, nori flake, 8 g ground ginger and 5 g poppy seed in a bowl; mix thoroughly by hand to distribute evenly, since the pieces vary widely in size and density and settle unevenly if just shaken together.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 2 months.
**Chef's notes:** grinding the citrus peel while it still has any moisture left produces a sticky paste rather than a powder — it must be fully brittle and snap cleanly before grinding.

name: Herbes de Provence
tagline: House-dried thyme, rosemary, savory and oregano in the classic southern French ratio.
story: Dried in-house from the herb beds around Bistro Mondo rather than bought, giving a blend that is noticeably more fragrant than the pre-packed version most kitchens use — mixed into a marinade, rubbed onto roasting chicken, or scattered over vegetables before they go into the wood oven.
method:
1. Pick 60 g thyme, 40 g rosemary, 30 g savory and 30 g oregano, discarding any damaged or yellowing leaves.
2. Spread each herb separately on a tray lined with a rack or mesh, since they dry at different rates.
3. Dry in an oven set to its lowest temperature (ideally under 50°C) with the door propped open, checking every 20 minutes — rosemary needles take longest, oregano and savory the shortest; each is ready when it crumbles to dust between the fingers with no give at all, typically 60-90 minutes total.
4. Once fully dry, strip leaves or needles from any woody stems and discard the stems.
5. Combine the dried herbs with 15 g dried lavender flower (optional, for the classic southern French style) and 10 g fennel seed, lightly crushed.
6. Mix thoroughly and store.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 3-4 months; check periodically for full dryness, as any residual moisture will mould the blend.
**Chef's notes:** rushing the drying with higher oven heat cooks the volatile oils out of the herbs before the water has left them — low and slow keeps both the colour and the aromatic punch.

name: Ibizan Herb Salt
tagline: House-dried rosemary, thyme and fennel from the finca, ground into a coarse island salt.
story: Built entirely from what grows on and around the property — wild rosemary, thyme and fennel fronds — so it is the one seasoning on both menus that is genuinely site-specific rather than sourced. Finished on the table at Bistro Mondo and used across the wood-oven vegetable and bread program.
method:
1. Pick 40 g wild rosemary, 30 g thyme and 20 g fennel fronds, washing and drying thoroughly.
2. Spread on a tray and dry in an oven at its lowest setting, under 50°C, door slightly ajar, for 60-75 minutes, until fully brittle and crumbling to dust between the fingers.
3. Strip any woody stems and discard.
4. Blitz the dried herbs in a spice grinder to a coarse, even texture.
5. Combine with 250 g coarse sea salt and mix thoroughly by hand.
6. Taste on a slice of bread with olive oil to check the herb-to-salt balance before finishing the full batch.
Holding: airtight, cool dry place away from light, 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** grinding the herbs too fine turns this into a green-tinted salt rather than a visibly herbed one — a coarse, textured grind is what makes it look and taste like something picked, not manufactured.

name: Classic Vinaigrette
tagline: The house three-to-one oil-and-vinegar dressing, whisked to a temporary emulsion.
story: The default dressing on both menus for any simple green salad — nothing to hide behind, so the vinegar and oil both have to be good. A small amount of mustard is there purely as an emulsifier, not as a flavour, and should not be tasted as mustard in the finished dressing.
method:
1. Whisk 10 g Dijon mustard with 15 g minced shallot and 100 g white wine vinegar in a bowl until combined.
2. Season with salt and let stand 5 minutes — this softens the raw bite of the shallot and lets the mustard begin to bind.
3. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 300 g olive oil in a thin, steady stream, starting very slowly, until fully emulsified and lightly thickened.
4. Adjust seasoning with salt and black pepper to taste; if too sharp, whisk in a few drops more oil, if too flat, a little more vinegar.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week; it will separate on standing, so whisk or shake vigorously before each use.
**Chef's notes:** oil added too fast, before the mustard and shallot have had time to bind, breaks the emulsion into an oily, separated dressing — go slow at the start, then increase the stream once it visibly thickens.

name: Dijon Vinaigrette
tagline: A mustard-forward vinaigrette, sharper and more textured than the classic house version.
story: Where the classic vinaigrette treats mustard as glue, this one treats it as a flavour — enough Dijon that it is clearly tasted, standing up to bitter leaves, charcuterie or a warm lentil salad without disappearing.
method:
1. Whisk 40 g Dijon mustard with 15 g honey and 15 g minced shallot in a bowl until smooth.
2. Whisk in 80 g red wine vinegar until fully combined.
3. Season with salt and black pepper, and let stand 5 minutes.
4. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 250 g olive oil in a thin stream until emulsified and noticeably thick — this dressing should coat a spoon heavily, unlike a thinner classic vinaigrette.
5. Taste and adjust; if too thick to pour, thin with a few drops of water.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 10 days; the high mustard content keeps the emulsion more stable than the classic version, though a stir before use is still good practice.
**Chef's notes:** using a mild American-style mustard instead of a sharp Dijon flattens the whole point of this dressing — use a proper strong Dijon and adjust the amount to taste, not the other way around.

name: Miso-Sesame Dressing
tagline: White miso, rice vinegar and toasted sesame oil blended into a thick, savoury dressing.
story: Built to carry raw or lightly cooked vegetables and cold noodle dishes — miso gives body and umami where a purely vinegar-based dressing would taste thin, and it needs no oil emulsification to hold together, which makes it forgiving to make ahead.
method:
1. Whisk 80 g white miso paste with 40 g rice vinegar and 15 g honey in a bowl until the miso is fully dissolved with no lumps.
2. Whisk in 15 g grated ginger and 10 g grated garlic.
3. Slowly whisk in 40 g toasted sesame oil and 100 g neutral oil until glossy and smooth.
4. Thin to the desired consistency with a little water, 20-40 g, whisked in gradually.
5. Taste — miso brands vary in salt, so hold back on any added salt until tasted.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 10 days.
**Chef's notes:** miso left in lumps rather than fully dissolved at the start will never smooth out once the oils go in — always dissolve it completely into the vinegar first. It thickens further in the fridge, so always taste and thin it again just before it goes out rather than relying on how it looked at the pass the day before.

name: Yuzu Kosho Dressing
tagline: Yuzu kosho whisked with rice vinegar and oil into a citrus-heat dressing.
story: Yuzu kosho — the fermented chili-citrus paste — is bought rather than made in-house, since a proper ferment needs weeks and a reliable source of fresh yuzu that does not exist locally. Whisked into a dressing, it gives citrus, salt and a slow chili heat all in one, over raw fish, cold vegetables or a simple leaf salad.
method:
1. Whisk 25 g yuzu kosho with 40 g rice vinegar and 15 g soy sauce until fully combined and smooth.
2. Add 10 g honey and whisk to dissolve.
3. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 200 g neutral oil in a thin stream until emulsified.
4. Taste — yuzu kosho varies significantly in salt and heat between brands, so build up gradually rather than following the amount blindly on an unfamiliar jar.
5. Thin with a little water if the dressing is too thick to pour cleanly.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 10 days; shake or whisk before use.
**Chef's notes:** yuzu kosho's heat continues to build for the first hour after mixing as the chili paste diffuses through the dressing — taste again just before service, not only right after mixing. Keep the jar of yuzu kosho itself tightly sealed between uses, since it dries out and loses its aromatic top note quickly once opened.

name: Buttermilk Ranch
