tagline: Buttermilk and mayonnaise dressing loaded with fresh dill, chive and garlic.
story: Kept on the menu at Bistro Mondo for grilled chicken and crudités because it does exactly one job extremely well — cool, tangy, herb-flecked richness — and no amount of fine-dining pressure has ever made Boris take it off.
method:
1. Whisk 150 g mayonnaise with 200 g buttermilk until smooth and no lumps of mayonnaise remain.
2. Whisk in 15 g grated garlic, 20 g finely chopped chive, 15 g finely chopped dill and 10 g finely chopped parsley.
3. Season with 10 g lemon juice, salt and black pepper to taste.
4. Whisk in a further 20-40 g buttermilk if a thinner, pourable consistency is wanted rather than a thicker dip consistency.
5. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes before serving to let the herbs infuse.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 5 days; the fresh herbs darken slightly over time but flavour holds well.
**Chef's notes:** adding the herbs to warm or room-temperature buttermilk dulls their colour fast — keep everything cold throughout mixing for a dressing that stays bright green-flecked rather than grey. Serve it well chilled; at room temperature the buttermilk tang flattens and it reads as a plain garlic mayonnaise rather than proper ranch.

name: Green Goddess
tagline: A herb-loaded, anchovy-backed mayonnaise dressing, blended vividly green.
story: Built with a genuinely heavy hand on soft herbs rather than a token sprinkle — this should look and taste like a herb purée loosened with mayonnaise, not a pale dressing with green flecks in it. The anchovy is there for savoury depth, not to be tasted as fish.
method:
1. Combine 150 g mayonnaise, 80 g sour cream, 60 g roughly chopped chive, 40 g tarragon leaves, 40 g parsley and 30 g basil in a blender.
2. Add 15 g salted anchovy fillets, 10 g grated garlic and 20 g lemon juice.
3. Blend on high, scraping down the sides as needed, until fully smooth and vividly green, about 1 minute.
4. Thin with a little water or extra sour cream if the dressing is too thick to pour.
5. Season with black pepper and salt to taste, tasting carefully given the anchovy.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 4-5 days; colour dulls a little each day, so make small batches often.
**Chef's notes:** using dried herbs or holding back on quantity produces a flat, mayonnaise-forward dressing rather than the intensely herbal one this should be — measure the fresh herbs by weight, not by eye, until the ratio is second nature.

name: Blue Cheese Dressing
tagline: Buttermilk and mayonnaise dressing chunky with folded blue cheese.
story: Kept deliberately lumpy rather than blended smooth — the point is to bite into distinct pockets of blue cheese against a tangy, creamy base, over a wedge of cos lettuce or alongside grilled meat.
method:
1. Whisk 120 g mayonnaise with 150 g buttermilk and 40 g sour cream until smooth.
2. Whisk in 15 g white wine vinegar and 5 g grated garlic.
3. Crumble 150 g good blue cheese into rough pieces; fold two-thirds of it into the dressing by hand, mashing a little as you fold to thicken the base and leave some texture.
4. Fold in the remaining third whole, keeping visible chunks intact.
5. Season with black pepper; taste before adding salt, since blue cheese is already salty.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 5-6 days; flavour deepens slightly over the first two days as the blue cheese permeates.
**Chef's notes:** folding all the cheese in at once and mixing thoroughly loses the textural contrast that makes this dressing work — always hold back a portion to fold in whole at the end. A stronger blue, such as Roquefort or a good Cabrales, gives a sharper dressing than a milder Gorgonzola dolce — choose the cheese to suit the dish it is going on.

name: Citrus-Shallot Dressing
tagline: Orange and lemon juice reduced lightly, whisked with shallot into a light dressing.
story: A lighter alternative to a straight vinegar vinaigrette for delicate leaves and raw fish — reducing the citrus juice slightly concentrates its flavour so the finished dressing does not taste diluted once the oil is whisked in.
method:
1. Combine 150 g fresh orange juice and 50 g fresh lemon juice in a small pot and reduce over medium heat to about 100 g total, roughly 8-10 minutes — watch closely near the end as it can scorch quickly once reduced.
2. Cool the reduction fully to room temperature.
3. Whisk in 10 g Dijon mustard and 20 g finely minced shallot.
4. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 200 g olive oil until emulsified.
5. Season with salt and black pepper to taste; a little orange zest whisked in at the end brightens it further.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week; whisk or shake before use as it will separate.
**Chef's notes:** whisking the oil into a still-warm reduction breaks the emulsion almost immediately — let the reduction come fully to room temperature or even slightly chilled before starting to add oil. Made fresh for service rather than held for a full week, since the citrus top note fades noticeably faster than a vinegar-based dressing.

name: Nuoc Cham
tagline: Fish sauce, lime, sugar, garlic and chili in the classic Vietnamese dipping sauce.
story: Gets the sweet-sour-salty-hot balance right in one bowl with no cooking at all — used as a dressing for herb-heavy salads and grilled meat as much as a dipping sauce, since the same balance works either way. The ratio matters more than the exact ingredients, and should be tasted and adjusted every time, since limes and chilies vary batch to batch.
method:
1. Dissolve 60 g sugar in 100 g warm water, stirring until fully clear.
2. Whisk in 80 g fish sauce and 80 g fresh lime juice.
3. Add 15 g finely minced garlic and 10 g finely minced fresh red chili (seeds in for more heat).
4. Taste against the four points of balance — sweet, sour, salty, hot — and adjust: more sugar if too sharp, more lime if too sweet, more fish sauce if flat, more chili if it needs more heat.
5. Let stand 10 minutes for the garlic and chili to mellow slightly before final tasting.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week; garlic flavour intensifies over the first day, so slightly under-season with garlic if making ahead.
**Chef's notes:** this sauce is never wrong to taste and adjust to the specific lime and chili in hand — treat the quantities as a starting ratio, not a fixed formula, since acidity and heat both vary significantly by batch.

name: Sesame-Ginger Dressing
tagline: Toasted sesame oil, soy, rice vinegar and fresh ginger whisked into a punchy dressing.
story: A fast, assertive dressing for raw or blanched vegetables and cold noodles — built around toasted sesame oil as the dominant flavour rather than as an accent, so it needs to be a genuinely good, dark toasted oil rather than a light or refined one.
method:
1. Grate 30 g fresh ginger and 10 g garlic finely.
2. Whisk with 60 g soy sauce, 40 g rice vinegar and 20 g honey until the honey is fully dissolved.
3. Whisking constantly, add 60 g toasted sesame oil and 120 g neutral oil in a thin stream until combined and glossy.
4. Stir in 10 g toasted sesame seed for texture.
5. Taste and adjust — more vinegar for sharper, more honey to round it out.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 10 days; shake before use as the sesame seed settles.
**Chef's notes:** using a light, refined sesame oil instead of a proper dark toasted one leaves this dressing tasting thin and one-dimensional no matter how much ginger and garlic go in — the toasted oil is doing most of the work here. Grate the ginger rather than mincing it, so its juice goes fully into the dressing instead of being left behind in fibrous scraps on the board.

name: Sherry Vinaigrette
tagline: Sherry vinegar and olive oil, sharpened with shallot and a touch of Dijon.
story: Sherry vinegar's nuttier, deeper acidity makes this the house choice over roasted vegetables, warm chickpeas and grilled meat where a plain wine vinegar would taste thin — a small everyday reminder of Spain on both menus.
method:
1. Whisk 10 g Dijon mustard with 20 g minced shallot and 100 g sherry vinegar in a bowl.
2. Season with salt and let stand 5 minutes to soften the shallot's raw edge.
3. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 280 g olive oil in a thin, steady stream until fully emulsified.
4. Taste; sherry vinegar varies in intensity by brand and age, so adjust the oil-to-vinegar ratio slightly if it tastes too sharp or too flat.
5. Finish with black pepper to taste.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 1 week; whisk or shake before use.
**Chef's notes:** a cheap, young sherry vinegar tastes thin and overly acidic compared to a properly aged one — use the best sherry vinegar available, since it is the entire point of the dressing and cannot be masked by more oil. Keep two bottles of sherry vinegar on hand — a younger one for everyday use and an aged reserve for a small batch when the dish calls for it.

name: Honey-Mustard Dressing
tagline: Dijon and honey whisked with cider vinegar into a sweet-sharp, family-friendly dressing.
story: The dressing that works for the widest range of palates on the Bistro Mondo menu — sweet enough for children, sharp enough for adults, and equally at home over a simple leaf salad or brushed onto grilled chicken as a glaze.
method:
1. Whisk 50 g Dijon mustard with 50 g honey in a bowl until fully combined and smooth.
2. Whisk in 60 g cider vinegar and 15 g minced shallot.
3. Whisking constantly, drizzle in 220 g olive oil in a thin stream until emulsified and glossy.
4. Season with salt and black pepper to taste.
5. Adjust sweetness or sharpness to preference by nudging the honey or vinegar slightly, tasting after each addition.
Holding: refrigerated, airtight, 10 days; the high mustard and honey content keeps this dressing more stable than a plain vinaigrette, though a stir before use is still recommended.
**Chef's notes:** this dressing thickens considerably in the fridge — let it come to room temperature and whisk briefly before plating rather than serving it straight from the cold well, where it pours poorly. Double as a glaze: brushed on chicken thighs in the last five minutes of roasting, it lacquers and browns rather than simply coating.

name: Sourdough Starter (Maintenance)
tagline: The house culture behind every loaf, focaccia and pizza base in both kitchens.
story: A stable, well-timed starter is the difference between predictable bakes and a coin-flip every morning. Bistro Mondo runs no commercial yeast, so this culture is the single point of failure for the whole bread and pizza program and gets treated that way — fed on a fixed schedule, at a fixed temperature, checked by eye and nose rather than by the clock alone.
method:
1. Discard all but 50g of existing starter, leaving it in the tub.
2. Add 250g strong white bread flour and 250g water at 28°C (1:5:5 ratio by weight of starter:flour:water). Mix to a thick, lump-free paste.
3. Mark the level on the tub with a band. Cover loosely (not airtight) and hold at 24°C.
4. Peak activity at 24°C is 4-6 hours: the culture should roughly double, dome, and just begin to recede at the centre, with a sour-yeasty, slightly fruity smell — not sharp acetone or paint-thinner, which signals it has gone too long hungry.
5. Use at or just past peak for baking. For a stiff levain build (pizza, enriched doughs), feed 1:2:2 with a firmer paste (reduce water to 200g) and hold 8-10 hours at 22°C until tripled.
6. Off-cycle storage: once daily needs are covered, refrigerate at 4°C and feed every 3-4 days. Bring back to room temperature and feed twice, 8-12 hours apart, before using for baking again.
7. Keep a frozen backup: dry a thin layer of mature starter on parchment, break into flakes, freeze in a sealed jar. Rehydrate with equal-weight water and resume daily feeds if the live culture is ever lost.

**Chef's notes:** a starter that only ever gets fed 'when someone remembers' drifts sour and weak — same time, same temperature, every day. If it stops doubling reliably, suspect chlorinated tap water or a feeding room that's dropped below 20°C before anything else.

name: Country Sourdough Loaf (Pain de Campagne au Levain)
tagline: The house loaf at Bistro Mondo — bread basket, crostini, and the reason there's no bread machine on site.
story: Boris's bread basket runs on this loaf alone, so it has to behave the same way every day whether it's baked for six covers or sixty. It is also the base for the kitchen's crostini, panzanella and stuffing whenever stale bread is called for, which is why it's written as a base recipe rather than a one-off.
method:
Baker's percentages (flour = 100%): white bread flour 70%, wholemeal flour 30%, water 72%, mature levain 20%, salt 2.2%.
1. Build levain the night before: 40g mature starter, 80g flour, 80g water, held 10-12 hours at 24°C until tripled and domed.
2. Autolyse: mix 700g strong white flour, 300g wholemeal flour and 720g water. Rest 45 minutes at room temperature.
3. Add 200g levain and 22g salt, mix to a smooth, elastic dough (windowpane test).
4. Bulk ferment 4 hours at 26°C. Give 4 sets of stretch-and-folds in the first 2 hours, then leave undisturbed.
5. Divide into 3 x ~950g pieces. Pre-shape loosely, bench rest 20 minutes.
6. Shape into tight boules or batards. Place seam-up in floured bannetons.
7. Retard 12-16 hours at 4°C.
8. Bake straight from the fridge: score, load into a preheated Dutch oven or steam-injected deck oven at 250°C. Bake covered/with steam 20 minutes, then uncovered at 220°C for 20-25 minutes until deeply coloured and internal temperature reaches 96°C.
9. Cool a minimum of 2 hours on a rack before cutting — the crumb is still setting.

Hold: 2 days at room temperature cut-side down; freezes well whole for up to 1 month, refresh in a hot oven 8 minutes from frozen.

**Chef's notes:** the retard is doing real work — pulling it cold and under-proofed gives a tight, gummy crumb no amount of oven spring will fix. If the dough doesn't pass a windowpane before bulk, don't start the clock; it will never catch up.

name: Focaccia (Sourdough)
tagline: High-hydration levain focaccia, cold-retarded overnight in the tray.
story: A wet, slow-fermented focaccia gives a big, open crumb and a crisp, oil-blistered base without touching a scrap of commercial yeast — in keeping with the house rule. It's cut for the bread basket, split for sandwiches at lunch, and toasted as the base for bruschetta service.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 80%, mature levain 20%, olive oil 8% (plus more for pan/finishing), salt 2.2%.
1. Mix 1000g strong white flour, 800g water and 200g mature levain to a shaggy, very wet dough. Rest 20 minutes.
2. Add 22g salt and 80g olive oil. Mix/fold in the bowl until incorporated and glossy — this dough is too loose to knead by hand in the conventional sense.
3. Bulk ferment 4 hours at 26°C with 3 gentle coil folds in the bowl during the first 2 hours.
4. Pour into two heavily oiled sheet trays (approx. 40x30cm), spreading gently — do not degas fully.
5. Retard, covered, 12-14 hours at 4°C directly in the trays.
6. Next day, bring to room temperature and let proof 2-3 hours at 24-26°C until visibly bubbled and puffy.
7. Dimple firmly all over with oiled fingers, right down to the tray. Drizzle with more oil, scatter flaky salt and rosemary if using.
8. Bake at 230-250°C for 18-22 minutes until deep golden and blistered.
9. Brush with olive oil the moment it comes out. Cool on a rack 15 minutes before cutting to hold the crumb structure.

Hold: 1 day at room temperature loosely wrapped; refreshes well in a hot oven 4-5 minutes.

**Chef's notes:** the dimpling step is what creates the oil pools that fry the base crisp — a timid dimple gives a flat, dry top instead of the characteristic craters.

ingredients.name: extra-virgin olive oil
ingredients.notes: plus more for pan and finishing

name: Pizza Dough, 24h Cold Ferment
tagline: Same-day-plus-one pizza base for service gaps when the 72h stock runs short.
story: This is the fast lane — a small amount of commercial yeast and a short cold retard get a usable, digestible dough on the board in a day, for the nights the 72h levain dough doesn't stretch far enough. It doesn't replace the house sourdough pizza, it backstops it.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 65%, salt 2.5%, fresh yeast 0.3%.
1. Combine 1000g '00' flour and 650g water at 20°C. Autolyse 20 minutes.
2. Dissolve 3g fresh yeast in a splash of the measured water if easier, then mix in with 25g salt.
3. Mix/knead to a smooth, elastic dough passing the windowpane test, about 8-10 minutes by machine.
4. Bulk ferment 2 hours at 22°C room temperature.
5. Divide into 250g balls, shape tight, place in a lidded tray with space to expand.
6. Retard 20-22 hours at 4°C.
7. Pull from the fridge 2 hours before use to come back to room temperature.
8. Stretch by hand from the centre out, leaving a raised cornicione. Bake in the wood oven, floor temperature 430-450°C, about 90 seconds, turning once, until the crust is leopard-spotted.

Hold: use within 24 hours of balling; do not re-retard a dough that has already been pulled and warmed.

**Chef's notes:** if the dough tears when stretched instead of relaxing, it's either under-fermented or was pulled from the fridge too close to bake time — give it more room-temperature rest, not more force.

name: Pizza Dough, 48h Cold Ferment
tagline: Lower-yeast, longer-retard pizza dough for a lighter, more digestible crust.
story: Halving the yeast and doubling the retard against the 24h version trades convenience for flavour and digestibility — more of the fermentation happens slowly in the fridge rather than fast at room temperature, which is what gives a crust that doesn't sit heavy.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 65%, salt 2.5%, fresh yeast 0.15%.
1. Mix 1000g '00' flour with 650g water at 18°C. Autolyse 20 minutes.
2. Add 1.5g fresh yeast dissolved in a little water, then 25g salt. Mix to a smooth, elastic dough, 8-10 minutes by machine.
3. Bulk ferment briefly, 1 hour at 20°C, just enough to get the yeast moving.
4. Divide into 250g balls, shape tight, place in a lidded tray with room to grow.
5. Retard 44-46 hours at 4°C.
6. Pull 2-3 hours before service to temper at room temperature — the dough should feel airy and extensible, not stiff.
7. Stretch by hand, bake in the wood oven at 430-450°C floor temperature for about 90 seconds, turning once.

Hold: use within a few hours of tempering; balls can sit refrigerated up to 60 hours total before quality drops off.

**Chef's notes:** at this low a yeast percentage, an under-heated proofing area in winter can stall fermentation almost completely — check the dough is visibly domed and jiggly by hour 40, not just trusting the clock.

name: Pizza Dough, 72h Sourdough
tagline: The house pizza base — no commercial yeast, three days on levain alone.
story: This is the standard dough for the pizza oven at Bistro Mondo: no packet yeast, built entirely on the same culture that runs the bread program, and given three days to develop the open crumb, blistered rim and mild tang that define the house pizza.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 70%, stiff mature levain 15%, salt 2.5%.
1. The night before mixing, build a stiff levain: 30g mature starter, 60g flour, 60g water, held 8-10 hours at 22°C until tripled and firm-domed.
2. Autolyse 1000g '00' flour with 700g water, 45 minutes.
3. Add 150g stiff levain and 25g salt. Mix to a smooth, elastic dough, windowpane test.
4. Bulk ferment 3 hours at 26°C, with 3 stretch-and-folds in the first 90 minutes.
5. Divide into 250g balls, shape tight, place in a lidded tray with space to expand at least double.
6. Retard 68-70 hours at 4°C.
7. Pull 3-4 hours before service to temper at room temperature; the balls should feel light, domed and jiggly, not stiff.
8. Stretch by hand from the centre, preserving a raised, air-filled cornicione. Bake in the wood oven, floor 450-480°C, 75-90 seconds, turning once, until well-leoparded.

Hold: balls hold refrigerated up to 4 days total; beyond that the crust turns brittle rather than blistered.

**Chef's notes:** the levain build is the whole recipe — a levain that hasn't tripled by mixing time will leave the dough underpowered for three full days in the fridge, giving dense, tight balls that won't stretch without tearing.

name: Pasta Fresca all'Uovo
tagline: Egg pasta dough for tagliatelle, ravioli and lasagne sheets.
story: A rich, all-yolk-leaning egg dough that rolls thin without tearing and holds a filling without going soft in the pot. It's the base for every stuffed and cut fresh pasta on the menu, made to order rather than held long, since fresh dough loses its bite fast.
method:
1. Mound 500g '00' flour on the bench or in a stand mixer bowl.
2. Whisk together 5 whole eggs (250g), 2 extra yolks (40g) and 10g olive oil.
3. Work the egg mixture into the flour gradually until it forms a shaggy mass, then knead by hand or on low speed with a dough hook for 10 minutes until smooth, firm and elastic — it should feel like an earlobe, not sticky.
4. Wrap tightly in plastic and rest a minimum of 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours refrigerated.
5. Divide into workable pieces, flatten, and pass through a pasta machine from the widest setting down, folding once or twice at the start to even the sheet.
6. Roll to the thickness suited to the shape: setting 6 for tagliatelle, setting 7-8 for ravioli.
7. Cut or shape immediately, dusting generously with semola to prevent sticking.
8. Cook fresh in well-salted boiling water 1.5-3 minutes depending on shape and thickness, until al dente.

Hold: fresh-cut pasta holds dusted with semola on trays, refrigerated, up to 24 hours; dough not yet rolled holds wrapped up to 2 days refrigerated. Freezes well cut and portioned, cook from frozen.

**Chef's notes:** a dough that's too soft to hold its shape on the machine is usually under-kneaded, not under-floured — resist adding flour at the rolling stage and knead longer next batch instead.

name: Pasta Secca Semolina (Extruded, Bronze Die)
tagline: Low-hydration durum dough for the bronze-die extruder — rough-surfaced, sauce-gripping pasta.
story: Bronze extrusion is what separates house-made dry pasta from anything bought in: the die drags and tears the dough surface instead of polishing it smooth, leaving a matte, porous finish that sauce actually clings to. Worth the extra equipment and time for anything that isn't fresh egg pasta on the menu.
method:
Baker's percentages: semolina 100%, water 38-40%.
1. Mix 1000g fine semola rimacinata with 380-400g water to a dry, shaggy, low-hydration dough — it should look under-hydrated, not smooth.
2. Rest, covered, 20-30 minutes to let the semolina fully hydrate.
3. Load into the extruder fitted with the bronze die for the shape required.
4. Extrude at low speed. Keep dough temperature below 40°C throughout — friction heat is the main enemy here; slow the auger or chill the barrel if it climbs.
5. Cut to length as it exits, laying pieces separately on trays or racks so they don't fuse.
6. Dry in a controlled environment: 40-50°C, 50-60% relative humidity, for 24-48 hours depending on shape thickness, until brittle and down to roughly 12% moisture.
7. Alternatively, cook a portion fresh off the die the same day without drying, in well-salted boiling water 3-5 minutes.

Hold: fully dried pasta keeps 6 months in a sealed container at room temperature, away from light.

**Chef's notes:** if the surface comes out shiny rather than matte, the die is overheating the dough — that alone will cost the sauce-cling that's the entire point of bronze extrusion. Dry too fast or too hot and the pasta cracks; too slow or humid and it moulds before it sets.

name: Brioche
tagline: Rich, butter-laminated-by-mixing enriched dough for loaves, buns and French toast.
story: The house enriched dough — the base for brioche buns under anything that wants a soft roll, and for the French toast that uses up loaf ends. Built butter-heavy and cold-retarded overnight so it's workable by hand the next morning instead of collapsing under its own richness.
method:
Baker's percentages (flour = 100%): sugar 12%, salt 2%, fresh yeast 3%, whole egg 50%, milk 12%, butter 60%.
1. Mix 500g strong white flour, 60g sugar, 10g salt, 15g fresh yeast, 250g whole egg (about 5 eggs) and 60g milk to a smooth, cohesive dough.
2. Knead on medium speed 8-10 minutes until it clears the bowl and starts to feel elastic.
3. With the mixer running, add 300g softened (not melted) butter in 3-4 additions, waiting for each to fully incorporate before adding the next.
4. Continue kneading until the dough is glossy, smooth and passes a windowpane test, 8-10 minutes more.
5. Bulk ferment 1 hour at room temperature, knock back, then retard overnight (8-12 hours) at 4°C — this firms the butter and makes the dough workable.
6. Divide and shape (loaf, brioche à tête, or 60g buns).
7. Final proof 2-2.5 hours at 26°C until doubled and visibly jiggly when the tin is tapped.
8. Egg wash, bake at 180°C: 25-30 minutes for loaves, 12-15 minutes for buns, until deep golden and internal temperature reaches 92-94°C.

Hold: 2 days at room temperature well wrapped; freezes baked or shaped-unbaked (thaw and proof from frozen).

**Chef's notes:** butter added too fast or too warm will slick out rather than incorporate — if the dough looks greasy and won't come together, stop, chill it 15 minutes, and resume on lower speed.

name: Croissant / Laminated Dough (Pâte Levée Feuilletée)
tagline: Yeasted laminated dough for croissants, pains au chocolat and other viennoiserie.
story: Croissant dough is a temperature-control exercise as much as a recipe — every fold either goes right at a stable butter temperature or fails silently and only shows up as flat, dense pastry the next morning. Written here as the one dough behind all of the studio's viennoiserie.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, liquid (water+milk) 44%, sugar 10%, salt 2%, fresh yeast 4%, détrempe butter 8%, lamination butter 50%.
1. Mix 1000g flour, 220g water, 220g milk, 100g sugar, 20g salt, 40g fresh yeast and 80g softened butter to a smooth, only lightly developed dough — do not overwork.
2. Shape into a flat rectangle, wrap, rest 1 hour at room temperature then retard 1 hour at 4°C.
3. Beat 500g cold butter into a 20x20cm block (beurre de tourage). Keep at 14-16°C — pliable but not soft.
4. Encase the butter in the dough. Give one double fold (book fold), rest 30-40 minutes at 4°C, then one single fold, rest 30-40 minutes at 4°C.
5. Final rest, wrapped, 8-12 hours (overnight) at 4°C.
6. Roll to 3.5-4mm, keeping dough between 14-16°C throughout — re-chill if it warms or resists.
7. Cut triangles, shape, and proof at 26-27°C for 2-2.5 hours until doubled, jiggly, and butter layers just visible at the cut edges.
8. Egg wash before and after proofing. Bake at 190°C for 4 minutes, then 180°C for 12-14 minutes until deeply golden with a shattering, layered crust.

Hold: bake same day for best lift; shaped, unproofed croissants freeze well — thaw and proof from frozen overnight in the fridge, then finish proofing at room temperature.

**Chef's notes:** butter that's too cold cracks and shatters through the layers on rolling; too warm and it melts into the dough and kills the lift entirely — 14-16°C is the whole window.

name: Pâte Feuilletée Inversée (Inverse Puff Pastry)
tagline: Butter-on-the-outside puff pastry — cleaner, more even lift than classic feuilletage.
story: With the butter block on the outside instead of the dough, inverse puff pastry laminates more evenly and shrinks less on baking, which matters for anything precise: vol-au-vent shells, mille-feuille layers, tart bases that need to hold a straight edge.
method:
1. Beurre manié (outer block): mix 375g cold butter with 150g flour until smooth and lump-free. Shape into a 20x20cm square, wrap, chill 1 hour at 4°C.
2. Détrempe (inner dough): mix 350g flour, 150g water, 5g white vinegar, 10g salt and 50g melted butter to a smooth dough. Shape into a 14x14cm square, wrap, chill 1 hour at 4°C.
3. Roll the beurre manié block larger than the détrempe. Place the détrempe in the centre and fold the butter block over it to fully enclose — butter on the outside, dough inside.
4. Roll out and give a single fold. Rest 30-40 minutes at 4°C.
5. Repeat for a total of 5-6 single turns (or a mix of double and single turns), always resting 30-40 minutes at 4°C between turns, and keeping the dough at 14-16°C when rolling.
6. Final rest a minimum of 4 hours, ideally overnight, at 4°C.
7. Roll to 2.5-3mm for the intended use, dock if needed, and rest 20 minutes before baking to reduce shrinkage.
8. Bake at 200°C for 10 minutes to set the lift, then reduce to 180°C and bake a further 15-20 minutes until fully risen and deep golden throughout, not just on the surface.

Hold: unbaked, wrapped dough keeps 3 days refrigerated or 1 month frozen.

**Chef's notes:** because the butter is on the outside, this dough tears if it's rolled while too cold or too warm — 14-16°C is non-negotiable; outside that window, stop and let it equalise rather than forcing the roll.

name: Pâte Brisée
tagline: Short, savoury tart pastry — the base for quiches and savoury tarts.
story: The plain shortcrust behind every savoury tart on the menu, built for structure rather than sweetness so it can carry a wet, custard-based filling without going soggy underneath.
method:
1. Rub 250g cold diced butter into 500g plain flour and 8g salt until the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs with some pea-sized pieces remaining — by hand or short pulses in a food processor.
2. Add 90-100g ice water gradually, bringing the dough together with a few folds. Stop as soon as it holds — overworking develops gluten and toughens the crust.
3. Shape into a disc, wrap, rest a minimum of 1 hour at 4°C (up to 3 days).
4. Roll to 3mm on a lightly floured surface, line the tart tin, chill the lined shell 20 minutes to relax the gluten before baking.
5. Dock the base, line with parchment and baking beans/weights.
6. Blind bake at 180°C for 15 minutes, then remove the weights and parchment and bake a further 8-10 minutes until pale gold and dry to the touch throughout the base.

Hold: unbaked dough keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen; baked, cooled shells hold 1 day airtight at room temperature before filling.

**Chef's notes:** warm butter is the main failure point — if it starts turning greasy or elastic instead of crumbly at any stage, stop and rest it in the fridge 15 minutes before continuing.

name: Pâte Sucrée
tagline: Sweet, sandy tart pastry for fruit tarts and custard shells.
story: The sweet counterpart to pâte brisée, creamed rather than rubbed so it bakes into a firm, biscuit-like shell that holds cream or custard fillings without collapsing at the edges.
method:
1. Cream 300g cold diced butter with 200g icing sugar and 3g salt just until combined — do not aerate heavily.
2. Add 4 egg yolks (80g) and mix until smooth.
3. Add 500g plain flour in one go and mix only until it comes together as a dough — overmixing here gives a tough, shrink-prone shell.
4. Shape into a disc, wrap, rest a minimum of 2 hours at 4°C.
5. Roll to 3mm between sheets of parchment (this dough is soft and short, harder to handle on a floured bench). Line the tart tin, chill the lined shell 20 minutes.
6. Dock, line with parchment and weights, blind bake at 170°C for 15-18 minutes until sandy gold at the edges.
7. If filling with anything wet, brush the warm shell with a thin layer of beaten egg and return to the oven 2 minutes to seal.

Hold: unbaked dough keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen; baked shells hold 1 day airtight before filling.

**Chef's notes:** this dough tears more easily than brisée when rolled warm — if it's sticking or stretching rather than cutting clean, chill it another 15 minutes rather than fighting it.

name: Pâte à Choux
tagline: Choux paste for éclairs, gougères and profiteroles, piped to order.
story: One paste covers both savoury and sweet service — gougères for the bread basket, éclairs and choux buns for dessert — so it's built neutral and adjusted with cheese or sugar downstream rather than baked into the base recipe.
method:
1. Bring 250g water, 250g milk, 220g butter, 5g salt and 10g sugar to a full boil.
2. Off the heat, tip in 300g flour all at once and beat vigorously until smooth.
3. Return to low heat and beat/dry the panade for 1-2 minutes until it pulls away from the pan sides and a thin film forms on the base — internal temperature around 80°C.
4. Transfer to a mixer or bowl and beat briefly to release steam and cool slightly, 2-3 minutes.
5. Beat in eggs (roughly 8, about 400g) gradually, a little at a time, until the paste falls from the beater in a slow, heavy ribbon that holds a V-shape — stop adding egg once this point is reached, even if some remains.
6. Pipe to shape immediately onto lined trays.
7. Bake with a shot of steam (or a splash of water thrown on the oven floor) at 200°C for 15 minutes without opening the door, then reduce to 170°C and bake a further 15-20 minutes until fully dry and deep golden — the paste must dry through or it collapses on cooling.
8. Pierce each piece with a skewer as it comes out to let steam escape, cool on a rack.

Hold: bake same day; unbaked piped paste can be frozen on trays and baked from frozen, adding a few minutes.

**Chef's notes:** opening the oven before the shells have fully coloured and set is the single most common cause of collapsed choux — resist checking before the minimum bake time is up.

name: Flatbread / Pita
tagline: Quick yeasted flatbread, blistered hot for a natural pocket.
story: A fast dough for the days that need bread on the table in under two hours — table flatbread, wraps for the grill station, or torn for mezze service.
method:
1. Mix 500g strong white flour, 320g water, 10g salt, 5g instant yeast and 15g olive oil to a smooth, slightly tacky dough. Knead 8 minutes until elastic.
2. Bulk ferment 1 hour at room temperature (24°C) until doubled.
3. Divide into 80g pieces, shape into balls, rest covered 15 minutes.
4. Roll each into a round, 4-5mm thick. Rest a further 10 minutes uncovered.
5. Bake on a very hot stone or steel (250-280°C), or near the mouth of the wood oven, for 60-90 seconds per side until puffed with a hollow pocket and lightly spotted.
6. Stack immediately under a clean cloth as they come off — this keeps them soft rather than crisping as they cool.

Hold: 1 day at room temperature wrapped; freezes well stacked with parchment between pieces, reheat directly from frozen on a hot surface 30 seconds per side.

**Chef's notes:** the pocket only forms if the surface is genuinely hot and the dough round is even in thickness — a thin patch blows out instead of puffing evenly.

name: Bagel Dough
tagline: Stiff, low-hydration dough, boiled in malt water before baking.
story: Bagels live or die on the boil, but the dough underneath has to be stiff enough to hold a ring shape through it — a wetter, softer dough (like most bread doughs) simply won't hold up.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 55%, salt 2%, instant yeast 0.6%, malt syrup 3%.
1. Mix 1000g high-gluten or strong bread flour, 550g water, 20g salt, 6g instant yeast and 30g barley malt syrup to a very stiff, dense dough — it should resist stretching, not extend easily.
2. Knead 10-12 minutes until smooth and fully developed despite the stiffness.
3. Bulk ferment 1 hour at room temperature.
4. Divide into 100g pieces, shape into rings by punching a hole through a ball and stretching gently to an even thickness.
5. Place on trays, cover, retard 12-16 hours at 4°C — this develops flavour and firms the dough for the boil.
6. Bring a large pot of water to a rolling boil with 60g malt syrup or honey per 4 litres.
7. Boil bagels straight from the fridge, 45-60 seconds per side, no longer or they turn wrinkled and dense.
8. Top immediately while wet (seeds, salt) and transfer to a tray.
9. Bake at 220°C for 18-20 minutes until deep mahogany-brown and firm.

Hold: 1 day at room temperature; freezes very well, refresh from frozen in a hot oven 8-10 minutes.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the retard and boiling straight after shaping gives a pale, flat bagel — the cold rest is what lets the surface set enough to hold its shape through the boil.

name: Ciabatta (Sourdough)
tagline: Wet-doughed, levain-leavened ciabatta with a big, irregular crumb.
story: Built on the house culture rather than a poolish, so it runs off the same starter schedule as everything else in the bakery. The dough is too slack to knead in the usual sense — the open, torn crumb comes precisely from leaving it alone once it's mixed.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, water 80%, mature liquid levain 20%, salt 2.2%.
1. Mix 1000g strong white flour, 800g water and 200g mature liquid levain to a very wet, shaggy dough.
2. Add 22g salt, fold in the bowl until incorporated.
3. Bulk ferment 3-4 hours at 26°C, with 3-4 gentle coil folds in the bowl during the first 2 hours, until visibly airy and full of bubbles.
4. Tip the dough gently onto a heavily floured surface — handle as little as possible to preserve the gas.
5. Cut into 6 logs (roughly 300g each) without pressing or degassing.
6. Transfer seam-down onto a well-floured couche or tray, proof 45 minutes.
7. Flip each piece onto a peel or tray so the textured, floured side faces up.
8. Bake with steam at 240°C for 20-22 minutes until deep golden and the loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the base.
9. Cool completely on a rack — the crumb is still setting for the first 30-40 minutes and will gum up if cut early.

Hold: 1 day at room temperature; freezes well, refresh from frozen in a hot oven 8-10 minutes.

**Chef's notes:** the instinct to knock this dough down and shape it neatly ruins it — the holes come from disturbing it as little as possible after bulk.

name: Pan de Molde (Sourdough Sandwich Loaf)
tagline: Soft, levain-leavened sandwich loaf for tostadas and service sandwiches.
story: The tinned loaf behind every sandwich and tostada that goes out, still built on the house culture rather than commercial yeast — softer and more enriched than the country loaf, but run through the same fermentation logic.
method:
Baker's percentages: flour 100%, combined liquid 45%, mature levain 20%, butter 8%, sugar 4%, salt 2%.
1. Mix 1000g strong white flour, 300g whole milk, 150g water and 200g mature levain to a rough dough. Rest 20 minutes.
2. Add 80g softened butter, 40g sugar and 20g salt. Knead 10-12 minutes to a smooth, elastic dough passing the windowpane test.
3. Bulk ferment 4 hours at 26°C, with 2 folds in the first 2 hours.
4. Divide into 3 pieces, shape to fit loaf tins (Pullman or standard, buttered).
5. Proof 3-4 hours at 26-28°C until the dough crowns 1-2cm above the rim of the tin.
6. For a square-top loaf, slide the lid on for the Pullman tin; for a domed top, leave open.
7. Bake at 190°C for 35-40 minutes until deep golden (or, for the lidded loaf, until it releases cleanly) and internal temperature reaches 94°C.
8. Brush the crust with melted butter on release from the tin. Cool fully, minimum 2 hours, before slicing.

Hold: 3 days at room temperature well wrapped, sliced for service; freezes sliced, toast directly from frozen.

**Chef's notes:** pulling this from the tin too early to 'check' collapses the sides while they're still setting — wait for the full cool before slicing for sandwich service.

ingredients.name: unsalted butter
ingredients.notes: softened, plus more for tins and finishing

name: Grissini
tagline: Thin, crisp breadsticks for the table before food arrives.
story: Something crisp and salty to put on the table the moment guests sit down, made in a batch large enough to hold in a sealed tin for several days of service rather than baked to order.
method:
1. Mix 500g strong white flour, 280g water, 30g olive oil, 10g salt and 5g instant yeast to a smooth, firm dough. Knead 8 minutes.
2. Bulk ferment 45 minutes at room temperature.
3. Divide into small pieces (about 15g each) and roll each by hand into a thin rope, 25-30cm long, tapering slightly at the ends.
4. Rest 10 minutes on trays.
5. Roll in semolina, sesame or fennel seed if using, pressing lightly to adhere.
6. Bake at 200°C for 12-15 minutes until evenly golden and crisp all the way through — they should snap cleanly, not bend.
7. Cool completely on a rack before storing.

Hold: 1-2 weeks in a fully airtight container; grissini lose their snap within hours if left uncovered or stored while even slightly warm.

**Chef's notes:** uneven rolling is the main defect — a rope that's thick in the middle stays soft there while the thin ends turn hard and dark; roll for even thickness over length, not just speed.

name: Tortilla de Maíz (Nixtamal Masa)
tagline: Fresh corn masa from scratch — lime-cooked, ground, and pressed to order.
story: Nixtamalization is a real technique, not a shortcut around masa harina, and it's what gives fresh corn tortillas their actual flavour and pliability — worth doing properly given the studio's cross-cultural menu leans on it more than once.
method:
1. Combine 1000g dried field corn, 10g food-grade calcium hydroxide (cal) and 3000g water in a non-reactive pot.
2. Simmer gently at 80-85°C for 45-60 minutes — do not let it boil hard. The corn is ready when the pericarp (outer skin) loosens and rubs off between the fingers, but the kernel is still firm, not mushy.
3. Remove from heat, cover, and steep 8-12 hours (overnight) in the cooking liquid (nejayote).
4. Rinse the corn thoroughly in several changes of water, rubbing to remove loosened hulls and excess lime, until the water runs mostly clear.
5. Grind through a stone mill or metate to a smooth, cohesive masa, adjusting with a little water to reach a soft, play-dough consistency that doesn't crack at the edges when pressed.
6. Press 40-45g balls of masa between sheets of plastic in a tortilla press.
7. Cook on a dry, very hot comal or plancha (260-280°C), 45-60 seconds per side, flipping as needed until it puffs slightly and browns in small spots.
8. Keep warm wrapped in cloth in a basket; serve within the hour for best texture.

Hold: fresh masa keeps 2 days refrigerated, wrapped; pressed tortillas are best cooked immediately, though extras hold a day refrigerated and reheat on the comal.

**Chef's notes:** nixtamalization is what unlocks the corn's flavour and nutrition — under-cooking the lime step gives a raw, chalky masa that won't hold together on the press or the comal.

name: Gyoza Wrappers
tagline: Hot-water wheat dough, rolled thin with a thicker centre for pleating.
story: A simple flour-and-water dough, but the hot-water scald is what gives it the pliability to fold and pleat without cracking — worth making in-house for anything filled and pan-fried rather than relying on shop-bought wrappers that tear at the seam.
method:
1. Place 250g plain flour in a bowl. Pour in 150g boiling water and mix immediately with a spoon or chopstick until it forms clumps — this partially gelatinises the starch for pliability.
2. Add a further 250g flour and 100g cold water, along with 5g salt, and bring together into a rough dough.
3. Knead 8-10 minutes until smooth and firm. Cover and rest 30 minutes at room temperature — this relaxes the gluten and makes rolling much easier.
4. Divide the dough into long ropes about 2.5cm thick, then cut into 12-15g pieces.
5. Roll each piece into a thin round, about 8cm across, keeping the centre slightly thicker than the edges — this stops the base from tearing under a filling while the edges pleat easily.
6. Dust rolled wrappers generously with cornstarch and stack with a layer of dusting between each to prevent sticking.
7. Fill and fold within a few hours, or wrap the stack airtight and freeze between parchment.

Hold: 4 hours at room temperature under a damp cloth; wrap airtight and refrigerate up to 1 day, or freeze up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the rest after kneading is the most common cause of wrappers that shrink back and won't roll thin — the dough needs the full 30 minutes to relax.

name: Pasta Verde (Spinach)
tagline: Spinach-enriched egg pasta dough for green tagliolini and lasagne.
story: The same egg-pasta base with wilted spinach worked in for colour and a subtle vegetal note, used wherever a striped or green pasta is on the menu — the technique lives or dies on getting the spinach bone dry before it goes in.
method:
1. Wilt 250g fresh spinach briefly in boiling water or a hot pan, then shock immediately in ice water to stop cooking and hold the colour.
2. Squeeze the spinach completely dry — twist hard in a clean cloth until no more water comes out. This step is critical; residual water will make the dough impossible to manage.
3. Finely chop or purée the dried spinach.
4. Mound 500g '00' flour, make a well, and add the spinach purée, 3 whole eggs (150g), 2 extra yolks (40g) and 10g olive oil.
5. Work into a shaggy dough, then knead by hand or machine 10 minutes until smooth, firm and elastic.
6. Wrap tightly and rest a minimum of 30-60 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours refrigerated.
7. Roll through a pasta machine from the widest setting down to the thickness needed (setting 6 for tagliolini, 7 for lasagne sheets), dusting with semola as needed.
8. Cut or shape immediately; cook fresh in well-salted boiling water 1.5-2.5 minutes until al dente.

Hold: cut pasta holds dusted with semola on trays, refrigerated, up to 24 hours; freezes well portioned.

**Chef's notes:** if the dough is sticky and won't firm up no matter how much flour is worked in, the spinach wasn't squeezed dry enough — start again rather than fighting it with extra flour, which just toughens the finished pasta.

name: Crème pâtissière
tagline: The base filling cream for éclairs, tarts and mille-feuille — silky, never floury.
story: Crème pâtissière is the most repeated cream in the section: it fills éclairs, layers a mille-feuille, backs a tarte aux fruits, and thins into crème diplomate for verrines. The whole difference between a clean custard and a raw-starch taste is cooking it out properly, not the recipe itself.
method:
1. Split the vanilla pod and scrape the seeds into the milk; bring milk, seeds and pod to just below a boil in a heavy pot.
2. Whisk egg yolks, sugar and cornstarch together until pale and ribboning — this also dissolves the starch so it doesn't clump.
3. Remove the vanilla pod. Temper: pour a third of the hot milk onto the yolk mixture, whisking constantly, then return everything to the pot.
4. Cook over medium heat, whisking continuously and scraping the base and corners, until it thickens and comes to a full rolling boil. Hold at the boil, still whisking, for 1–2 minutes — this cooks out the raw starch taste.
5. Off the heat, whisk in the cold diced butter until glossy.
6. Pass through a fine sieve onto a shallow tray, spread thin, press cling film directly onto the surface to stop a skin forming, and chill rapidly (ice bath or blast chiller) to below 4°C within 90 minutes.
7. Before use, whisk vigorously until smooth and pipeable.

Holds 48 hours refrigerated in a sealed container. Do not freeze — it splits into a grainy, weeping mess on thawing.

**Chef's notes:** the failure point is always time at the boil, not temperature — pull it 30 seconds early and every filling made from it will taste faintly of raw flour. Let it boil properly, whisking hard so it doesn't catch.

name: Crème anglaise
tagline: The mother custard sauce — pours beside desserts, becomes ice-cream base with more cream.
story: Crème anglaise is the plain sauce behind half the dessert pass: poured warm beside a tarte, chilled under a soufflé that's already falling, or built up with extra cream into an ice-cream base. It lives or dies on a few degrees — nappe consistency, never a scramble.
method:
1. Split the vanilla pod, scrape the seeds, and heat with the milk, cream and half the sugar to just below a boil.
2. Whisk the yolks with the remaining sugar until pale.
3. Temper the hot milk into the yolks gradually, whisking.
4. Return to the pot and cook over low-medium heat, stirring constantly with a spatula in a figure-eight (covering the base evenly), until it reaches 82–84°C: it should coat the back of a spoon and hold a clear line when you run a finger through it. Do not let it boil.
5. Strain immediately into a bowl set over ice and stir to stop the cooking.
6. Cool fully, then refrigerate.

Holds 2 days refrigerated, tightly covered. Use cold as a sauce, or fold into more cream to build an ice-cream base.

**Chef's notes:** past about 85°C the yolks scramble and there is no bringing it back — keep a thermometer in the pot until the visual cue is second nature, and pull the pot a couple of degrees early since residual heat keeps cooking it in the pan.

name: Crème diplomate
tagline: Crème pâtissière stabilised with gelatin and lightened with cream — holds a piped line.
story: Plain crème pâtissière is too dense to pipe cleanly or hold overnight without weeping. Gelatin fixes the base so folded whipped cream keeps its air, which is what a fraisier, a Paris-Brest or a verrine needs to still look clean the next service.
method:
1. Bloom the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5 minutes, squeeze dry.
2. Warm 150g of the crème pâtissière to about 40°C, melt the gelatin into it, then whisk this back into the remaining cold crème pâtissière until completely smooth with no lumps.
3. Whip the cream to soft-medium peaks only — it must still be able to fold, not already stiff.
4. Fold the whipped cream into the crème pâtissière in two additions, cutting and turning with a spatula until no streaks of white remain.
5. Use at once for piping or layering, or cover and refrigerate up to 24 hours — beyond that the gelatin sets it too firm to pipe cleanly.

Do not freeze; it weeps badly on thawing.

**Chef's notes:** fold, never whisk, once the cream goes in — overworking it collapses the air you just built and you are left with expensive plain crème pâtissière.

name: Ganache oscura
tagline: Cream and dark chocolate, near enough 1:1 — glaze, filling and truffle centre in one base.
story: Dark ganache is the most repeated ratio in the book, nudged a few points either way for pouring glaze versus firm piping filling. It underlies the entremet glaze, the chocolate tart filling and the bonbon centre without changing method.
method:
1. Chop the chocolate finely, or use callets, and place in a heatproof bowl.
2. Bring the cream and glucose to a full boil.
3. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate in two additions, letting it sit 30 seconds each time before stirring from the centre outward with a spatula until fully melted and glossy.
4. If the ganache looks grainy or oily (split), blend briefly with a stick blender held just below the surface to bring it back into emulsion.
5. At around 35°C, whisk in the diced butter for extra shine and a smoother mouthfeel.
6. For glazing, use warm at 35–40°C. For piping or truffles, cool to room temperature, then refrigerate until it holds a clean line off a spatula.

Store covered at room temperature up to 2 days, or refrigerated up to 10 days; bring back to working temperature gently in a bain-marie, never direct high heat.

**Chef's notes:** a split ganache is almost always cream added too hot or too fast — fix it with a stick blender before reaching for more cream, which only masks the problem.

name: Ganache de leche
tagline: Softer, sweeter than dark ganache — needs less cream to set because the chocolate carries more fat and sugar.
story: Milk chocolate already carries milk solids and more sugar, so it sets softer than dark ganache at the same ratio — the cream has to come down or the filling never firms. This is the standard filling for milk chocolate bonbons and a softer glaze where dark reads too bitter.
method:
1. Chop the chocolate finely or use callets, place in a heatproof bowl.
2. Bring the cream and glucose to a full boil.
3. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate in two additions, resting 30 seconds each time, then stir from the centre outward until smooth and glossy.
4. If it splits, bring it back together with a brief pass of the stick blender just under the surface.
5. At around 35°C, whisk in the diced butter.
6. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate until it holds a clean line off a spatula for piping, or use warm at 32–35°C for glazing.

Store covered, refrigerated, up to 10 days; bring back to temperature gently.

**Chef's notes:** do not use the dark-ganache ratio here out of habit — milk ganache made 1:1 with cream never sets and stays a sauce; if it looks too soft after a full chill, it is under-chocolated, not under-chilled.

name: Ganache blanca
tagline: White chocolate holds almost no structure of its own — the cream ratio has to drop hard to get a set.
story: White chocolate is mostly cocoa butter, milk solids and sugar with no cocoa mass to help it set, so a white ganache needs noticeably less cream than dark or milk to firm up at all. It is the base for a lot of the pale glazes and mousse fillings in the fine-dining kitchen, and the one most likely to split from careless heat.
method:
1. Chop the white chocolate finely or use callets, place in a heatproof bowl.
2. Bring the cream to just below a boil — white chocolate scorches and grains more easily than dark, so do not let the cream get any hotter than it needs to.
3. Pour the hot cream over the chocolate, wait 30 seconds, then stir gently from the centre outward until smooth.
4. If it looks split or grainy, bring it back with a brief stick-blender pass just below the surface — do not add extra cream to fix it, that only dilutes the set further.
5. Whisk in the diced butter once the mixture is around 30°C.
6. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 4 hours before piping or moulding; it sets more slowly than dark or milk ganache.

Store covered, refrigerated, up to 7 days — white ganache is the most perishable of the three on flavour, not just food safety.

**Chef's notes:** the commonest fault is treating it like dark ganache and using too much cream out of habit — if it will not firm up after a proper chill, the fix is more chocolate next batch, not more time in the fridge.

name: Ganache montada
tagline: A cold-whipped ganache, light enough to pipe like a mousse, that holds its shape without gelatin problems.
story: Whipped ganache solves the gap between a dense set ganache and an unstable chocolate mousse: made with a two-stage cream addition and rested overnight, it whips up light and stable enough to pipe onto a tart or into a verrine and still hold a crisp edge the next day.
method:
1. Chop the chocolate finely, place in a heatproof bowl.
2. Bring a third of the cream (the 'hot' portion) to a full boil with the glucose.
3. Pour over the chocolate and stir from the centre outward until smooth and fully melted.
4. Whisk in the remaining cold cream in a steady stream — this brings the whole mixture down in temperature and starts the emulsion that will let it whip later.
5. Pass through a fine sieve, cover with cling film touching the surface, and refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight, to let the fat crystallise fully.
6. Whip in a stand mixer on medium speed — not high — until it just holds a soft, glossy peak. Stop the moment it holds; it goes from whipped to grainy and broken within seconds if overrun.
7. Pipe or spread immediately.

Once whipped it does not hold well — use it within the hour. The unwhipped base keeps refrigerated up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** the whole method fails if the base isn't cold enough before whipping — a warm ganache never builds structure and just turns to chocolate cream; if in doubt, chill it another hour rather than force it in the mixer.

name: Crème Chantilly
tagline: Sweetened, vanilla-scented whipped cream — the fastest finish on the pass.
story: Crème Chantilly is whipped cream done properly: cold equipment, cold cream, sugar added gradually, stopped at soft-medium peak. It finishes a tart, lightens a mousse, or sits plain beside a slice of tarta de Santiago — simple enough that the only real risk is overwhipping it to butter.
method:
1. Chill the bowl and whisk in the fridge or freezer for 10 minutes before starting — warm equipment is the main cause of a slow, unstable whip.
2. Pour the cold cream into the bowl and start whisking on medium speed.
3. Once it starts to thicken, add the sugar and vanilla in a steady stream, still whisking.
4. Continue to soft-medium peaks — it should hold a soft point that folds over, not a stiff spike.
5. Use immediately for piping (chill the piping bag beforehand) or fold into other mixtures.

Holds 4 hours refrigerated before it starts to weep; whisk briefly to bring it back once, no more.

**Chef's notes:** the line between whipped cream and butter is about ten seconds at the end — stop the machine as soon as it holds, and finish the last few turns by hand if piping is not immediate.

name: Merengue italiano
tagline: Egg whites cooked by a hot sugar syrup — the most stable meringue, safe to eat unbaked.
story: Italian meringue is made by pouring a 121°C sugar syrup into whipping whites, which cooks the egg through and gives a glossy, stable foam that holds for hours without weeping. It is the meringue for a lemon-pie topping that gets torched rather than baked, for macaron shells, and for lightening buttercream.
method:
1. Put the egg whites in a stand mixer bowl, ready to whip but not started yet.
2. In a small pot, combine sugar and water; cook to 121°C, brushing down the sides with a wet pastry brush to stop crystallisation.
3. When the syrup reaches about 114°C, start whipping the whites on medium-high speed to soft peaks.
4. Once the syrup hits 121°C, reduce mixer speed to medium and pour the syrup in a thin, steady stream down the side of the bowl, avoiding the whisk.
5. Increase speed back to high and whip until the bowl is cool to the touch (about 10 minutes) and the meringue is thick, glossy and holds a stiff, shiny peak.

Use immediately — it starts to lose gloss and volume after about 2 hours at room temperature. Piped and torched, or folded into other bases, it does not keep as a stand-alone item.

**Chef's notes:** the single failure point is pouring the syrup onto the whisk instead of the side of the bowl — it flings hot sugar onto the walls and never incorporates, so the meringue stays runny no matter how long you whip it.

name: Merengue suizo
tagline: Whites and sugar warmed together over a bain-marie before whipping — dense, glossy, easy to pipe and bake.
story: Swiss meringue sits between French and Italian in effort and result: warming the whites with the sugar first dissolves it completely, giving a dense, marshmallow-textured foam that pipes cleanly and holds its shape through baking. It is the standard for piped meringue shells, kisses and buttercream bases that do not need a hot sugar stage.
method:
1. Combine egg whites and sugar in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of gently simmering water, bowl not touching the water.
2. Whisk by hand continuously until the sugar is fully dissolved and the mixture reaches 55–60°C — test by rubbing a little between your fingers; it should feel completely smooth, no grains.
3. Transfer to a stand mixer and whip on high speed until it triples in volume, turns bright white and glossy, and holds a stiff peak, and the bowl has cooled to room temperature (8–10 minutes).
4. Pipe or spread as needed at once.

For crisp meringue shells, pipe and bake at 90–100°C for 90–120 minutes until they lift cleanly off the paper and sound hollow when tapped; cool fully before storing airtight up to 2 weeks (they soften fast in humidity).

**Chef's notes:** rushing the bain-marie stage is the usual mistake — if the sugar is not fully dissolved before whipping, the shells weep sugar syrup as they bake and never crisp properly.

name: Merengue francés
tagline: Raw whites whipped straight with sugar — the simplest meringue, always baked or torched before serving.
story: French meringue is whites whipped with sugar and nothing else — no cooked syrup, no bain-marie — which makes it the fastest of the three but also the least stable, and it must always be baked through before it reaches a plate. It is what goes under a pavlova shell and into dacquoise and other nut meringues where a long, slow bake is already planned.
method:
1. Make sure the bowl and whisk are completely grease-free — any trace of yolk or fat stops the whites from whipping properly.
2. Whip the egg whites on medium speed until foamy, then add the cream of tartar (or a few drops of lemon juice) to stabilise.
3. Once soft peaks form, add the sugar gradually, a third at a time, whipping on high between additions.
4. Continue whipping until the meringue is stiff, glossy and holds a firm peak, and no sugar grains are felt when rubbed between fingers.
5. Use immediately — piped for pavlova shells or spread thin for dacquoise-style bases — as it begins to weep and lose volume within 20–30 minutes if left standing.

Always bake fully before serving; raw French meringue is not a finished product.

**Chef's notes:** adding the sugar too fast is the main failure — dumped in all at once it never fully dissolves, and the meringue weeps syrup and deflates in the oven instead of drying out.

ingredients.name: cream of tartar
ingredients.notes: or a few drops lemon juice

name: Praliné y gianduja
tagline: Caramelised hazelnuts ground to a paste, then folded with chocolate to become gianduja.
story: Praliné is hazelnuts and sugar taken past caramel and ground until the oils release into a paste — the base flavouring for fillings, ice creams and bonbon centres. Fold in melted milk chocolate and cocoa butter while it's still warm and the same batch becomes gianduja, the moulded Piedmontese paste that needs nothing else to be a finished bonbon.
method:
1. Toast the hazelnuts and almonds at 160°C for 12–15 minutes until deep golden under the skin; keep warm.
2. Make a dry caramel with the sugar in a wide pan over medium heat, swirling rather than stirring, until deep amber (170–175°C).
3. Pour the caramel over the warm nuts on a lined tray, spread out, and let cool completely and harden (about 30 minutes).
4. Break into pieces and blitz in a food processor — first to a coarse sand, then keep processing in bursts, letting the machine rest so it doesn't overheat, until it turns into a smooth, pourable paste as the nuts release their oil. Add the salt.
5. Praliné is finished here: pass through a fine sieve for a very smooth product, or leave as is; store airtight at room temperature up to 3 months.
6. For gianduja, melt the milk chocolate and cocoa butter together to 40°C and fold into 500g of the still-warm (around 30°C) praliné until fully homogeneous. Pour into moulds or a lined tray and set at cool room temperature or in the fridge until firm.

**Chef's notes:** stopping the processor too early, at a coarse cookie-butter stage rather than pushing on until it turns fully liquid, is the most common fault — the nuts need to release their oil completely or the paste stays grainy and never sets cleanly as gianduja.

name: Caramelo de mantequilla salada
tagline: Dry caramel finished with salted butter and cream — the Breton sauce that goes on everything.
story: Caramel au beurre salé is Brittany's contribution to the pastry section: a dark caramel stopped with hot cream and good salted butter, used as a sauce, a filling for tarts and choux, or folded into ice cream. The margin between right and burnt is measured in seconds, not minutes.
method:
1. Warm the cream separately, almost to a boil, to avoid a cold-cream shock later; keep it hot.
2. In a heavy, wide pot, melt the sugar in stages — sprinkle, let it melt, sprinkle more — over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pot only, until it is a deep amber caramel at around 180°C, just short of smoking.
3. Off the heat, carefully whisk in the hot cream in a thin stream — it will bubble violently — until smooth.
4. Return briefly to low heat, stirring to dissolve any hardened sugar lumps, then remove from the heat.
5. Cool to about 60°C and whisk in the diced salted butter until glossy and fully emulsified.
6. Pass through a fine sieve if any lumps remain. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate in a sealed jar.

Holds 3 weeks refrigerated; rewarm gently to pour.

**Chef's notes:** the caramel keeps darkening for a few seconds after it comes off the heat from residual heat in the pot — stop a shade lighter than the final colour you want, especially the first few times, since a genuinely burnt caramel cannot be saved by adding cream.

name: Frangipane
tagline: Almond cream lightened with crème pâtissière — the raw filling that bakes into a tart's centre.
story: Frangipane is crème d'amande — butter, sugar, almond flour and egg beaten together — cut with crème pâtissière so it bakes soft rather than dense. It goes raw into a tart shell and bakes with it, which is what gives a galette des rois or a pear tart its moist, almond-rich centre instead of a dry paste.
method:
1. Cream the softened butter and sugar together until pale and smooth — do not overwhip to the point of aerating heavily, or the frangipane puffs and cracks in the oven.
2. Add the eggs one at a time, beating in fully between each addition.
3. Fold in the almond flour until just combined.
4. Stir in the rum.
5. Fold in the cold crème pâtissière in two additions until smooth and homogeneous.

Use at once to fill raw tart shells (spread or pipe 1.5–2cm deep) and bake at 180°C for 25–35 minutes depending on the tart, until golden and set with a slight give in the centre. Unbaked, it holds refrigerated 3 days or piped into portions and frozen up to 2 months — bake straight from frozen, adding 5–8 minutes.

**Chef's notes:** the crème pâtissière has to be properly cold when folded in, or the butter in the almond cream softens too far and the mixture splits — fix a split frangipane by folding in a spoonful more cold almond flour, not by beating harder.

name: Streusel / crumble
tagline: Cold butter rubbed into flour, sugar and ground almonds — a crisp topping baked separately from the fruit.
story: Streusel and crumble are the same idea by two names: cold fat rubbed roughly into flour and sugar so it bakes into crisp, uneven clumps rather than a smooth crust. Baking it separately on a tray, rather than only on top of a fruit dish, keeps it genuinely crisp — added to a tart or clafoutis-style bake at the pass rather than going soft under fruit juice in the oven.
method:
1. Dice the cold butter small and keep it cold until the last moment.
2. Combine the flour, sugar, ground almonds and salt in a bowl.
3. Rub the butter in by hand, or on low speed with a paddle attachment, only until it forms uneven pea-sized clumps — do not work it to a fine, sandy crumb, or it bakes flat and biscuit-like instead of textured.
4. Spread loosely on a lined tray and chill 30 minutes.
5. Bake at 170°C for 15–18 minutes, stirring once at the halfway point to break up any large clumps and colour it evenly, until golden throughout.
6. Cool completely on the tray before storing — it crisps further as it cools.

Store airtight at room temperature up to 2 weeks, or freeze the raw, unbaked mix up to 2 months and bake straight from frozen, adding a few minutes.

**Chef's notes:** overworking the butter into the flour is the one mistake that ruins it — the moment it starts to look like a smooth dough rather than clumps, it has gone too far and will bake dense rather than crisp.

name: Sablé breton
tagline: A rich, salted Breton butter biscuit baked in rings — sandy and short, not crunchy.
story: Sablé breton takes its name from 'sableux' — sandy — the texture it should shatter into, thanks to a high butter and yolk content and minimal gluten development. Baked in rings so it holds a clean disc shape, it is the base for a fraisier, a plated tart base, or served plain as a petit four.
method:
1. Cream the softened butter and sugar together until pale and fluffy.
2. Add the egg yolks one at a time, beating well between each addition.
3. Sift the flour, baking powder and fleur de sel together and fold in on low speed, just until the dough comes together — stop as soon as no dry flour remains.
4. Wrap and rest the dough in the fridge at least 1 hour, or overnight.
5. Roll to 1cm thick, cut into rounds, and set inside buttered rings on a lined tray.
6. Bake at 170°C for 15–18 minutes until the edges are golden and the centre is set but still pale.
7. Cool in the rings for 5 minutes before unmoulding onto a rack.

Store airtight at room temperature up to 1 week, or freeze raw discs, well wrapped, up to 2 months.

**Chef's notes:** overworking the dough once the flour goes in builds gluten and turns a sablé, which should shatter, into a tough biscuit — mix only until it holds together, no further.

name: Pain de Gênes
tagline: An almond-paste sponge whipped to full volume — denser and more moist than a genoise.
story: Pain de Gênes is built from almond paste rather than ground almonds, whipped with whole eggs until it triples before the flour goes in, which gives it a close, moist crumb that keeps well — better suited to a plated base that needs to survive a day or two than a genoise does.
method:
1. Warm the almond paste briefly (a few seconds in the microwave, or over a bain-marie) to soften it, then beat in a stand mixer with a little of the egg and the sugar until smooth with no lumps.
2. Add the remaining eggs gradually, whipping on high speed, until the mixture triples in volume and falls in a thick, pale ribbon (about 10 minutes).
3. Sift the flour, cornstarch and baking powder together and fold in gently in two additions.
4. Temper the melted butter with a spoonful of the batter, then fold it in in three additions down the side of the bowl.
5. Pour into a buttered and lined 20cm mould and bake at 165°C for 30–35 minutes, until a skewer comes out clean and the centre springs back to a light touch.
6. Cool 10 minutes in the tin, then turn out onto a rack.

Holds wrapped at room temperature 3 days, or freeze whole, well wrapped, up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** folding in the melted butter too quickly deflates all the volume just built — drizzle it down the side of the bowl and fold in gently over three additions, never all at once.

name: Genoise
tagline: Whole eggs and sugar whipped warm over a bain-marie — the plain sponge that soaks well for layer cakes.
story: Genoise is the workhorse layer sponge: whipped with no chemical raising agent, its lift comes entirely from air beaten in while the eggs are warm. It is drier and plainer than a butter cake by design, meant to be brushed with syrup and layered rather than eaten alone.
method:
1. Whisk the eggs and sugar together in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of simmering water (not touching the water) until warm, about 45°C, and the sugar has dissolved.
2. Transfer to a stand mixer and whip on high speed until tripled in volume, pale and thick enough to hold a ribbon trail for a few seconds (8–10 minutes).
3. Sift the flour over the mixture in three additions, folding gently each time to keep the volume.
4. Temper the melted butter with a spoonful of batter, then fold it in gently.
5. Pour into a buttered and lined tin and bake at 180°C for 20–25 minutes, until it springs back to a light touch and the edges pull slightly from the tin.
6. Cool on a rack for 10 minutes, then unmould.

Holds wrapped at room temperature 3 days, or freeze whole up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** the bain-marie stage is what gives genoise its lift without any raising agent — skip it and whip the eggs cold, and the sponge stays dense no matter how long it's whipped.

name: Joconde sponge
tagline: A thin almond sponge lightened with a separate meringue — flexible enough to roll, thin enough to layer.
story: Joconde is baked thin, almost like a flexible sheet rather than a cake, so it can wrap around a mousse in a roulade or stack into fine, even layers in an entremet without adding bulk. The almond flour gives it flavour and moisture that a plain sponge cannot match at that thickness.
method:
1. In a stand mixer, whisk the almond flour, icing sugar and whole eggs together on high speed until pale and tripled in volume, about 5 minutes.
2. Sift the flour over and fold in gently.
3. Fold in the melted butter.
4. In a separate clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, add the sugar gradually, and whip to a stiff, glossy meringue.
5. Fold the meringue into the almond batter in two additions, keeping as much air as possible.
6. Spread thinly (3–4mm) onto lined sheet trays with an offset spatula.
7. Bake at 220°C for 6–8 minutes, until lightly golden and springing back to a light touch.
8. Cool covered with a clean cloth to keep it flexible if it needs to roll; otherwise cool uncovered and trim to size for layering.

Wrap and refrigerate up to 2 days, or freeze between sheets of paper up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** bake it a shade underdone rather than fully coloured if it has to roll — an overbaked joconde cracks the moment it's curved.

name: Dacquoise
tagline: A nut meringue, crisp outside and soft within — the layer that gives an entremet its bite.
story: Dacquoise is a French meringue folded with ground nuts instead of left plain, baked to a crisp shell with a soft, chewy centre. It gives a mousse cake the structural layer and textural contrast that a plain sponge or biscuit base can't — the point where a bite stops being all cream.
method:
1. Whip the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually add the sugar, whipping to a stiff, glossy French meringue.
2. Sift together the ground almonds, ground hazelnuts, icing sugar and cornstarch.
3. Fold the nut mixture into the meringue in two additions, cutting and turning gently to keep as much air as possible.
4. Pipe or spread into discs or sheets on lined trays; dust the surface with extra icing sugar for a crackled finish.
5. Bake at 160°C for 18–22 minutes, until pale golden and firm to the touch but still a little tender in the centre.
6. Cool completely on the tray before peeling off the paper.

Store airtight at room temperature up to 3 days — humidity softens it quickly — or freeze layered with paper up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** folding the nut mixture in too roughly is the usual fault — a dacquoise should stay light inside a crisp shell, not turn dense; fold only until no dry streaks remain.

name: Chiffon cake
tagline: Oil-based sponge that climbs an ungreased tube pan — as light as angel food, richer in flavour.
story: Chiffon cake uses oil instead of butter, so it stays soft and moist straight from the fridge, and relies on a whipped-egg-white lift climbing the ungreased sides of a tube pan, which is why it's baked and cooled upside down. It's a useful base wherever a very light, neutral sponge is needed under fruit or cream.
method:
1. Whisk the flour, half the sugar, baking powder and salt together in a bowl.
2. Whisk in the oil, egg yolks, water and vanilla until smooth.
3. In a separate clean bowl, whip the egg whites with the cream of tartar to soft peaks, then gradually add the remaining sugar and whip to a stiff, glossy peak.
4. Fold the whites into the yolk batter in three additions, keeping as much air as possible.
5. Pour into an ungreased tube pan — the batter needs to grip the sides to climb.
6. Bake at 165°C for 40–45 minutes, until it springs back to a light touch and a skewer comes out clean.
7. Invert the pan immediately (over its feet, or hung on a bottle neck) and cool completely upside down before unmoulding, to stop it collapsing.

Holds wrapped at room temperature 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** greasing the pan is the classic mistake — the batter needs to cling to the sides while it climbs during baking, and a greased pan lets it slide back down and sink as it cools.

name: Tuile de almendra
tagline: Thin almond batter baked to lace, shaped while still hot — a crisp, decorative finish.
story: A tuile is baked flat and thin, then shaped in the few seconds it's still pliable off the tray, before it sets crisp as it cools — the name comes from the curved roof-tile shape it takes over a rolling pin. It gives height and crunch to a plated dessert without adding any real weight to the plate.
method:
1. Whisk the icing sugar and egg whites together until smooth — no need to whip to a foam.
2. Whisk in the melted butter, then the sifted flour, until a smooth, pourable batter forms.
3. Fold in the flaked almonds.
4. Spread thin circles (a spoonful, smoothed flat with the back of a spoon, or through a stencil) onto silicone baking mats, spacing them well apart.
5. Bake at 170°C for 6–8 minutes, until the edges are deep golden and the centre is pale gold.
6. Working fast while still hot, lift each tuile with a palette knife and drape it over a rolling pin, or press into a mould, to shape — they set crisp within seconds as they cool.

Store airtight with a food-safe desiccant sachet up to 5 days; they soften within minutes in any humidity.

**Chef's notes:** shaping has to happen in the first 10–15 seconds out of the oven — keep the rolling pin right beside the oven door and bake one tray at a time until the timing is second nature.

name: Base de almíbar para sorbete
tagline: A stock sugar syrup measured to 30° Baumé — diluted with fruit purée to build any sorbet.
story: Rather than weighing sugar fresh for every sorbet, the section keeps a concentrated stock syrup measured precisely to 30° Baumé with a hydrometer, then dilutes it with fruit purée and lemon juice to hit the right final density for each fruit — usually 14–18° Baumé depending on the fruit's own sugar and acid. One correctly measured base keeps every sorbet consistent from batch to batch.
method:
1. Combine the water, sugar and glucose syrup in a pot and bring to a boil, stirring until fully dissolved.
2. Simmer for 2 minutes, skimming any scum from the surface.
3. Cool to 20°C — density readings are only accurate at this temperature.
4. Pour into a tall, narrow container and float a Baumé hydrometer in it; read the scale at eye level where the syrup surface meets the stem.
5. Adjust: if the reading is above 30°B, add a little water and re-check; if below, return to the heat, reduce briefly, cool and re-check.
6. Once at exactly 30°B, store in sealed containers.

Refrigerate up to 1 month. This is a base, not a finished product — blend with fruit purée and a little lemon juice, then re-check the Baumé of the finished mix before freezing (churn once the mix is fully chilled to below 4°C).

**Chef's notes:** always read the hydrometer with the syrup at 20°C — a hot or cold reading gives a false density, and every sorbet built from a mis-measured base comes out either icy and hard or soft and never quite freezing properly, regardless of how careful the rest of the recipe is.

name: Masa y relleno de cannoli
tagline: Fried Sicilian shells wrapped around a well-drained sweet ricotta filling, piped only to order.
story: Cannoli fail for one reason more than any other: wet ricotta. Properly drained overnight, beaten smooth with sugar and studded with candied peel and chocolate, the filling stays firm inside a fried shell that must itself stay bone dry until the moment it's piped, or the whole point of the contrast — crisp shell, soft filling — is lost within minutes.
method:
