1. Dough: mix the flour, sugar, cocoa powder and salt; rub in the lard or butter until sandy. Add the Marsala and vinegar and bring together into a firm dough; knead 5 minutes until smooth. Wrap and rest in the fridge at least 1 hour, up to overnight.
2. Roll the dough thin (about 2mm, pasta machine setting 5–6) and cut into 10cm rounds.
3. Wrap each round around a greased metal cannoli tube, sealing the overlap with a little beaten egg.
4. Fry in oil at 180°C for 2–3 minutes, turning, until deep golden and blistered.
5. Drain on paper, cool completely, then carefully slide the shells off the tubes. Store airtight at room temperature up to 5 days — any humidity softens them.
6. Filling: drain the ricotta overnight in a cheesecloth-lined sieve over a bowl in the fridge — this step is not optional. Beat the drained ricotta with the icing sugar until smooth, then fold in the candied orange peel and chocolate chips. Refrigerate.
7. Pipe the filling into the shells only at the moment of service.

Filled cannoli lose their crunch within 15–20 minutes; keep shells and filling separate until then.

**Chef's notes:** an unrushed overnight drain on the ricotta is what separates a cannolo that shatters from one that goes soggy from the inside before it reaches the table — do not shortcut it with a quick squeeze.

name: Macarons
tagline: Italian-method shells, built on a hot-sugar meringue for a stable batter and a consistent foot.
story: The Italian method — folding almond paste into a meringue that's already been cooked with hot sugar syrup — gives a sturdier, more forgiving batter than the French method, which is why most professional kitchens use it for volume. The whole recipe comes down to macaronage: knowing exactly when to stop folding.
method:
1. Sift the ground almonds and icing sugar together, or blitz briefly in a food processor, then mix with the first portion of egg whites to a thick, smooth paste (the 'tant pour tant').
2. Make an Italian meringue: cook the sugar and water to 118°C; meanwhile whip the second portion of egg whites to soft peaks. Pour the hot syrup in a thin, steady stream down the side of the bowl and whip to a glossy, stiff, warm meringue.
3. Fold a third of the meringue into the almond paste to loosen it, then fold in the rest in two additions.
4. Macaronage: continue folding, pressing the batter against the side of the bowl, until it falls off the spatula in a slow, thick ribbon that dissolves back into the mass within about 20 seconds. Under-mixed batter peaks when piped; over-mixed spreads flat.
5. Pipe 3.5cm rounds onto lined trays and tap the trays firmly on the counter to release air bubbles.
6. Rest uncovered at room temperature 30–45 minutes until a dry skin forms — no batter should stick to a light touch.
7. Bake at 145–150°C for 13–15 minutes, one tray at a time, rotating halfway, until a defined foot has formed and the shells lift cleanly off the mat.
8. Cool completely before peeling off. Sandwich with ganache, praliné or crème diplomate.

Unfilled shells freeze well up to 1 month; filled macarons mature best 24 hours refrigerated before serving and hold 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** macaronage is judged by eye and feel, not a fold count — stop the moment the batter ribbons and settles back in 20 seconds, since the difference between a clean shell and a cracked, hollow or footless one usually comes down to a handful of folds either way.

name: Brownie
tagline: Dense, fudgy chocolate tray bake — pulled from the oven before the skewer comes out clean.
story: A brownie is judged entirely by the bake: pulled early it stays fudgy, pushed to a clean skewer it turns dry and cakey. Walnuts add crunch but are optional; the chocolate-to-butter ratio and the underbake are what actually define it.
method:
1. Melt the chocolate and butter together gently, over a bain-marie or in short bursts in the microwave, stirring until smooth.
2. Whisk in the sugar.
3. Whisk in the eggs one at a time until the mixture is glossy and slightly thickened.
4. Sift the flour, cocoa powder and salt over and fold in just until no dry streaks remain.
5. Fold in the walnuts if using.
6. Pour into a lined tray and bake at 175°C for 22–25 minutes, until a crust has formed on top and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out with a few moist crumbs clinging to it — not wet batter, and not clean.
7. Cool completely in the tin before cutting; cutting warm crumbles the edges.

Store airtight at room temperature up to 4 days, or freeze cut squares up to 2 months.

**Chef's notes:** pull it for moist crumbs, never a clean skewer — a brownie keeps cooking in its own residual tray heat, and a clean skewer at the oven already means a dry, cakey brownie once it's cooled.

name: Pavlova
tagline: A slow-baked meringue shell, crisp outside and marshmallow-soft within, filled only at the last moment.
story: The vinegar and cornstarch folded into the meringue at the end are what give pavlova its signature contrast — a crisp shell over a soft, marshmallow centre — rather than a meringue that dries all the way through. It is assembled with cream and fruit at the very last moment, since it collapses within the hour once filled.
method:
1. Whip the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually add the sugar, whipping to a stiff, glossy meringue — rub a little between your fingers to check the sugar has fully dissolved.
2. Gently fold in the cornstarch, vinegar and vanilla at the end, keeping as much air as possible.
3. Shape into a 20cm disc on a lined tray, building the edges slightly higher than the centre.
4. Bake at 120°C for 70–75 minutes, until the outside is dry and pale ivory.
5. Turn the oven off and leave the pavlova inside to cool completely with the door ajar, about 1 hour — this prevents cracking and collapse.
6. Top with whipped Chantilly and fresh fruit only immediately before serving.

The baked, unfilled shell holds in an airtight container at room temperature 2 days. Assembled, serve within the hour — fruit juice and humidity collapse it fast.

**Chef's notes:** the vinegar and cornstarch are not optional flourishes — leave either out and the meringue dries through completely instead of keeping the soft marshmallow centre that makes it a pavlova.

name: Tiramisù
tagline: Mascarpone lightened with a cooked sabayon and meringue, layered with coffee-dipped ladyfingers.
story: Cooking the yolks briefly over a bain-marie before folding in the mascarpone gives tiramisù a stable, safely cooked base without losing the light, mousse-like texture the dish depends on. It needs a genuine rest — a minimum of six hours — for the layers to settle into clean slices rather than sliding apart.
method:
1. Whisk the egg yolks with half the sugar over a bain-marie, whisking constantly, until it reaches 70°C, thickens and turns pale and ribbony. Remove from the heat and let cool slightly.
2. Whisk the mascarpone into the cooled yolk mixture until completely smooth.
3. In a separate clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, gradually add the remaining sugar, and whip to a stiff meringue. Fold into the mascarpone mixture in two additions.
4. Combine the cooled espresso and coffee liqueur in a shallow dish. Dip each ladyfinger briefly — about a second per side, not a soak — and lay in a single layer in a dish.
5. Spread half the mascarpone cream over the biscuits, add a second layer of dipped ladyfingers, then the remaining cream, smoothing the top.
6. Refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
7. Dust generously with cocoa powder just before serving.

Holds refrigerated, covered, up to 2 days.

**Chef's notes:** dip the biscuits fast — a full soak turns them to mush and the layers slide apart on the cut instead of holding a clean line; the coffee should flavour the biscuit, not drown it.

name: Panna cotta
tagline: Sweetened cream set with just enough gelatin to hold a gentle wobble, never a rubbery disc.
story: Panna cotta means 'cooked cream,' not boiled cream — the whole dish is a demonstration of restraint, gently warmed and barely set, so a spoon meets the same softness a good crème anglaise would give if it could hold its own shape.
method:
1. Bloom the gelatin sheets in cold water for 5 minutes.
2. Split the vanilla pod, scrape the seeds, and heat the cream, milk, sugar, seeds and pod together to just below a boil.
3. Remove from the heat, discard the pod, squeeze out the gelatin and whisk it into the warm mixture until fully dissolved.
4. Strain through a fine sieve.
5. Pour into moulds or serving glasses and cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 4 hours until set — it should hold a gentle, even wobble, not sit liquid or turn rubbery.
6. To unmould, dip the mould briefly in warm water and invert onto a plate.

Holds refrigerated, covered, up to 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** treat the heat gently and stop well short of a boil — pushing it too hot skins the surface and can weaken the final set, giving a grainy top rather than the clean, glossy wobble panna cotta should have.

name: Zabaglione
tagline: Yolks, sugar and Marsala whisked over gentle heat to a warm, airy foam — served the moment it's ready.
story: Zabaglione is one of the few desserts with no shelf life at all: whisked continuously over a bain-marie until it triples in volume, it has to reach the table within minutes of coming off the heat, poured warm over fruit or biscuits or served alone in a glass.
method:
1. Combine the egg yolks, sugar and Marsala in a heatproof bowl, or a copper zabaglione pot if the kitchen has one.
2. Set over a pan of gently simmering water, bowl not touching the water.
3. Whisk constantly and vigorously — this is not a mixture that can be left to sit even briefly — until it triples in volume, turns pale and holds a thick, foamy ribbon, about 8–10 minutes. It should never exceed about 70°C; test by feel, it will coat the whisk thickly.
4. Pour into warmed glasses and serve immediately, alone or over fruit or biscuits.

Zabaglione does not hold, refrigerate or reheat — make it to order.

**Chef's notes:** it has to reach the table the moment it's made — zabaglione has no structure to hold once it starts to cool, and there is no saving a batch that has been left waiting even ten minutes.

name: Semifreddo
tagline: A frozen mousse built on a cooked pâte à bombe — soft enough to cut cleanly straight from the freezer.
story: Semifreddo gets its churn-free softness from a pâte à bombe base — yolks whipped with a hot sugar syrup until cold and thick — folded with whipped cream so no ice cream machine is needed. It freezes to a texture between mousse and ice cream, sliceable straight from the mould.
method:
1. Cook the sugar and water to 121°C.
2. Meanwhile whip the egg yolks to pale in a stand mixer. Once the syrup is ready, pour it in a thin, steady stream down the side of the bowl, whipping continuously, then keep whipping until the mixture triples, thickens and cools fully to room temperature, about 10 minutes.
3. Whip the cream to soft peaks.
4. Fold the whipped cream into the cooled pâte à bombe in stages, along with the vanilla and praliné if using, keeping as much air as possible.
5. Pour into lined moulds or a terrine and freeze at least 6 hours, ideally overnight, at –18°C.
6. To unmould, dip briefly in warm water or wrap with a hot towel; slice with a knife run under hot water and wiped dry between cuts.

Holds frozen, well wrapped, up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** the pâte à bombe must be fully cooled before the cream goes in — folded in warm, the cream deflates on contact and the semifreddo freezes hard and icy instead of staying soft-set.

name: Crema catalana
tagline: Cinnamon-and-citrus custard, thickened on the stove and finished under the torch at the last minute.
story: Crema catalana is a stovetop custard, not a baked one, infused with cinnamon and citrus zest and thickened with cornstarch and yolks until it holds its own shape in a shallow dish. The brittle sugar crust is a last-second finish, not part of the make — torched too early it turns to syrup on the cold custard.
method:
1. Heat the milk, cream, cinnamon stick and citrus zests to just below a boil, then remove from the heat and let steep for 15 minutes. Strain and discard the aromatics.
2. Whisk the egg yolks, half the sugar and the cornstarch together until pale.
3. Temper the hot infused milk into the yolk mixture, then return everything to the pot.
4. Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly, until thickened to a custard that coats a spoon thickly — a touch thicker than a crème anglaise.
5. Pour into shallow terracotta dishes (cazuelas) and cool, then refrigerate at least 4 hours.
6. Just before serving, sprinkle a thin, even layer of the remaining sugar over the top and caramelise with a blowtorch until deep amber and brittle.

Refrigerate the un-torched custard up to 3 days; torch each portion to order.

**Chef's notes:** torch it only at the pass, never ahead of time — the crisp sugar crust weeps into syrup within 10–15 minutes sitting on the cold custard underneath.

name: Flan de queso
tagline: Cream cheese flan baked in a water bath over a hard caramel — pulled while the centre still trembles.
story: Where a plain flan de huevo relies only on eggs and milk to set, flan de queso folds in cream cheese for a denser, richer curd closer to a baked cheesecake, still built over the same hard caramel base. It has to come out of the oven while the centre is still visibly unset, since the water bath keeps finishing the custard for several minutes afterward.
method:
1. Make a caramel with the sugar and water, cooking to a deep amber, and pour immediately into the base of the mould, tilting to coat the bottom evenly. Let it harden.
2. Blend the cream cheese, condensed milk, evaporated milk, eggs and vanilla together until completely smooth, with no lumps of cheese remaining.
3. Pour the mixture over the hardened caramel.
4. Cover the mould with foil and bake in a bain-marie at 160°C for 45–55 minutes, until just set with a gentle wobble left in the centre — a skewer near the middle should come out mostly clean, not fully clean.
5. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
6. Run a knife around the edge and invert onto a plate with a lip, to catch the caramel sauce as it releases.

Holds refrigerated, covered, up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** pull it while the centre still wobbles — residual heat in the water bath keeps setting the custard for several more minutes, and a fully firm centre at the oven door means a rubbery, weeping flan once it's cold.

name: Tarta de Santiago
tagline: A Galician almond cake with no flour at all, finished with the stencilled Cross of Saint James in sugar.
story: Tarta de Santiago has no flour — the crumb comes entirely from ground almonds, eggs and sugar, which is what keeps it moist for days rather than drying out like a sponge. The stencilled cross on top is the traditional marker of the dish, dusted on only once the cake has cooled fully.
method:
1. Whisk the eggs and sugar together until pale and slightly thickened — no need for full ribbon stage.
2. Stir in the ground almonds, lemon zest and cinnamon until you have a smooth, thick batter.
3. Pour into a buttered 24cm tin (traditionally baked with no pastry base).
4. Bake at 170°C for 30–35 minutes, until golden on top, set, and a skewer comes out clean — the crumb should stay moist from the almonds even when fully baked.
5. Cool completely in the tin, then turn out.
6. Lay a Cross of Saint James stencil on top and dust generously with icing sugar; lift the stencil straight up and away.

Holds wrapped at room temperature up to 4 days — the flavour actually improves after the first day as the almond settles.

**Chef's notes:** dust the stencil only once the cake is completely cool — any residual warmth melts the icing sugar into the surface instead of leaving a crisp white cross.

name: Flaó ibicenco
tagline: Ibiza's fresh-cheese tart, defined by raw spearmint and aniseed — nothing like a plain cheesecake.
story: Flaó is often described to outsiders as an Ibizan cheesecake, which undersells it: the identity of the dish is fresh hierbabuena (spearmint) and ground matalahúva (aniseed) folded raw into a fresh cheese filling, baked in a lard-and-anís pastry shell. Leave out the fresh mint or substitute dried, and it stops tasting like Ibiza and just tastes like a plain baked cheese tart.
method:
1. Pastry: rub the lard into the flour with the sugar and salt until sandy. Add the anís liqueur and water and bring together into a smooth dough. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.
2. Roll the dough thin and line a 24–26cm shallow tart mould; trim the edges and chill 20 minutes.
3. Filling: press any excess whey out of the fresh cheese, then whisk it with the eggs and sugar until well combined — a little texture from the cheese is traditional, it does not need to be perfectly smooth.
4. Stir in the finely chopped fresh spearmint and ground aniseed, and the lemon zest if using, at this last stage, raw.
5. Pour the filling into the lined case.
6. Bake at 180°C for 40–45 minutes, until the top is golden and puffed and the centre has a gentle set wobble — it will deflate slightly as it cools, which is normal.
7. Cool to room temperature before slicing; flaó is traditionally served just warm or at room temperature, not served cold, so the mint stays fragrant.

Holds at room temperature or refrigerated up to 2 days — the mint aroma fades noticeably by day three.

**Chef's notes:** the defining flavour is fresh hierbabuena, never dried mint or extract, and it must go in raw and chopped at the very end — cooking it any earlier flattens the aroma that makes flaó taste of Ibiza rather than a plain cheesecake.

ingredients.name: fresh Ibizan cheese
ingredients.notes: fresh sheep's or goat's cheese, whey pressed out

name: Greixonera
tagline: Ibiza's bread pudding, built on stale ensaïmada soaked in cinnamon milk — named after the dish it's baked in.
story: Greixonera exists to use up stale ensaïmada rather than throw it out — torn, soaked in cinnamon-and-citrus milk, bound with egg and baked in the earthenware dish that gives it its name. It should keep visible pockets of soft bread rather than blend into a smooth custard.
method:
1. Tear the stale ensaïmada into rough pieces into a bowl.
2. Heat the milk with the cinnamon stick and lemon zest to just below a boil, then let cool slightly.
3. Pour the warm milk over the bread and let it soak 20 minutes, until fully softened. Remove the cinnamon stick and zest.
4. Whisk in the eggs and most of the sugar until combined — the mixture should stay lumpy with bread, not blend smooth.
5. Pour into a buttered earthenware dish and sprinkle the remaining sugar over the top.
6. Bake at 180°C for 20–25 minutes, until puffed, golden and just set with a slight wobble in the centre — or finish the last few minutes under a hot grill for a caramelised top.
7. Dust with ground cinnamon and serve warm or at room temperature.

Holds refrigerated up to 2 days; reheat briefly before serving.

**Chef's notes:** greixonera should keep texture from the bread, not turn into a smooth flan — resist over-soaking or blending it, since the contrast between soft custard and pockets of bread is the point of the dish.

name: Orelletes
tagline: Ibizan anís fritters rolled paper-thin so they blister into a light, crisp lace when fried.
story: Orelletes take their name from their thin, almost translucent shape once rolled and fried — traditionally made for local festivities. The whole dish depends on rolling the dough far thinner than instinct suggests, so it bubbles into a crisp lace rather than frying heavy in the middle.
method:
1. Combine the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and ground aniseed in a bowl.
2. Whisk the eggs, olive oil, anís liqueur and orange zest together, then work into the dry ingredients to form a smooth, firm dough. Knead briefly until elastic, wrap and rest 30 minutes.
3. Roll the dough very thin — 1–2mm, almost translucent — on a pasta machine or by hand, and cut into 10cm rounds or ovals.
4. Fry in batches in oil at 175°C for 1–2 minutes per side, until pale golden and blistered, keeping the batches small so the oil temperature doesn't drop.
5. Drain on paper and dust generously with sugar while still warm.

Store airtight at room temperature up to 1 week — they crisp further as they dry.

**Chef's notes:** roll the dough thinner than feels right — orelletes should bubble and blister into a light, crisp lace when fried; rolled too thick, they fry heavy and doughy in the centre.

name: Financiers
tagline: Small almond cakes built on browned butter, named for their traditional gold-bar mould shape.
story: The whole point of a financier is the beurre noisette — butter cooked past melted into nutty and brown — folded into an almond and egg-white batter with no yolks at all. A rest overnight before baking noticeably improves the dome and the crumb.
method:
1. Make a beurre noisette: melt the butter over medium heat until it foams, then turns deep amber-brown with a nutty smell — watch it closely, as it goes from perfect to burnt in seconds. Strain through a fine sieve to remove the dark solids and cool slightly.
2. Whisk the egg whites lightly, just to loosen — no need to whip.
3. Whisk in the icing sugar, ground almonds, sifted flour and baking powder until smooth.
4. Whisk in the honey, then the warm (not hot) brown butter in a steady stream.
5. Cover and rest the batter in the fridge at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.
6. Pipe or pour into buttered financier moulds, filling three-quarters full.
7. Bake at 200°C for 15–18 minutes, until golden brown at the edges and springy on top.
8. Unmould while still warm onto a rack.

Holds airtight at room temperature up to 3 days, or freeze baked and cooled up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** the beurre noisette is the entire point of a financier — stop it the moment it smells nutty and turns amber, since a few seconds more burns the milk solids bitter and ruins the whole batch.

name: Madeleines
tagline: Small shell-shaped sponges that hump in the oven only when the batter goes in properly cold.
story: A madeleine's signature hump is thermal shock — cold, rested batter dropped into hot buttered moulds in a hot oven. Skip the rest or let the batter warm up and they bake flat, still tasting fine but missing the point of the shape.
method:
1. Whisk the eggs, sugar and honey together until pale and slightly thickened.
2. Sift the flour and baking powder over and fold in.
3. Fold in the melted (slightly cooled) butter and the lemon zest until smooth.
4. Cover and refrigerate at least 2 hours, ideally overnight — this rest is what gives the characteristic hump.
5. Butter and flour the madeleine moulds well, or use a well-seasoned non-stick tray, and chill them.
6. Pipe or spoon the cold batter into the moulds, filling two-thirds full.
7. Bake at 220°C for 4 minutes, then reduce the oven to 180°C and bake a further 6–8 minutes, until humped in the centre and golden at the edges.
8. Unmould immediately onto a rack.

Best eaten the day they're baked; holds airtight up to 2 days.

**Chef's notes:** the hump comes from cold batter meeting a hot mould and a hot oven — do not skip the rest or use a lukewarm batter, or the madeleines bake flat with no dome at all.

name: Mousse de chocolate
tagline: Melted chocolate lightened with whipped whites and cream — airy, not a set custard.
story: This is the classic French chocolate mousse: warm chocolate loosened with yolks, then lifted with whipped whites and finished with a little whipped cream for a finer, less eggy texture. The whole method depends on folding the whites into chocolate that is still warm enough to stay fluid.
method:
1. Melt the chocolate gently over a bain-marie to 45–50°C.
2. Off the heat, whisk in the egg yolks until smooth and glossy.
3. In a separate clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually add the sugar and whip to a stiff, glossy meringue.
4. In another bowl, whip the cream to soft peaks.
5. Fold a third of the meringue into the warm chocolate base to loosen it, then fold in the remaining meringue in two additions, keeping as much air as possible.
6. Fold in the whipped cream last, gently.
7. Spoon or pipe into glasses or moulds and refrigerate at least 3 hours before serving.

Holds refrigerated, covered, up to 2 days.

**Chef's notes:** the chocolate base needs to stay warm and fluid, around 30–35°C, when the whites go in — a cooled, stiffened base seizes the instant cold meringue hits it, leaving the mousse grainy with unmixed chocolate flecks.

name: Lemon posset
tagline: Cream set by lemon acid alone — no gelatin, no eggs, just fat and citrus in the right ratio.
story: Posset sets purely on the interaction between the fat in cream and the acid in lemon juice, with no gelatin or eggs required at all — which makes it fast, but only works reliably at full-fat cream; anything lighter simply will not set.
method:
1. Combine the cream, sugar and lemon zest in a pot and bring to a gentle boil.
2. Simmer for 3 minutes, stirring, to infuse the zest and fully dissolve the sugar.
3. Remove from the heat and stir in the lemon juice.
4. Strain if a completely smooth texture is wanted (the zest can also be left in for texture).
5. Pour into serving glasses and cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 4 hours until set to a soft, spoonable custard.

Holds refrigerated up to 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** the set relies entirely on the fat-to-acid ratio — substitute a lower-fat cream and the posset will not set at all, no matter how long it chills.

name: Arroz con leche
tagline: Short-grain rice simmered slowly in cinnamon milk until creamy — needs constant attention near the end.
story: Arroz con leche is patience more than technique: rice simmered gently in milk infused with cinnamon and lemon, stirred often so it thickens evenly instead of catching on the bottom of the pot in the last stretch.
method:
1. Rinse the rice under cold water.
2. Combine the milk, cinnamon stick and lemon zest in a wide, heavy pot and bring to a gentle simmer.
3. Add the rice and cook over low heat, stirring frequently, for 35–40 minutes, until the rice is tender and the mixture has thickened to a creamy, still slightly loose consistency — it thickens further as it cools.
4. Stir in the sugar for the last 10 minutes of cooking (adding it earlier can slow the rice's cooking and toughen it slightly).
5. Remove the cinnamon stick and zest, and stir in the butter if using.
6. Pour into a shallow dish or individual bowls and dust with ground cinnamon.

Serve warm or chilled. Holds refrigerated up to 3 days; loosen with a splash of milk when reheating.

**Chef's notes:** keep the heat low and stir often — arroz con leche scorches easily on the bottom of the pot as it thickens in the final stretch, and a scorched pot flavours the whole batch.

name: Churros con chocolate
tagline: Piped fried dough, no egg needed, served with a thick drinking chocolate for dipping.
story: Spanish churro dough is simpler than it looks — water, flour, salt and a little butter, no egg — cooked briefly on the stove before piping directly into hot oil. The dipping chocolate is made thick, almost a sauce rather than a drink, specifically so it clings to the churro.
method:
1. Bring the water, butter, salt and sugar to a boil.
2. Off the heat, add the flour all at once and stir vigorously until it forms a smooth, thick dough that pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pot.
3. Let cool for 5 minutes, then transfer to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip.
4. Pipe lengths directly into oil at 180°C, cutting them off with scissors as they drop in.
5. Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden and crisp all over.
6. Drain briefly and toss immediately in the cinnamon sugar while still hot.
7. For the chocolate: heat the milk, whisk in the sugar and the cornstarch (mixed first with a splash of cold milk to avoid lumps), then whisk in the chopped chocolate over low heat until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
8. Serve the churros hot alongside the warm chocolate for dipping.

Churros lose their crunch within 15–20 minutes — fry to order rather than ahead.

**Chef's notes:** hold the oil at a steady 180°C, no hotter — churros dropped into oil that's too hot brown on the outside before the centre cooks through, leaving a raw, gummy core.

name: Clafoutis
tagline: A thin, custard-like batter baked over whole cherries — served just warm, never straight from the oven or fridge.
story: Clafoutis is closer to a baked crêpe batter than a cake — thin enough to pour, set just enough to hold its shape once cooled to warm. Traditionalists leave the pits in the cherries, which is said to add a faint bitter-almond note during baking.
method:
1. Butter a baking dish and arrange the cherries in a single layer.
2. Whisk the eggs and sugar together until pale.
3. Whisk in the flour, then gradually whisk in the milk, cream and vanilla until you have a smooth, thin, pourable batter.
4. Pour the batter over the cherries.
5. Bake at 180°C for 30–35 minutes, until puffed, golden and just set — a slight wobble in the centre is fine, it firms further as it cools.
6. Cool to just warm before dusting with icing sugar and serving; clafoutis is traditionally served neither hot nor fridge-cold.

Holds refrigerated up to 2 days; rewarm gently before serving.

**Chef's notes:** if serving the traditional way with pits left in, warn the table — it's intentional, said to add a faint almond note during baking, not an oversight.

name: Tarte Tatin
tagline: Apples cooked in caramel on the stove, topped with pastry and baked, then inverted at the table's pace, not the oven's.
story: Tarte Tatin is built upside down and finished by inversion, which means the whole dish depends on timing that flip correctly: too hot and the caramel floods the plate, too cold and the pastry tears against the set sugar.
method:
1. Peel, halve and core the apples.
2. In an ovenproof, heavy pan, melt the sugar dry over medium heat until it becomes a deep amber caramel, then whisk in the butter off the heat until smooth.
3. Arrange the apple halves tightly, rounded side down, packed into the caramel — they will shrink as they cook.
4. Cook over medium-low heat on the stovetop for 15–20 minutes, until the apples soften slightly and the caramel deepens, basting occasionally.
5. Roll the pastry into a circle slightly larger than the pan and lay it over the apples, tucking the edges down inside the rim.
6. Bake at 200°C for 25–30 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and well puffed.
7. Rest out of the oven for 5–10 minutes — this lets the caramel firm slightly so it doesn't all run out on inverting.
8. Place a plate over the pan and invert confidently in one motion.

Best made and served the same day, warm, ideally with crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream. Can be assembled a day ahead (apples in caramel, pastry on top, refrigerated) and baked to order.

**Chef's notes:** invert it while still warm, not straight from the oven and not fully cooled — hot caramel runs everywhere on the plate, while a cold tatin can stick and tear the pastry on release.

name: Tarte au chocolat
tagline: A dense chocolate ganache tart, baked at a low temperature just enough to set the egg without scrambling it.
story: This is closer to baking a ganache than baking a custard: the low oven temperature is what keeps the egg from scrambling inside the cream and chocolate, so the filling sets into a dense, clean-cutting slice rather than a grainy one.
method:
1. Blind bake the tart shell fully at 170°C until golden and cooked through; let cool completely.
2. Heat the cream and milk to just below a boil.
3. Pour over the chopped chocolate, let sit 30 seconds, then stir from the centre outward until smooth.
4. Whisk in the eggs and sugar until just combined — do not whisk in excess air.
5. Whisk in the softened butter.
6. Pour into the cooled tart shell.
7. Bake at 150°C for 12–15 minutes, until just set at the edges with a gentle wobble left in the centre; it should not puff or crack.
8. Cool to room temperature before slicing — the filling firms further as it cools, like a set ganache.

Holds refrigerated up to 3 days; bring to cool room temperature before serving for the best texture.

**Chef's notes:** this bakes at a much lower temperature than most tarts on purpose — pushed hotter, the egg scrambles inside the ganache and the filling turns grainy instead of setting into a dense, clean slice.

name: Basque cheesecake
tagline: Baked hot and fast with no water bath, deliberately burnished black on top and wobbling underneath.
story: Tarta de queso vasca inverts every normal cheesecake rule: no water bath, no low-and-slow bake, no fear of a dark top or a heavily wobbling centre — those are the goal, not signs it's gone wrong, and it firms fully only once cold.
method:
1. Line a springform tin generously with parchment, letting it rise well above the rim in loose, crumpled folds — this is what gives the classic rustic, burnt edge.
2. Beat the cream cheese and sugar together until smooth.
3. Add the eggs one at a time, beating in fully between each.
4. Add the cream, then the sifted flour and salt, mixing just until smooth — do not overbeat air into it.
5. Pour into the lined tin.
6. Bake at 220–230°C, with no water bath, for 40–45 minutes, until deeply burnished to near-black on top and the centre still wobbles significantly — this looks underdone, which is correct.
7. Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate at least 4 hours before unmoulding and slicing; it firms considerably as it chills.

Holds refrigerated up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** the burnt top and a heavily wobbling centre are the point, not a mistake — pull it while it still looks underdone, since it finishes setting entirely as it cools, and a cake that looks fully done at the oven door will be dry and overbaked once cold.

name: Kardemummabullar
tagline: Swedish cardamom-spiced yeasted buns, twisted and knotted, finished with pearl sugar.
story: Kardemummabullar depend on genuinely fresh-ground cardamom and on the butter being worked into the dough gradually rather than dumped in — rushed, it greases the gluten instead of laminating through it, and the bun bakes dense instead of light and pull-apart.
method:
1. Warm the milk to about 37°C and dissolve the yeast in it.
2. In a mixer, combine the flour, sugar, cardamom and salt. Add the milk-yeast mixture and the egg, mix to a shaggy dough, then knead on medium speed for 8–10 minutes.
3. Add the softened butter gradually, a little at a time, kneading until fully incorporated and the dough is smooth, elastic and passes a windowpane test.
4. Cover and proof in a warm place for 1–1.5 hours, until doubled.
5. Meanwhile, beat the filling butter with the sugar and spices to a soft, spreadable paste.
6. Roll the dough into a large rectangle (about 40x60cm) and spread the filling edge to edge.
7. Fold into thirds like a letter, roll lightly to seal, then cut into strips; twist each strip and knot into the classic bun shape.
8. Place on lined trays, cover, and proof a further 45–60 minutes until visibly puffy.
9. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with pearl sugar.
10. Bake at 200°C for 10–12 minutes, until deep golden.

Best the day they're baked; holds airtight up to 2 days, or freeze the baked buns up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** do not rush the butter into the dough — added too fast it greases the gluten instead of laminating into it, and the buns bake dense rather than showing the light, pull-apart layers a proper kardemummabulle should have.

name: Cinnamon roll
tagline: A yeasted dough rolled into a cinnamon-sugar log, sliced and baked, finished with cream cheese icing while warm.
story: Where kardemummabullar are twisted and knotted, this dough is rolled into a tight log and sliced into rounds, which is what gives it the visible spiral. Icing it while still warm lets the frosting melt slightly into the swirls instead of sitting as a hard cap.
method:
1. Warm the milk to about 37°C and dissolve the yeast in it.
2. Combine the flour, sugar and salt in a mixer; add the milk-yeast mixture and the egg, mix to a dough, then knead 8–10 minutes.
3. Add the softened butter gradually, kneading until smooth, elastic and fully incorporated.
4. Cover and proof in a warm place 1–1.5 hours, until doubled.
5. Beat the filling butter with the brown sugar and cinnamon to a spreadable paste.
6. Roll the dough into a large rectangle and spread the filling edge to edge.
7. Roll tightly into a log from the long edge and pinch the seam firmly to seal.
8. Slice into rounds about 4cm thick using a sharp serrated knife or a length of dental floss — do not press down with a blunt blade, it squashes the spiral flat.
9. Place cut-side up in a lined tray with space to expand, cover, and proof 30–45 minutes until puffy.
10. Bake at 190°C for 18–20 minutes, until golden.
11. Whisk the icing sugar, cream cheese and milk together until smooth, and spread over the rolls while still warm.

Holds airtight up to 2 days, or freeze sliced, unbaked rolls up to 1 month — proof fully after thawing before baking.

**Chef's notes:** seal the seam firmly and slice with a sawing motion, never a pressing cut — a squashed cut flattens the spiral and the rolls lose their defined swirl once baked.

name: Soufflé de chocolate
tagline: A chocolate base lightened with whipped whites and baked to order — timed to the minute, served the moment it's pulled.
story: A chocolate soufflé is really two separate jobs: a stable chocolate base that can be made ahead, and a meringue folded in at the last possible moment before baking. Everything about the recipe — the buttering, the flour in the base, the fold — exists only to get it to climb cleanly and hold for the seconds it takes to reach the table.
method:
1. Butter the ramekins thoroughly with upward strokes (this helps the soufflé climb rather than stick and stall), coat with sugar, tap out the excess, and chill.
2. Melt the chocolate and butter together gently.
3. Warm the milk, whisk in the flour to a smooth paste, and cook for 1–2 minutes to remove the raw flour taste.
4. Whisk this into the melted chocolate, then whisk in the egg yolks off the heat until smooth. This base can be made up to 4 hours ahead and held at room temperature.
5. When ready to bake, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, gradually add the sugar, and whip to a glossy, stiff (not dry) meringue.
6. Fold a third of the meringue into the chocolate base to loosen it, then fold in the rest in two additions, keeping as much air as possible.
7. Fill the ramekins to the top, level with a palette knife, and run a thumb around the inner rim to help it rise evenly.
8. Bake at 190°C for 12–14 minutes, until well risen with a slight wobble in the centre — do not open the oven door for the first 10 minutes.
9. Serve immediately.

A soufflé begins to fall within 60–90 seconds of leaving the oven — it must go straight to the table.

**Chef's notes:** the base has to be warm, not hot, when the whites are folded in — a hot base deflates the meringue on contact and the soufflé will not climb no matter how well it was whipped.

name: Espagnole
tagline: The classic brown mother sauce; the base every small brown sauce and demi-glace builds on.
story: Espagnole is the reason a kitchen keeps brown veal stock on hand at all. It is rarely served as itself — it is reduced further into demi-glace or finished into bordelaise, Robert, diable — but every one of those depends on this base being built correctly: a properly coloured roux, real brown stock, and a long, patient, well-skimmed simmer.
method:
1. Heat the oil in a heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrot and celery and sweat 8-10 minutes until soft but not coloured.
2. Stir in the flour and cook, stirring constantly, until the roux turns a light hazelnut brown, 8-10 minutes — this is what gives espagnole its colour and nutty flavour; do not let it catch or blacken.
3. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes to lose its raw acidity.
4. Gradually whisk in the hot brown veal stock, a ladle at a time, to avoid lumps. Bring to a gentle simmer.
5. Add the bouquet garni and crushed peppercorns. Simmer uncovered at a bare bubble for 3-4 hours, skimming fat and scum from the surface every 20-30 minutes.
6. Strain through a fine chinois, pressing lightly on the solids. The sauce should coat the back of a spoon lightly; if thin, reduce further.
7. Season with salt only at the end, since it will be reduced again in most applications.
Holding: cool quickly in an ice bath, refrigerate up to 4 days, or freeze flat in bags up to 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** the roux colour is the whole sauce — pale roux gives a flat, floury result, and a roux taken too dark turns bitter and thins the sauce's body. Cook it low and watch it, not the clock.

name: Béchamel
tagline: White mother sauce built from a blond roux and infused milk; the base for Mornay and soubise.
story: Béchamel is the fastest of the mother sauces to make and the one used most often, because it underlies gratins, Mornay, soubise and a dozen bound vegetable dishes. Getting it right is about patience with the roux and infusing the milk properly rather than rushing to a boil.
method:
1. Warm the milk with the onion clouté (onion studded with the clove, bay leaf tucked against it) over low heat until just below a simmer. Remove from heat and let infuse 10 minutes, then strain and keep warm.
2. Melt the butter in a heavy saucepan over low-medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook, whisking, for 3-4 minutes without colouring — this is a blond (white) roux.
3. Off the heat, whisk in the warm milk gradually, a third at a time, whisking out any lumps before adding more.
4. Return to low heat and cook, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and any raw flour taste is gone, 8-10 minutes.
5. Season with salt, white pepper and a light grating of nutmeg.
6. Pass through a fine sieve for a perfectly smooth finish if using for Mornay or a delicate gratin.
Holding: press cling film directly onto the surface to stop a skin forming; refrigerate up to 3 days. Reheat gently, whisking, adding a splash of milk if it has tightened.
**Chef's notes:** the roux must cook long enough to lose its raw-flour taste but not colour — colouring it turns this into a pale velouté-adjacent sauce, not béchamel.

name: Velouté
tagline: Blond roux thickened white stock; the mother sauce behind suprême and every white pan sauce.
story: Velouté is what separates a kitchen that makes real white sauces from one that only makes béchamel. Built from a good white stock rather than milk, it carries the flavour of whatever bird or fish that stock came from, and it is the base for suprême sauce, allemande and most veloutéd soups.
method:
1. Melt the butter in a heavy saucepan over medium-low heat. Whisk in the flour and cook 3-4 minutes, stirring, without colouring, to make a blond roux.
2. Off the heat, gradually whisk in the hot white stock, working out lumps as you go.
3. Return to the heat and bring to a gentle simmer, whisking. Cook 20-25 minutes at a bare simmer, skimming any scum that rises.
4. The sauce is ready when it coats the back of a spoon and no longer tastes of raw flour.
5. Season with salt and white pepper. Strain through a fine chinois for service.
Holding: cool and refrigerate up to 3 days with a film of cling on the surface, or freeze up to 2 months. Whisk in a little more hot stock when reheating if it has thickened too far.
**Chef's notes:** the stock must be good enough to drink on its own — a weak stock makes a weak velouté no amount of roux can fix. Use white chicken stock for chicken dishes, fish fumet for fish velouté; never mix stock types.

ingredients.name: white chicken stock
ingredients.notes: hot, or fish fumet for a fish velouté

name: Hollandaise
tagline: Warm egg-yolk and butter emulsion; the mother sauce behind béarnaise and every eggs Benedict.
story: Hollandaise is judged in seconds — it can split in the time it takes to answer a question. A kitchen keeps it on the pass for eggs, asparagus and poached fish because nothing else gives the same rich, barely-set texture, and every cook needs to be able to rebuild it fast when it breaks.
method:
1. Clarify the butter and keep warm (not hot) — around 60°C.
2. In a heatproof bowl, whisk the egg yolks with the water over a bain-marie of barely simmering water, off direct heat contact with the bowl base.
3. Whisk constantly until the yolks ribbon and thicken to a pale, mousse-like sabayon, 3-4 minutes. Do not let the bowl get hot enough to scramble the eggs — lift it off the heat periodically.
4. Remove from the heat. Whisking constantly, add the warm clarified butter in a very thin stream, building the emulsion the way you would a mayonnaise.
5. Once all the butter is incorporated, whisk in the lemon juice, a pinch of cayenne and salt to taste.
6. Adjust consistency with a teaspoon of warm water if too thick.
Holding: hold at 55-60°C (a warm spot near the stove, not over direct heat) for up to 1.5 hours; it does not reheat or refrigerate well and should be made fresh per service.
**Chef's notes:** if it splits, whisk a fresh yolk with a teaspoon of water in a clean bowl and gradually whisk the split sauce into it — this rebuilds the emulsion. The single biggest cause of splitting is heat, not speed.

name: Sauce Tomate
tagline: Escoffier's fifth mother sauce: pork, mirepoix and tomato simmered to a savoury base sauce.
story: This is not an Italian tomato sauce — it is a French mother sauce, built with salt pork and a light roux to give it body and depth rather than pure acidity. It is kept for classical dishes that call for it by name and as a component in other preparations, not as the house pasta sauce.
method:
1. Render the diced salt pork in a heavy pot over medium heat until the fat runs, 5 minutes.
2. Add the onion and carrot and sweat 8 minutes until softened.
3. Stir in the flour and cook 2-3 minutes without colouring.
4. Add the crushed tomatoes, white stock, garlic, bouquet garni, sugar and salt. Bring to a simmer.
5. Cover and cook in a 160°C oven or on the stovetop at a bare simmer for 1-1.5 hours, stirring occasionally, until thickened and the vegetables are fully broken down.
6. Remove the bouquet garni, pass the sauce through a food mill or blend and pass through a sieve for a smooth finish.
7. Adjust seasoning; the sauce should taste rounded, not sharply acidic — add a touch more sugar if needed.
Holding: refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze up to 3 months.
**Chef's notes:** the roux is there for body, not flavour — keep it pale and don't skip the long, slow cook, which is what breaks down the acidity of the tomatoes into something rounder.

name: Beurre Blanc
tagline: Cold butter whisked into a shallot and wine reduction; the classic sauce for poached fish.
story: Beurre blanc is pure technique with almost no ingredients — it lives or dies on temperature control while the butter is worked in. A kitchen keeps it for delicate white fish and vegetables where a heavier sauce would overwhelm the dish.
method:
1. Combine the shallot, white wine and vinegar in a heavy-bottomed pan. Bring to a simmer and reduce until almost dry — a few tablespoons of syrupy liquid remain, 8-10 minutes.
2. Reduce the heat to very low. Add the cold butter a few cubes at a time, whisking constantly and continuously, letting each addition melt into a creamy emulsion before adding more.
3. Keep the pan just warm enough that the butter softens and emulsifies but never fully melts to an oily liquid — pull off the heat periodically if it looks close to breaking.
4. Once all the butter is incorporated, the sauce should be pale, opaque and lightly coating. Season with salt, white pepper and a few drops of lemon juice if desired.
5. Strain out the shallot for a classic smooth finish, or leave it in for a rustic version.
Holding: this sauce does not hold or reheat — it will split. Make it to order, or hold briefly (20 minutes maximum) in a warm spot off direct heat, such as near the stove, not on it.
**Chef's notes:** the entire sauce is temperature management — too hot and it breaks into melted butter and liquid; too cold and the butter won't emulsify. Work in small batches near service.

name: Béarnaise
tagline: Hollandaise built on a tarragon and vinegar reduction; the standard sauce for grilled steak.
story: Béarnaise is hollandaise's derivative for red meat: the tarragon-shallot-vinegar reduction gives it the acidity and aniseed edge that cuts through a grilled steak or chateaubriand. It is kept on the pass at any kitchen that serves grilled meat as a main.
method:
1. Combine the shallot, half the tarragon stems, crushed peppercorns, vinegar and wine in a pan. Reduce over medium heat until almost dry, 8-10 minutes. Strain and cool slightly; this is the reduction base.
2. Whisk the egg yolks with the strained reduction and a tablespoon of water in a heatproof bowl over a bain-marie of barely simmering water.
3. Whisk constantly until pale, thick and doubled in volume, 3-4 minutes, keeping the bowl from getting too hot.
4. Off the heat, whisk in the warm clarified butter in a thin stream to build the emulsion.
5. Fold in the chopped fresh tarragon and chervil. Season with salt and cayenne.
Holding: hold warm (55-60°C) near the stove for up to 1.5 hours; does not refrigerate or reheat well — make fresh per service.
**Chef's notes:** the reduction must be fully cooled below the point of scrambling the yolks before you start the sabayon, and it must be strained clean of solids or the finished sauce looks and eats gritty.

name: Mornay
tagline: Béchamel enriched with gruyère and egg yolk; the sauce behind every classic gratin.
story: Mornay is béchamel's most direct child — add cheese and a yolk to enrich and it becomes the sauce for gratinéed fish, eggs and vegetables. A kitchen keeps it because it browns beautifully under a salamander and holds its shape rather than weeping.
method:
1. Bring the béchamel to a gentle simmer in a heavy saucepan.
2. Off the heat, whisk in the grated gruyère and parmesan gradually, stirring until fully melted and smooth.
3. Temper the egg yolk with a spoonful of the hot sauce, then whisk it back into the pan off the heat — do not let it boil again once the yolk is added, or it may split.
4. Season with a light grating of nutmeg and salt to taste; the cheese already carries plenty of salt, so taste before adjusting.
5. Use immediately, spread over the dish to be gratinéed, and finish under a hot salamander or grill until golden and blistered.
Holding: keep warm no more than 30 minutes once the yolk is added; for longer holding, prepare the base without the yolk and add it just before use. Refrigerate the yolk-free base up to 3 days.
**Chef's notes:** boiling the sauce after the yolk goes in is the one mistake that ruins it — it will curdle into a grainy, broken sauce that no amount of whisking fixes.

name: Sauce Vierge
tagline: Warm, uncooked olive oil dressing of tomato, herbs and citrus for grilled fish and vegetables.
story: Sauce vierge is barely a sauce in the classical sense — it is warmed just enough to bloom the herbs and coriander seed without cooking anything. It is kept for simply grilled fish and summer vegetables where the dish needs brightness, not richness.
method:
1. Toast the coriander seeds in a dry pan over low heat until fragrant, 1-2 minutes, then crush lightly.
2. Warm the olive oil in a small pan over the lowest possible heat with the shallot and garlic — it should never fry or bubble, just become fragrant, 2-3 minutes.
3. Remove from the heat and stir in the tomato concassé, crushed coriander seed and lemon juice.
4. Let stand off the heat 5-10 minutes to let the flavours combine, then stir in the basil just before serving so it stays bright green.
5. Season with salt and pepper. Serve warm, spooned over the dish rather than under it.
Holding: best made fresh the day of service; the tomato and basil lose freshness quickly. If needed, hold the oil-shallot-garlic base up to 2 days refrigerated and add the tomato, citrus and herbs just before serving.
**Chef's notes:** the oil must stay below a simmer throughout — if it fries the garlic, the sauce turns from bright and fresh to heavy and one-note.

name: Salsa Verde
tagline: Chopped parsley, caper, anchovy and mustard sauce for boiled meats and grilled fish.
story: The Italian salsa verde, distinct from the Mexican one, is a workhorse condiment built to cut through boiled beef (bollito misto) and rich grilled fish. The soaked bread is what gives it body without needing much oil.
method:
1. Soak the bread in the red wine vinegar for 5 minutes, then squeeze out excess liquid and set aside.
2. Finely chop the parsley, anchovy fillets, capers and garlic together by hand, or pulse briefly in a food processor — the texture should stay coarse, not a purée.
3. Combine the chopped mixture with the soaked bread, mustard and olive oil in a bowl. Stir to combine.
4. Taste and adjust with more vinegar, salt or oil — the anchovy and capers bring salt, so season carefully.
5. Let rest 15 minutes before serving to let the flavours settle.
Holding: refrigerate in an airtight container up to 2 days; the parsley darkens after that. Bring to room temperature before serving.
**Chef's notes:** chop, do not purée — a food processor run too long turns this into a pesto-like paste and loses the rustic texture that defines it.

name: Mignonette
tagline: Shallot and cracked pepper steeped in red wine vinegar; the classic oyster accompaniment.
story: Mignonette exists for one purpose: raw oysters. The acidity and pepper heat wake up the oyster without masking it, which is exactly why nothing more elaborate belongs on the same spoon.
method:
1. Finely mince the shallot.
2. Crack the black peppercorns coarsely with the flat of a knife or in a mortar — the texture should be visible, not ground fine.
3. Combine the shallot, cracked pepper and red wine vinegar in a small bowl or jar. Stir to combine.
4. Let steep at room temperature for at least 30 minutes before serving to let the shallot mellow into the vinegar.
Holding: refrigerate up to 5 days in a sealed jar; the flavour improves after a day.
**Chef's notes:** mince the shallot fine enough to sit on a spoon with the oyster — large pieces overwhelm the bite. Serve very cold, spooned directly onto the oyster just before eating.

name: Ponzu
tagline: Citrus and soy dipping sauce steeped with kombu and katsuobushi; sharp, savoury, versatile.
story: Ponzu is kept for sashimi, grilled fish, hot pot dipping and as a bright counterpoint to fatty dishes. The overnight steep with kombu and katsuobushi is what separates a kitchen's ponzu from a bottled citrus-soy mix.
method:
1. Combine the soy sauce, mirin and rice vinegar in a non-reactive container.
2. Add the kombu and let it soak 30 minutes to soften.
3. Add the katsuobushi and citrus juice, stir, and cover.
4. Refrigerate and let steep for 24 hours, stirring once or twice.
5. Strain through a fine sieve or cheesecloth, pressing lightly on the katsuobushi to extract the liquid, then discard the solids.
6. Taste and balance — add a touch more citrus for brightness or mirin for roundness if needed.
Holding: refrigerate in a sealed bottle up to 3 weeks; the flavour deepens over the first few days.
**Chef's notes:** use a mix of citrus (yuzu if available, or lemon and lime) rather than one alone — yuzu's floral note is hard to replace with a single substitute, but a blend gets close.

name: XO Sauce
tagline: Dried shrimp, scallop and cured ham cooked slowly in oil; a savoury condiment, not a table sauce.
story: XO sauce earns its keep as a spoonable finishing condiment — stirred into fried rice, noodles or spooned over steamed fish — because the rehydrated dried seafood and rendered ham give a depth no fresh ingredient reaches. It takes real time and should be made in a batch large enough to justify the effort.
method:
1. Soak the dried shrimp and dried scallop separately in warm water until softened, about 30 minutes. Reserve the soaking liquid.
2. Shred the softened scallop by hand into fine threads; finely chop the dried shrimp.
3. Heat the oil in a wok or heavy pot over medium-low heat. Add the shallot and garlic and fry gently, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, 10-12 minutes — do not let them brown too fast or they turn bitter.
4. Add the diced cured ham and cook 5 minutes until it renders slightly.
5. Add the chopped dried shrimp and shredded scallop. Cook over low heat, stirring frequently, for 30-40 minutes until deeply fragrant and the oil separates and turns a rich amber-red.
6. Stir in the dried chili flakes, sugar and fish sauce. Cook a further 10 minutes.
7. Season with salt to taste. The finished sauce should be a thick, oil-rich paste, not a liquid.
Holding: cool completely and store in a sealed jar under a film of oil, refrigerated, up to 3 weeks.
**Chef's notes:** the whole process is about patience on low heat — anything cooked too fast browns the aromatics before the dried seafood has time to release its flavour into the oil.

ingredients.name: cured ham
ingredients.notes: diced, such as jinhua or serrano

name: Nam Jim
tagline: Pounded chili, garlic, lime and palm sugar dipping sauce; sweet, sour, salty and hot in one spoon.
story: Nam jim is the base dipping sauce behind grilled meats, seafood and the classic green papaya salad — the exact ratio of the four flavours shifts by dish, but the technique of pounding rather than chopping the aromatics is what releases their oils properly.
method:
1. Pound the garlic, coriander root and bird's eye chili together in a mortar and pestle to a coarse paste — this releases far more flavour than chopping with a knife.
2. Add the palm sugar and continue pounding until it dissolves into the paste.
3. Stir in the fish sauce and lime juice, stirring until the sugar is fully dissolved.
4. Taste and adjust the balance — it should hit sour, salty, sweet and hot distinctly, with no single note dominating.
Holding: best made fresh within a few hours, as the lime juice turns bitter over time; if needed, hold the pounded paste (before adding lime) refrigerated up to 2 days and add lime juice just before serving.
**Chef's notes:** taste constantly while adjusting — nam jim has no fixed ratio, only a target balance, and it shifts with how hot the chilies are and how sour the limes are that day.

name: Gremolata
tagline: Raw chopped parsley, lemon zest and garlic; the classic finish for osso buco.
story: Gremolata is minimal by design — three ingredients, chopped fine, scattered over a braise at the very last moment. It exists to cut the richness of a long-cooked dish like osso buco with a burst of raw, sharp freshness.
method:
1. Wash and thoroughly dry the parsley to prevent it from clumping when chopped.
2. Finely chop the parsley leaves.
3. Zest the lemon finely, avoiding the bitter white pith.
4. Mince the garlic very fine, almost to a paste.
5. Combine all three on a board and chop together briefly to blend evenly.
6. Use immediately, scattered over the finished dish just before serving — never cooked.
Holding: does not hold well; the parsley wilts and the garlic sharpens unpleasantly within a few hours. Make it to order or no more than 30 minutes ahead, covered, at room temperature.
**Chef's notes:** the garlic must be minced very fine and used sparingly — this is a garnish, and raw garlic in coarse pieces will overpower the dish rather than lift it.

name: Salmoriglio
tagline: Warm Sicilian emulsion of olive oil, lemon and oregano for grilled fish and lamb.
story: Salmoriglio is Sicily's answer to a butter sauce — no butter at all, just olive oil worked with warm water until it emulsifies into something creamy. It is brushed onto fish or lamb straight off the grill, not served as a side sauce.
method:
1. Warm the water gently — it should be warm to the touch, not hot.
2. In a bowl, whisk the olive oil and warm water together vigorously, or shake in a jar, until the mixture emulsifies into a pale, creamy consistency.
3. Whisk in the lemon juice, garlic and dried oregano.
4. Season with salt and pepper. Whisk again just before use, as it will separate on standing.
5. Brush or spoon generously over grilled fish, lamb chops or vegetables immediately after they come off the grill, so the residual heat helps it soak in.
Holding: make fresh per service; it separates within an hour and does not re-emulsify cleanly once cold. Keep any extra at room temperature and re-whisk before using.
**Chef's notes:** the warm water is what makes this emulsify without egg or mustard — cold water will not work the same way, so don't skip warming it.

name: Sauce Bordelaise
tagline: Red wine and shallot reduction finished with espagnole and bone marrow; the classic steak sauce.
story: Bordelaise is named for the red wine of the region and kept for grilled or roasted beef — the poached bone marrow stirred in at the end is what gives it a silky, almost custard-like richness beyond what the reduction alone provides.
method:
1. Combine the red wine, shallot, thyme, bay leaf and crushed peppercorns in a saucepan. Bring to a simmer and reduce by three-quarters, 15-20 minutes, until syrupy.
2. Strain out the solids and return the reduction to the pan.
3. Whisk in the espagnole (or demi-glace) and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook 15 minutes, skimming any impurities, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
4. Meanwhile, poach the diced bone marrow in barely simmering salted water for 1-2 minutes until just softened; drain.
5. Off the heat, whisk in the butter to finish and gloss the sauce, then fold in the poached marrow gently so it doesn't break apart.
6. Season with salt to taste. Serve immediately.
Holding: the sauce without the marrow and butter holds refrigerated up to 3 days; finish with marrow and butter fresh per service, as the marrow does not reheat well.
**Chef's notes:** poach the marrow separately and fold it in at the very end — simmering it directly in the sauce turns it grainy and can make the sauce greasy.

name: Sauce Robert
tagline: Onion and white wine espagnole derivative finished with mustard; the classic pork accompaniment.
story: Sauce Robert is one of espagnole's oldest small sauces, built specifically to go with grilled or roasted pork, where its mustard bite and mellow cooked onion cut through the fat.
method:
1. Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the onion and cook gently until soft and translucent but not browned, 8-10 minutes.
2. Add the white wine and reduce by half, 5 minutes.
3. Stir in the espagnole sauce and sugar. Simmer gently 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly thickened.
4. Remove from the heat and whisk in the mustard — do not boil the sauce again after this point, or the mustard turns bitter and loses its sharpness.
5. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
Holding: the sauce without mustard holds refrigerated up to 4 days; whisk in the mustard fresh, off the heat, at the point of service.
**Chef's notes:** adding the mustard off the heat is the key step — boiled mustard turns flat and slightly bitter, losing the very bite the sauce is built around.

name: Sauce Diable
tagline: Sharp shallot, wine and cayenne espagnole derivative; a spiced sauce for grilled poultry and game.
story: Sauce diable — 'devil's sauce' — gets its bite from a hard vinegar-wine reduction and a clear hit of cayenne, kept in the repertoire for grilled chicken, guinea fowl and other dishes that need something sharper than a straight demi-glace.
method:
1. Combine the shallot, white wine, white wine vinegar and crushed peppercorns in a saucepan. Bring to a simmer and reduce until nearly dry, 10-12 minutes.
2. Whisk in the espagnole sauce and bring to a gentle simmer. Cook 10 minutes, skimming as needed, until slightly thickened.
3. Strain if a smooth sauce is wanted, or leave the shallot in for texture.
4. Stir in the cayenne pepper and season with salt to taste — the sauce should have a clean, sharp heat, not an overwhelming one.
Holding: refrigerate up to 4 days; reheat gently, whisking, without boiling hard.
**Chef's notes:** add the cayenne at the end and taste as you go — its heat builds after a few minutes off the stove, so it is easy to overshoot.

name: Sabayon Salé
tagline: Savoury egg-yolk sabayon whisked with wine and fish fumet; a light gratin sauce for poached fish.
story: The savoury sabayon swaps the sugar of its dessert cousin for fish fumet and white wine, giving a light, airy sauce that can be glazed under a salamander over poached fish or vegetables without the heaviness of a full hollandaise.
method:
1. Combine the egg yolks, white wine and fish fumet in a heatproof bowl.
2. Set over a bain-marie of barely simmering water, making sure the bowl does not touch the water.
3. Whisk constantly and vigorously until the mixture triples in volume and becomes a thick, pale, airy foam that holds a ribbon trail, 6-8 minutes. Keep the heat gentle — direct high heat will scramble the yolks.
4. Remove from the heat and whisk in the cold butter a piece at a time to enrich and stabilise the foam.
5. Season with lemon juice, a pinch of cayenne and salt to taste.
6. Use immediately — spoon over fish or vegetables and glaze quickly under a hot salamander until lightly golden, or serve as is as a light sauce.
Holding: does not hold; this sauce must be made and used within minutes of finishing, as the foam collapses on standing.
**Chef's notes:** whisk hard and constantly from the moment the bowl goes over the heat — any pause lets the yolks near the bowl's edge overcook before the rest catches up.

name: Soubise
tagline: Béchamel enriched with slow-cooked onion purée; sweet, mild, classic with lamb and eggs.
story: Soubise turns béchamel into something rounder and sweeter by folding in onion cooked down until it nearly melts. It is kept as a base for gratins and as a sauce for lamb and roasted poultry where a plain white sauce would be too flat.
method:
1. Melt the butter in a heavy pan over low heat. Add the sliced onion, cover, and sweat very gently for 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until completely soft and translucent with no colour — this slow, covered cook is what gives soubise its sweetness.
2. Purée the cooked onion in a blender or food processor until smooth.
3. Combine the onion purée with the hot béchamel in a saucepan and simmer gently 10 minutes to marry the flavours.
4. Pass through a fine sieve for a silky, restaurant finish if desired.
5. Season with a light grating of nutmeg, salt and white pepper.
Holding: refrigerate up to 3 days; reheat gently, whisking, adding a little milk if it has thickened too much.
**Chef's notes:** covering the pan while the onion sweats is essential — uncovered, the onion will catch and colour before it fully softens, which turns the sauce brown and loses the clean sweetness soubise is meant to have.

name: Pistou
tagline: Provençal basil and garlic paste worked with olive oil; no cheese, no nuts, unlike its Ligurian cousin.
story: Pistou is often confused with pesto, but the Provençal version leaves out the pine nuts and cheese, staying purely basil, garlic and olive oil. It is stirred into soupe au pistou at the last moment, never cooked, so the basil stays bright.
method:
1. Strip the basil leaves from their stems and wash and dry thoroughly.
2. Pound the garlic to a paste in a mortar and pestle, or crush finely with the flat of a knife.
3. Add the basil leaves and continue pounding, working in a little of the olive oil at a time, until a rough, bright green paste forms.
4. Alternatively, pulse the basil and garlic briefly in a food processor, streaming in the oil, taking care not to over-process into a smooth purée or overheat the blade.
5. Season with salt to taste.
6. Stir into soup or a finished dish off the heat, just before serving — pistou should never be cooked, or it loses its colour and fresh aroma.
Holding: refrigerate up to 2 days under a film of olive oil to prevent oxidation; the colour dulls after that.
**Chef's notes:** work by hand with a mortar and pestle when possible — a food processor's blade generates heat that can turn the basil dull and slightly bitter.

name: Sauce Gribiche
tagline: Cold mayonnaise-style sauce built from hard-boiled egg yolk, mustard and chopped cornichon.
story: Gribiche is a cold sauce, not an emulsion of raw egg like mayonnaise — the yolks are cooked first, then mashed and worked with oil the same way. It is the classic pairing for calf's head, poached tongue and cold poached fish.
method:
1. Boil the eggs for 9-10 minutes for a fully set yolk with no grey ring. Cool in ice water, then peel. Separate the yolks from the whites; chop the whites and set aside.
2. Mash the cooked yolks to a smooth paste in a bowl with the dijon mustard.
3. Whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in a thin stream, building an emulsion the same way as a mayonnaise, until thick and glossy.
4. Whisk in the white wine vinegar to loosen slightly and season.
5. Fold in the chopped egg white, cornichons, capers, parsley, chervil and tarragon.
6. Season with salt and pepper. The finished sauce should be thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon, studded with the chopped garnish.
Holding: refrigerate up to 3 days in a sealed container; the herbs darken slightly but the sauce holds well.
**Chef's notes:** mash the yolks completely smooth before adding oil — any lumps left at that stage will not smooth out later and the emulsion will look grainy.

name: Ravigote
tagline: Sharp mustard vinaigrette with shallot, capers and fine herbs, for cold poached meats and offal.
story: Ravigote is a punchy, herb-heavy vinaigrette kept for calf's head, tongue, poached poultry and other dishes that need real acidity and texture to stand up to them, rather than a plain dressing.
method:
1. Whisk the white wine vinegar and dijon mustard together in a bowl until combined.
2. Whisking constantly, add the neutral oil in a slow stream to build a loose emulsion.
3. Stir in the shallot, capers, parsley, chervil and tarragon.
4. Season with salt and pepper. The sauce should be sharp and herbaceous, pourable rather than thick.
5. Let stand 10 minutes before serving so the shallot softens slightly in the acid.
Holding: refrigerate up to 3 days; whisk again before serving as it will separate.
**Chef's notes:** keep the herbs freshly chopped and add them last — chopped too far ahead, they blacken and turn the sauce dull rather than vividly green-flecked.

name: Agrodolce
tagline: Sicilian sweet-and-sour reduction of vinegar, sugar and onion, used across meat, game and vegetables.
story: Agrodolce is Sicily's core sweet-sour base, built simply from vinegar and sugar cooked down with onion, and used across dishes from caponata to braised game — the ratio can be pushed sweeter or sharper depending on what it will dress.
method:
1. Warm the olive oil in a saucepan over medium heat. Add the sliced red onion and cook until softened and lightly golden, 8-10 minutes.
2. Add the sugar and cook, stirring, until it dissolves and starts to lightly caramelise around the onion, 2-3 minutes.
3. Pour in the red wine vinegar carefully — it will steam vigorously — and stir to deglaze.
4. Add the raisins and simmer gently until the liquid reduces to a syrupy consistency that coats the onion, 10-12 minutes.
5. Season with salt to taste. The finished sauce should balance clearly sweet and clearly sour, with neither masking the other.
Holding: refrigerate up to 1 week; the flavour deepens after a day. Reheat gently before serving.
**Chef's notes:** taste as the vinegar reduces — cooking it too far concentrates the acidity sharply, so pull it just before it tastes exactly right, since it will tighten slightly more as it cools.

name: Salsa de Tomate Asada
tagline: Charred tomato, onion and chile salsa; smoky, simple, the base table salsa of a Mexican kitchen.
story: This is the salsa built from direct char rather than raw ingredients — the tomatoes, onion, garlic and chile are blistered hard before blending, which is what gives it a smoky depth a raw pico de gallo doesn't have.
method:
1. Heat a dry comal, cast iron pan or grill over high heat. Char the tomatoes, onion (cut in thick slices) and garlic cloves, turning occasionally, until blackened and blistered in spots and softened, 10-15 minutes. Char the serrano chile alongside for 5-6 minutes.
2. Let everything cool slightly, then peel the garlic.
3. Combine the charred tomatoes, onion, garlic and chile in a blender with the cilantro and a pinch of salt. Pulse to a coarse, rustic texture — do not purée completely smooth.
4. Transfer to a bowl and stir in the lime juice.
5. Taste and adjust salt and chile heat by adding more raw or charred chile as needed.
Holding: refrigerate up to 4 days in a sealed container; flavour improves slightly after a few hours.
**Chef's notes:** char hard, past the point that feels comfortable — real blackening on the skins is what gives this salsa its smoky backbone, not a light roast.

name: White Chicken Stock
tagline: Raw chicken bones simmered gently with aromatics; the clean base stock for velouté and soup.
story: This is the everyday stock of the kitchen — used for velouté, risotto, braising liquid and soup — kept clear and clean by starting from raw bones and never letting it boil hard.
method:
1. Rinse the raw chicken bones under cold water to remove surface blood and impurities.
2. Place the bones in a stockpot and cover with cold water. Bring slowly to a bare simmer over medium heat — never a boil, which clouds the stock.
3. Skim the scum that rises to the surface thoroughly in the first 20-30 minutes, before adding vegetables.
4. Add the onion, carrot, celery, leek and bouquet garni. Return to a bare simmer.
5. Simmer uncovered, skimming occasionally, for 3.5-4 hours. The liquid should barely move — one or two bubbles breaking the surface at a time.
6. Strain through a fine chinois lined with cheesecloth. Do not press the solids, which clouds the stock.
7. Cool quickly in an ice bath before refrigerating.
Holding: refrigerate up to 4 days, or freeze flat in bags up to 4 months.
**Chef's notes:** the difference between a clear, professional stock and a cloudy home one is entirely temperature control — a rolling boil emulsifies the fat and scum into the liquid and cannot be fixed after the fact.

name: Brown Chicken Stock
tagline: Roasted chicken bones and mirepoix for a deeper, darker stock than the white version.
story: Roasting the bones and vegetables first before simmering gives this stock a colour and roundness the white version doesn't have, making it the better base for chicken jus and darker chicken sauces.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 220°C. Spread the chicken bones on a roasting tray and roast 35-40 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden brown.
2. Add the onion and carrot to the tray for the final 15 minutes to colour alongside the bones.
3. Transfer the bones and vegetables to a stockpot. Deglaze the roasting tray with a little water over heat, scraping up the browned bits, and add this to the pot.
4. Stir the tomato paste into the tray or pot to dissolve, then add the celery, cold water and bouquet garni.
5. Bring slowly to a bare simmer, skimming the surface thoroughly. Simmer uncovered 4-4.5 hours, skimming occasionally.
6. Strain through a fine chinois lined with cheesecloth, without pressing the solids.
7. Cool quickly in an ice bath before refrigerating.
Holding: refrigerate up to 4 days, or freeze up to 4 months.
**Chef's notes:** roast the bones hard enough to get real colour, not just pale tan — under-roasted bones give a muddy, weak brown stock instead of a rich one.

name: Fond de Veau Brun
tagline: Roasted veal bones simmered a full day; the foundation stock for espagnole and demi-glace.
story: Veal stock is the backbone of the classical sauce repertoire — its natural gelatine gives body no chicken or vegetable stock can match, and a kitchen that serves red meat dishes with real sauces keeps this simmering in the background most days.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 230°C. Roast the veal bones on a tray for 45-60 minutes, turning occasionally, until very deeply browned.
2. Add the onion and carrot to the tray for the last 20 minutes to colour.
3. Transfer everything to a large stockpot. Deglaze the tray with water, scraping up the fond, and add to the pot along with the tomato paste, celery and cold water.
4. Bring slowly to a bare simmer, skimming thoroughly for the first hour before adding the bouquet garni and peppercorns.
5. Simmer uncovered at the barest bubble for 7-8 hours, topping up water if it reduces below the bones, and skimming periodically.
6. Strain through a fine chinois lined with cheesecloth without pressing.
7. Cool in an ice bath quickly; the stock should set to a loose jelly when fully chilled, a sign of good gelatine extraction.
Holding: refrigerate up to 5 days, or freeze up to 6 months.
**Chef's notes:** a properly made veal stock sets firm and jelly-like when cold — if it stays liquid in the fridge, the bones were under-roasted, the simmer too short, or too much water was used relative to bone.

name: Fish Fumet
tagline: White fish bones sweated with vegetables and wine; a fast, delicate stock for fish velouté and sauces.
story: Fumet is deliberately short-cooked compared to a meat stock — fish bones give up their flavour quickly and turn bitter and glue-like if simmered too long. Use only white, lean fish bones, never oily fish.
method:
1. Rinse the fish bones and heads under cold water, removing any blood, gills, and trimming away fins.
2. Melt the butter in a wide pot over medium-low heat. Add the onion, celery and leek and sweat gently 5 minutes without colouring.
3. Add the fish bones and mushroom trim, and sweat a further 5 minutes, stirring, until the bones turn opaque.
4. Add the white wine and let it reduce by half, 3-4 minutes.
5. Add the cold water, bouquet garni and white peppercorns. Bring to a bare simmer.
6. Simmer gently, skimming, for no more than 25-30 minutes — longer extraction turns the stock cloudy and slightly bitter.
7. Strain through a fine chinois lined with cheesecloth without pressing the solids.
8. Cool quickly in an ice bath.
Holding: refrigerate up to 2 days only, or freeze up to 2 months — fish fumet does not keep as long as meat stocks.
**Chef's notes:** never let fumet simmer past 30 minutes or boil at any point — both extract bitterness and gelatine breakdown that a longer meat stock actually benefits from but fish bones do not.

name: Shellfish Stock
tagline: Roasted prawn and crab shells simmered with mirepoix and brandy; the base for bisque and shellfish sauces.
story: This stock is built the same way a brown meat stock is — hard roasting of the shells first, then a proper mirepoix and reduction — because shells alone give up their flavour much more readily under high heat than a gentle simmer.
method:
1. Heat the olive oil in a heavy pot over high heat. Add the shells and heads and cook, stirring and crushing them with a spoon, until well coloured and fragrant, 8-10 minutes.
2. Add the onion, carrot, celery and garlic and cook a further 5 minutes.
3. Stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes.
4. Add the brandy and flambé or reduce until nearly evaporated, then add the white wine and reduce by half.
5. Add the cold water and bouquet garni. Bring to a simmer, skimming any foam.
