**Chef's notes:** don't skip the toasting step — it's what develops the grain's smoky character further rather than leaving it flat and one-note.

name: Quinoa
tagline: Rinsed and simmered plain — the base for salads, bowls and sides.
story: A neutral, gluten-free base kept simple so it can go in any direction — warm as a side, cold in a salad, folded into a tasting-menu component. The only real technique is rinsing off the natural saponin coating so it doesn't taste bitter or soapy.
method:
1. Rinse quinoa thoroughly in a fine sieve under cold running water for at least 1 minute, rubbing the grains between your fingers, until the water runs clear — this removes the bitter saponin coating.
2. Combine quinoa with water or stock in a ratio of 1:1.75 by volume, add a pinch of salt.
3. Bring to a boil, then cover and reduce to the lowest simmer.
4. Cook 15-16 min undisturbed until the liquid is absorbed and small white spirals (the germ) appear around each grain.
5. Remove from heat, keep covered, rest 5 min to steam through.
6. Fluff with a fork.
7. Cool on a tray if using cold, or serve warm. Keeps refrigerated up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the rinse is the most common cause of a bitter, off-tasting batch — always rinse regardless of whether the packet says pre-washed.

name: Sushi rice
tagline: Short-grain rice, seasoned warm with a vinegar dressing (shari).
story: The base for any raw-fish or vegetable roll or nigiri on the tasting menu — the rice, not the fish, is what a sushi chef is actually judged on. Washing until the water runs clear and seasoning while the rice is still warm are the two steps that cannot be shortcut.
method:
1. Wash short-grain sushi rice in several changes of cold water, swirling and draining, until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Drain and let sit dry in the sieve 20-30 min.
3. Cook rice and water in a rice cooker or covered pot at a 1:1.1 ratio; if on the stove, bring to a boil, cover, reduce to lowest heat 12-13 min, then rest covered off heat 10 min.
4. Meanwhile warm rice vinegar, sugar and salt gently just until dissolved — do not boil.
5. Turn the hot cooked rice into a wide wooden or non-reactive tray.
6. Pour the vinegar mixture evenly over the rice, and fold gently with a cutting motion (not stirring, which mashes the grains) while fanning to cool it quickly to body temperature — this is what gives the rice its characteristic sheen.
7. Cover with a damp cloth and use within a few hours; sushi rice does not refrigerate well as it hardens.

**Chef's notes:** seasoning cold rice is the classic mistake — the vinegar only absorbs properly into rice that is still hot, and fanning while folding is what creates the glossy finish.

name: Basmati pilaf
tagline: Whole-spiced rice, steamed to fully separate grains.
story: A fragrant, separate-grain rice side built on the same steam-then-rest logic that governs most good pilafs: whole spices bloomed in fat, rice toasted briefly, then left completely undisturbed to steam so the grains stay distinct rather than clumping.
method:
1. Rinse basmati rice in several changes of cold water until it runs clear, then soak 20-30 min and drain well.
2. Warm ghee or butter in a heavy pot, bloom whole spices (cardamom pods, a cinnamon stick, cloves, bay leaf) 1 min until fragrant.
3. Add sliced onion, cook until golden, 8 min.
4. Add the drained rice, stir gently to coat in fat, toast 1-2 min without breaking the grains.
5. Add hot water or stock at a 1:1.5 ratio, season with salt, bring to a boil.
6. Cover tightly, reduce to the lowest heat, cook 12-15 min without lifting the lid.
7. Remove from heat and rest, still covered, 10 min.
8. Fluff gently with a fork just before serving, taking care not to break the grains.

**Chef's notes:** lifting the lid during cooking is the main failure — every peek lets steam escape and risks an unevenly cooked pot; trust the timing instead.

name: Jasmine rice
tagline: Fragrant steamed rice, plain, for anything that needs a neutral base.
story: The daily-use steamed rice for anything Thai, Southeast Asian or simply needing a soft, fragrant base — a workhorse recipe made right every time rather than left to guesswork with a rice cooker on a default setting.
method:
1. Rinse jasmine rice in cold water until it runs mostly clear.
2. Combine rice and water at a 1:1.25 ratio in a pot with a tight lid.
3. Bring to a boil uncovered, then immediately cover, reduce to the lowest heat, and cook 12-13 min.
4. Remove from heat, keep covered, and rest 10 min without lifting the lid — this finishes the cooking with residual steam.
5. Fluff gently with a fork or rice paddle just before serving.
6. Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days; reheat covered with a splash of water, steaming rather than drying it out.

**Chef's notes:** resist stirring or fluffing too early — disturbing the rice before the rest period is complete breaks the grains and releases starch, making the batch gummy.

name: Congee
tagline: Rice simmered to a savoury porridge, long and low, until it breaks down.
story: A long-simmer rice porridge kept on both menus as a savoury, comforting base for breakfast service or a light course — the rice is deliberately cooked well past al dente until it breaks down into the broth itself, which is the opposite instinct to every other rice dish in the kitchen.
method:
1. Rinse short-grain or jasmine rice briefly.
2. Combine rice with water or light stock at a ratio of roughly 1:8 to 1:10 in a heavy pot.
3. Add a few slices of ginger.
4. Bring to a boil, then reduce to the lowest simmer, partially covered, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking.
5. Simmer 1.5-2 hours, topping up with hot water as it reduces, until the rice has broken down into a thick, creamy porridge with no distinct grains remaining.
6. Season with salt to taste near the end (salting too early can toughen the rice).
7. Serve hot, topped to order — sliced scallion, fried shallot, soy sauce, a soft egg, or shredded poached chicken all work.
8. Keeps refrigerated 3 days; thins on reheating, so add a splash of water or stock and stir over low heat.

**Chef's notes:** rushing the simmer with high heat scorches the base of the pot long before the rice has broken down — keep it at the lowest possible simmer and stir regularly instead.

name: Overnight oats
tagline: Oats soaked cold overnight in milk and chia — no cooking, no morning rush.
story: A no-cook breakfast base for both kitchens' morning service, prepped the night before so the pass isn't slowed at breakfast. The soak softens the oats and the chia thickens the mix into something closer to a pudding than dry cereal.
method:
1. Combine rolled oats, chia seeds and a pinch of salt in a container.
2. Add whole milk (or a milk of choice) and natural yogurt, stir well to combine.
3. Sweeten lightly with honey or maple syrup to taste.
4. Cover and refrigerate overnight, minimum 6 hours, until the oats have softened and the mixture has thickened.
5. Stir well before serving; loosen with a splash of milk if too thick.
6. Portion into bowls or jars, top to order with fresh fruit, nuts or granola.
7. Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days, covered.

**Chef's notes:** don't skip the chia — without it the mixture stays thin and separates, closer to milk-soaked oats than the thick, spoonable texture the dish is meant to have.

name: Granola (house)
tagline: Oats and nuts baked low and slow into loose, crunchy clusters.
story: The house breakfast granola, baked in trays low and slow so clusters form without burning — moved and stirred too often and it never clumps, left completely alone too long and the edges scorch before the centre sets.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 150°C.
2. Combine rolled oats, chopped mixed nuts and a pinch of salt in a large bowl.
3. Warm honey and oil together gently until runny, pour over the oats and nuts, mix thoroughly until every piece is coated.
4. Spread in an even, firmly pressed layer on a lined baking tray — pressing it down is what helps clusters form.
5. Bake 30-35 min, turning the tray once halfway, until golden all over; avoid stirring, which breaks up the clusters.
6. Remove and cool completely on the tray without disturbing it — it crisps fully as it cools.
7. Once cold, break into clusters by hand, fold through dried fruit if using.
8. Store airtight at room temperature up to 3 weeks.

**Chef's notes:** stirring during baking is the main way clusters are lost — press the mix down firmly before baking and leave it alone until it comes out of the oven.

name: Muesli
tagline: Raw oats, nuts and dried fruit — the unbaked cousin of granola.
story: Kept alongside the baked granola for guests who want something lighter — no oil, no baking, just oats and dried fruit mixed to be soaked in milk or yogurt overnight, or eaten dry over fruit.
method:
1. Combine rolled oats, chopped mixed nuts, seeds and dried fruit in a large bowl.
2. Mix thoroughly to distribute evenly.
3. Store airtight at room temperature up to 1 month.
4. To serve, portion and soak in milk, yogurt or juice for at least 15 min (or overnight for a softer texture), or serve dry alongside fresh fruit and yogurt.

**Chef's notes:** keep any add-ins (banana chips, coconut) dry and add them at the point of storage, not mixed with wetter dried fruit, or the batch clumps and softens in storage before it's used.

name: Porridge
tagline: Oats cooked slow in milk and water, stirred to creamy, not gluey.
story: Breakfast porridge kept to a simple ratio and a gentle hand — a mix of milk and water so it doesn't catch or turn too rich, and constant low, slow stirring so the starch releases evenly rather than clumping at the base of the pot.
method:
1. Combine rolled oats with equal parts milk and water in a heavy-based pot (roughly 1:3.5 oats to total liquid).
2. Add a pinch of salt.
3. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat, stirring frequently.
4. Reduce heat to low, continue cooking, stirring regularly, 7-9 min until thick and creamy with the oats fully softened.
5. Adjust consistency with a splash more hot milk if too thick; it will also continue to thicken slightly off the heat.
6. Serve immediately, topped to order — honey, fruit, nuts, a knob of butter.

**Chef's notes:** high heat is the main failure — it catches the oats on the base of the pot and scorches the batch, which no amount of stirring afterward will fix.

name: Bulgur tabbouleh
tagline: A herb salad with a little bulgur in it, not the other way round.
story: Done properly, tabbouleh is mostly parsley — the bulgur is a minor component, soaked rather than cooked, present for texture and bulk, not as the base of the dish. Getting the ratio backwards is the most common way kitchens outside the Levant get this wrong.
method:
1. Soak fine bulgur in a little cold water or lemon juice for 15-20 min until just softened, then drain any excess liquid and fluff — it should not be cooked.
2. Finely chop a large quantity of flat-leaf parsley and a smaller amount of mint — by volume, the herbs should far outweigh the bulgur.
3. Finely dice ripe tomato and drain off excess juice and seeds so the salad doesn't turn watery.
4. Finely dice spring onion.
5. Combine the soaked bulgur, parsley, mint, tomato and spring onion in a bowl.
6. Dress with fresh lemon juice, good olive oil and salt, tossing well.
7. Taste and adjust acidity — it should be bright and sharp with lemon.
8. Rest 10 min before serving to let the flavours settle, but serve the same day — it turns watery on long standing.

**Chef's notes:** too much bulgur and too little parsley is the single most common mistake outside the region — herbs should be the bulk of the dish, bulgur the minor addition.

name: Farro salad
tagline: Whole farro, simmered to a firm chew, dressed while warm.
story: Semi-pearled farro gives the best balance of quick cooking and a chew that holds up in a salad without the long soak whole farro needs — dressed while still warm so the grain takes on the vinaigrette properly, then finished cold with whatever vegetables and herbs are in season.
method:
1. Rinse semi-pearled farro.
2. Simmer in plenty of well-salted water, uncovered like pasta, 25-30 min until tender with a firm, nutty chew — taste from 20 min.
3. Drain well.
4. While still warm, dress with a lemon and olive oil vinaigrette, salt and pepper — dressing it warm lets the grain absorb the flavour.
5. Fold in diced roasted or raw seasonal vegetables, chopped soft herbs and a soft cheese such as feta or ricotta salata if using.
6. Cool to room temperature or chill lightly before serving.
7. Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days; dress again lightly before serving as the grain continues to absorb the vinaigrette on standing.

**Chef's notes:** draining the farro and letting it sit before dressing wastes the one window where it actually absorbs flavour well — dress it warm, every time.

name: Cooked chickpeas from dry
tagline: Dried chickpeas soaked and simmered soft — the base under hummus, stews and salads.
story: A base kept from dry rather than tinned wherever volume allows — the texture and flavour are simply better, and the cooking liquid (chickpea aquafaba) is worth keeping for emulsifying or as a vegan binder elsewhere in the kitchen.
method:
1. Soak dried chickpeas in plenty of cold water with a pinch of bicarbonate of soda, at least 8 hours or overnight. Drain and rinse.
2. Place in a large pot, cover generously with fresh water (at least double the volume of chickpeas).
3. Add a few whole garlic cloves, a bay leaf and a halved onion — no salt yet, which toughens the skins if added too early.
4. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer.
5. Cook 60-90 min, topping up water as needed to keep them covered, until fully tender and creamy at the centre, not just soft on the outside.
6. Salt generously in the last 15-20 min of cooking.
7. Cool in their liquid to keep them from drying out and splitting.
8. Store submerged in their cooking liquid, refrigerated, up to 5 days; freeze in the liquid up to 3 months.

**Chef's notes:** salting too early is the classic mistake — it keeps the skins tough no matter how long you cook them afterward. Always salt near the end.

name: White beans al fiasco
tagline: Cannellini beans cooked long and slow with sage, garlic and oil, no stock.
story: A Tuscan technique traditionally done in an empty wine flask buried in the embers — done here in a low oven or on the lowest stovetop simmer, the point is the same: beans cooked in nothing but water, oil, garlic and sage until the liquid itself becomes a light, savoury broth.
method:
1. Soak dried cannellini beans overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain.
2. Place in a heavy pot (or ovenproof jar) with whole garlic cloves, a few sage leaves and a generous glug of olive oil.
3. Cover with fresh water by about 4 cm, no salt yet.
4. Cover and cook at the lowest possible simmer (or in a low oven at 120°C), undisturbed as much as possible, 1.5-2 hours, until the beans are fully tender and creamy but holding their shape.
5. Salt generously in the last 20 min.
6. Finish with a final drizzle of raw olive oil.
7. Serve warm as a side, or cool and store in their liquid, refrigerated, up to 5 days.

**Chef's notes:** stirring or boiling hard breaks the skins and turns the pot starchy and cloudy — the gentlest possible heat, left mostly alone, is what keeps the beans whole.

name: Black beans
tagline: Dried black beans simmered with onion, garlic and cumin until deeply savoury.
story: A base kept ready for anything from a simple side to a base for refried beans — the aromatics go in from the start of cooking rather than added after, so the beans themselves taste seasoned rather than the liquid around them.
method:
1. Soak dried black beans overnight in plenty of cold water. Drain and rinse.
2. Place in a pot with a halved onion, whole garlic cloves and a bay leaf. Cover generously with fresh water.
3. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer.
4. Cook 60-90 min, topping up water as needed, until fully tender.
5. In the last 20 min, add ground cumin and salt.
6. Remove the onion halves and bay leaf.
7. For a looser side, serve as is with some of the cooking liquid; for refried beans, mash and fry in a little oil.
8. Store in their liquid, refrigerated, up to 5 days; freeze up to 3 months.

**Chef's notes:** old, long-stored dried beans take noticeably longer and can stay tough regardless of cooking time — check stock rotation if a batch won't soften.

name: Lentil dal
tagline: Split red lentils simmered soft, finished with a hot spiced tempering (tadka).
story: A dal kept simple: split lentils cooked down to a soft, thick purée, then finished with a separately fried tempering of spice poured over at the very last moment, which is what keeps the spice aromatic rather than muddy.
method:
1. Rinse split red lentils until the water runs mostly clear.
2. Combine with water, turmeric and a halved garlic clove in a pot, bring to a boil, skim any foam.
3. Reduce to a simmer, cook uncovered 20-25 min, stirring occasionally, until the lentils fully break down to a thick, soft purée. Add water if it thickens too much before the lentils are done.
4. Season with salt.
5. Separately, warm ghee in a small pan, add cumin seeds, sliced garlic and dried chilli, fry until the garlic is golden and the seeds are fragrant, about 1 min — watch closely, this burns fast.
6. Pour the hot tempering over the finished dal immediately before serving, stirring it through at the table or just before.
7. Finish with chopped coriander.
8. Keeps refrigerated 4 days; the tempering is best made fresh each time it's served.

**Chef's notes:** the tempering must go in hot and last — poured in too early or left to sit, the fried spices lose their aroma and the dish tastes flat.

name: Lentil salad
tagline: Puy lentils, cooked to hold their shape, dressed warm in mustard vinaigrette.
story: A cold starter built on the one lentil that holds its structure through cooking — Puy lentils keep a firm bite where most others collapse, which is what lets this be dressed while warm and served as a proper composed salad rather than a mash.
method:
1. Rinse Puy lentils, no soaking needed.
2. Simmer in unsalted water or light stock with a bay leaf and a halved carrot, 20-25 min, until tender but still holding their shape distinctly. Salt only in the last 5 min.
3. Drain well, discard the bay leaf and carrot, and while still warm, dress with a mustard vinaigrette (Dijon mustard, red wine vinegar, olive oil, salt, pepper) — dressing them warm lets the lentils absorb the flavour properly.
4. Fold through finely diced shallot and chopped soft herbs (parsley, chives).
5. Taste and adjust acidity and salt once cooled, as flavours mute slightly with chilling.
6. Serve at room temperature or lightly chilled.
7. Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days; dress a touch more before serving if the lentils have absorbed most of the vinaigrette.

**Chef's notes:** overcooking is the main risk — Puy lentils go from firm to mushy quickly past the point of doneness, so start checking at 18 minutes.

name: Fava purée
tagline: Yellow split peas simmered to a smooth purée, finished with oil and lemon.
story: Despite the name, this Greek meze is made from split yellow peas, not fava beans — simmered without salt until they break down completely and blended smooth, it is one of the simplest and most reliable meze bases on the menu.
method:
1. Rinse yellow split peas well.
2. Combine with water in a pot (roughly 3x the volume of peas), add a halved onion, no salt yet.
3. Bring to a boil, skim any foam thoroughly — split peas throw a lot of foam.
4. Reduce to a simmer, cook uncovered 35-40 min, stirring occasionally, until fully broken down and soft, topping up water if needed.
5. Remove the onion, blend the purée smooth with a stick blender.
6. Salt to taste, then beat in olive oil and lemon juice gradually until glossy and smooth.
7. Adjust consistency with a little hot water if too thick — it should be soft enough to spread but hold its shape on a spoon.
8. Serve warm or at room temperature, drizzled with more olive oil, chopped raw onion and capers on top.
9. Keeps refrigerated 4 days; thins slightly on standing, re-blend or beat with a little oil to bring back together.

**Chef's notes:** salting before the peas have fully broken down toughens them and stalls the cook — always salt at the very end.

name: Fabada asturiana
tagline: Fabes beans stewed with chorizo, morcilla and pork until the broth turns silken.
story: A one-pot Asturian stew where the beans (fabes) are the point and the cured meats are there to season the pot, not dominate it — cooked long and gently enough that the bean skins stay intact even as the broth thickens to a natural, silky body.
method:
1. Soak dried fabes beans (or large white beans) overnight in cold water. Drain.
2. Place in a large pot with pork belly, a piece of ham bone or hock, and cover generously with fresh water. Bring to a boil, skim thoroughly.
3. Add a whole onion, garlic cloves and a good pinch of saffron threads.
4. Reduce to the gentlest simmer, cover partially, and cook 1.5 hours, topping up with cold water occasionally (a Spanish technique called "assustar" — shocking the beans with cold water helps keep the skins intact).
5. Add whole chorizo and morcilla sausages, continue simmering a further 40-50 min until the beans are fully tender and the broth has thickened naturally.
6. Remove the meats, slice, and either return to the pot or serve alongside.
7. Season with salt. The stew should be thick enough to coat a spoon but still have a visible broth.
8. Best made a day ahead and reheated gently, which is when the flavours settle. Keeps refrigerated up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** boiling hard splits the bean skins and clouds the broth — the "assustar" technique of adding cold water and never letting it rise back to a rolling boil is what keeps this dish's texture correct.

name: Cassoulet
tagline: White beans, duck confit and pork, baked under a breadcrumb crust until it cracks.
story: A restaurant-scale cassoulet built in stages rather than one pot: beans cooked with aromatics, meats browned separately, then everything layered and baked long enough to form and break the breadcrumb crust two or three times, which is the traditional mark of a properly finished cassoulet.
method:
1. Cook dried white beans (soaked overnight) with onion, garlic, a bouquet garni and pork rind until just tender, about 1 hour; reserve the cooking liquid.
2. Brown Toulouse sausage, pork belly (cubed) and garlic sausage separately in a heavy pan; set aside.
3. In the same fat, soften diced onion and carrot, add tomato paste, cook briefly.
4. Layer in a large earthenware dish: beans, browned meats, duck confit legs, the softened vegetables, moistening with the reserved bean liquid to just below the top layer.
5. Top generously with fresh breadcrumbs.
6. Bake at 150°C for about 2.5-3 hours, breaking the crust that forms on top and pushing it back into the liquid two or three times during cooking, finishing with a final crust left intact.
7. The cassoulet is ready when the top is deeply golden and cracked, and the beans have absorbed most of the liquid into a rich, creamy sauce.
8. Rest 15 min before serving. Keeps refrigerated 3 days, reheats well covered in a low oven; freezes without the final crust, re-crumbed before reheating.

**Chef's notes:** a cassoulet that isn't basted and re-crusted during baking dries out on top before the beans have fully absorbed the fat and liquid — the breaking and reforming of the crust is not decorative, it's what builds the final texture.

name: Edamame
tagline: Boiled soybeans in the pod, salted hard and hot.
story: The simplest thing on the menu and one of the easiest to get wrong through neglect — properly salted while still steaming hot is the entire difference between a forgettable bowl and one guests actually finish.
method:
1. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil (salted as strongly as pasta water).
2. Add frozen or fresh edamame pods, boil 3-4 min until tender but still with a slight bite.
3. Drain immediately and thoroughly.
4. While still hot and slightly wet, toss with flaky sea salt generously — the residual moisture is what makes the salt stick.
5. Serve immediately, hot, in the pod.

**Chef's notes:** salting once the pods have cooled is nearly useless — the salt needs the hot, damp surface to adhere, so salt within seconds of draining.

name: Tofu (house-pressed)
tagline: Fresh soy milk curdled and pressed in-house, firmer and sweeter than bought.
story: Made in-house because fresh tofu is a genuinely different product from anything sold in a tub — sweeter, with a clean bean flavour that fades within days of pressing. Kept as a base for both raw preparations and searing, depending on how firm it's pressed.
method:
1. Heat unsweetened fresh soy milk gently in a heavy pot to about 75-80°C, stirring to prevent scorching on the base.
2. Dissolve nigari (or a substitute such as food-grade calcium sulphate, or lemon juice) in a little warm water.
3. Remove the soy milk from the heat, stir in the coagulant gently with a few slow strokes, then stop stirring and let it sit undisturbed 10-15 min — curds will separate from a clear yellowish whey.
4. Ladle the curds gently into a cloth-lined mould, folding the cloth over the top.
5. Press with a light weight for a softer tofu (15-20 min) or a heavier weight for a firm, sliceable tofu (30-40 min), draining off the whey.
6. Unmould, and hold submerged in cold water, refrigerated, changing the water daily, up to 4 days.

**Chef's notes:** stirring after the coagulant goes in breaks up the curd structure and gives a grainy, weak tofu — add the coagulant, stir briefly, then stop completely and let the chemistry work undisturbed.

name: Tempeh marinade
tagline: Soy, ginger and rice vinegar marinade to season tempeh's natural bitterness.
story: A base marinade built to counter tempeh's slightly bitter, mushroomy edge with sweetness, acidity and umami — steaming the tempeh briefly before marinating opens its structure so it actually absorbs the liquid instead of sitting on the surface.
method:
1. Steam sliced tempeh for 8-10 min before marinating — this softens its structure and removes some of the natural bitterness, letting it absorb the marinade properly.
2. Whisk together soy sauce, rice vinegar, grated ginger, grated garlic, a little brown sugar, sesame oil and a splash of water.
3. Pour the marinade over the warm steamed tempeh, ensuring every piece is coated.
4. Marinate refrigerated at least 30 min, ideally 2-4 hours, turning once.
5. Pan-fry, grill or bake the marinated tempeh until caramelised at the edges, basting with any extra marinade as it cooks.
6. Unused marinade (that hasn't touched raw meat/tempeh) keeps refrigerated 5 days; marinated tempeh keeps 3 days raw, refrigerated.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the steaming step is the main reason tempeh tastes bitter and underseasoned on the plate — the marinade barely penetrates unsteamed tempeh's dense surface.

name: Salmorejo
tagline: Cordoban chilled tomato and bread soup, thicker and richer than gazpacho.
story: Salmorejo is often mistaken for a thicker gazpacho, but the bread ratio is what actually defines it — enough stale bread blended in that the soup sets almost to a purée, finished with a slick of good olive oil and the classic garnish of chopped hard-boiled egg and jamón.
method:
1. Soak stale white bread (crusts removed) in a little water until soft, then squeeze lightly.
2. Blend ripe tomatoes, the soaked bread, garlic and a pinch of salt until completely smooth.
3. With the blender running, stream in olive oil steadily until the soup emulsifies to a thick, velvety texture that coats a spoon.
4. Add a splash of sherry vinegar, blend again, and pass through a fine sieve for a silky finish.
5. Adjust salt and acidity, chill at least 2 hours before serving.
6. Serve very cold, topped with finely chopped hard-boiled egg and diced jamón, with a final drizzle of olive oil.
7. Keeps refrigerated up to 3 days; the surface may need re-emulsifying with a quick whisk before serving.

**Chef's notes:** thin, watery salmorejo means either not enough bread or oil added too fast without emulsifying properly — stream the oil in slowly with the blender running the whole time.

name: Ajoblanco
tagline: Chilled almond and garlic soup, finished with grapes or melon.
story: Older than gazpacho and often overshadowed by it, this Malaga soup is built entirely from almonds, bread, garlic and oil — pale, cooling and closer to a savoury almond milk than a vegetable soup, traditionally served with a scatter of sweet grapes to cut the garlic.
method:
1. Soak stale white bread in water until soft, squeeze lightly.
2. Blanch blanched almonds briefly if not already skinless, or use pre-skinned blanched almonds.
3. Blend the almonds, soaked bread, garlic and a pinch of salt with a little cold water until as smooth as possible.
4. With the blender running, stream in olive oil steadily to emulsify.
5. Add sherry vinegar to taste, thin to a pourable soup consistency with iced water.
6. Pass through a fine sieve for a silky texture, discarding the almond solids left behind.
7. Chill at least 2 hours, ideally overnight for the flavours to mellow — the raw garlic is sharp when freshly made.
8. Serve very cold, garnished with halved green grapes or diced melon and a drizzle of olive oil.

**Chef's notes:** garlic mellows significantly with an overnight rest — if made and served the same day, use less garlic than a recipe suggests and adjust up only if needed.

name: Minestrone
tagline: Seasonal vegetables, beans and small pasta simmered into a full-bodied soup.
story: A soup with no fixed recipe by tradition, but a fixed method: a proper soffritto base, vegetables added by cooking time so nothing turns to mush, and pasta cooked in at the end so it doesn't bloat and thicken the whole pot into a stew.
method:
1. Build a soffritto of finely diced onion, carrot and celery in olive oil, cook 10 min until soft.
2. Add diced potato and any firmer seasonal vegetables (courgette, green beans), cook 5 min.
3. Add crushed tomatoes and vegetable stock, bring to a simmer.
4. Add cooked white beans and simmer 20 min until the vegetables are tender.
5. Add a parmesan rind if available, for depth, and remove before serving.
6. About 10 min before serving, add small dried pasta (ditalini or similar) and simmer until al dente, adding a little more stock if the pot thickens too much.
7. Fold in shredded leafy greens (cavolo nero or spinach) in the last 3-4 min.
8. Season with salt and pepper, finish with a drizzle of olive oil and grated parmesan at the table.

**Chef's notes:** adding the pasta too early is the most common fault — it keeps absorbing liquid on standing and turns a soup into a stodgy stew by the time it's served.

name: Ribollita
tagline: Tuscan bread and bean soup, thick enough to stand a spoon in.
story: Literally 'reboiled' — a soup built from leftovers, traditionally made a day ahead and reheated, which thickens it further as the stale bread breaks down completely into the vegetables and beans. Cavolo nero, unlike other greens, holds its structure through the long simmer.
method:
1. Build a soffritto of onion, carrot and celery in olive oil, cook 10 min.
2. Add cavolo nero (stemmed, chopped) and cook until wilted, 5 min.
3. Add crushed tomatoes, vegetable stock and half the cooked cannellini beans.
4. Purée the remaining half of the beans and stir in, to thicken the base.
5. Simmer 30-40 min until the vegetables are fully tender and the soup has thickened.
6. Season with salt and pepper.
7. Tear stale country bread into pieces and stir into the pot, letting it soak and break down completely, 10-15 min.
8. The soup should end up thick enough that a spoon stands upright in it briefly.
9. Best made a day ahead and reheated the next day — hence the name — adding a little water or stock if it's too thick on reheating.
10. Serve with a drizzle of raw olive oil at the pass.

**Chef's notes:** using fresh, springy bread instead of properly stale, dense bread gives a gluey rather than a thick, cohesive result — day-old or older country bread is essential.

name: French onion soup
tagline: Onions caramelised low and slow, in a beef broth under a gruyère crust.
story: The whole dish rests on how far the onions are taken — properly caramelised, deep mahogany brown, takes the better part of an hour and cannot be rushed with high heat. Everything after that is straightforward.
method:
1. Slice onions thinly and evenly.
2. Melt butter with a little oil in a heavy pot over medium-low heat, add the onions with a pinch of salt.
3. Cook, stirring regularly, 45-60 min, lowering the heat if they start to catch, until deeply caramelised to a dark mahogany brown — do not rush this with higher heat, which browns unevenly and can turn bitter.
4. Deglaze with a splash of dry white wine or sherry, scraping up any fond, reduce briefly.
5. Add rich beef stock, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme, simmer 25-30 min.
6. Season with salt and pepper.
7. Ladle into oven-proof bowls, top each with a slice of toasted baguette and a generous layer of grated gruyère.
8. Place under a hot grill until the cheese is melted and deeply bubbled and browned.
9. Serve immediately, very hot.

**Chef's notes:** pale, sweet-tasting onion soup almost always means the onions were rushed at too high a heat — true caramelisation takes the better part of an hour and there's no shortcut worth taking.

name: Vichyssoise
tagline: Leek and potato soup, silked smooth and served ice-cold.
story: Essentially a leek and potato soup finished and served differently — puréed until completely smooth, enriched with cream, and chilled thoroughly rather than served warm, which is what turns a humble soup into a refined starter.
method:
1. Sweat sliced leeks (white and pale green only) and diced onion gently in butter, without colour, 10 min.
2. Add diced potato and light chicken or vegetable stock, season lightly.
3. Simmer 20-25 min until the potato is fully tender and falling apart.
4. Blend thoroughly until completely smooth, then pass through a fine sieve for a silky texture with no fibre.
5. Stir in cream, adjust seasoning — flavours mute when chilled, so season slightly assertively while warm.
6. Chill thoroughly, at least 4 hours, ideally overnight.
7. Taste again once cold and adjust salt and acidity (a small squeeze of lemon can help lift it).
8. Serve very cold, garnished with snipped chives and a drizzle of cream or olive oil.

**Chef's notes:** skipping the sieve leaves leek fibres that ruin the intended silky texture — always pass it through, however smooth the blender made it look.

name: Sopa de ajo
tagline: Castilian garlic and bread soup, coloured with paprika, finished with a poached egg.
story: A rustic Castilian soup born of stale bread and little else — the garlic is cooked twice, once in the oil and again once the paprika and bread go in, building a depth that a raw-garlic soup could never manage. A poached or lightly cooked egg dropped in at the end turns it into a full plate.
method:
1. Warm olive oil in a pot, add thinly sliced garlic, cook over low heat until golden but not browned, 3-4 min.
2. Add torn stale bread, stir to coat in the oil and garlic, toast 2 min.
3. Add sweet paprika, stir off the heat briefly to avoid scorching, then return to the heat for a few seconds.
4. Add hot water or light stock, season with salt, bring to a simmer.
5. Simmer 15 min, breaking up the bread with a spoon, until it has broken down into a thick, rustic soup.
6. Crack an egg per portion directly into the simmering soup (or into individual bowls under the hot soup), and poach gently until the white sets but the yolk stays soft, 3-4 min.
7. Serve immediately, piping hot, with a little extra paprika and olive oil on top.

**Chef's notes:** letting the paprika sit too long in the hot oil before the liquid goes in burns it bitter almost instantly — move quickly from paprika to liquid.

name: Tom yum
tagline: Hot and sour prawn broth, built on bruised lemongrass, galangal and lime leaf.
story: A soup defined entirely by its aromatics — lemongrass, galangal and kaffir lime leaf bruised and simmered to release their oils, then balanced hard against fish sauce, lime and chilli. Prawn shells go into the broth itself so nothing of the prawn is wasted.
method:
1. Peel prawns, reserve the shells. Sauté the shells in a little oil until pink and fragrant, add water, simmer 15 min to make a quick stock, then strain.
2. Bruise lemongrass stalks, sliced galangal and torn kaffir lime leaves with the flat of a knife to release their oils.
3. Bring the prawn stock to a simmer with the bruised aromatics, simmer 10 min to infuse.
4. Add sliced mushrooms, cook 3-4 min.
5. Season the broth with fish sauce and a little sugar.
6. Add the peeled prawns, cook just until pink and curled, 2 min — do not overcook.
7. Off the heat, add fresh lime juice and sliced bird's eye chilli to taste — adding lime off the heat keeps its aroma bright rather than cooking it flat.
8. Taste and balance: it should hit hot, sour, salty and a touch of sweet all at once, with no single note dominating.
9. Serve immediately, garnished with coriander leaves. Does not hold well once the prawns and lime are in.

**Chef's notes:** boiling the lime juice or adding it too early flattens the whole soup's brightness — always finish it off the heat, at the very last moment.

name: Miso soup
tagline: Dashi and miso, never boiled once the paste goes in.
story: The simplest soup on the menu and one of the most frequently ruined by heat — boiling miso after it's added drives off its aroma and turns it flat and cloudy rather than clean and fragrant.
method:
1. Make a dashi stock: steep kombu in cold water, warm slowly, remove the kombu just before boiling, add bonito flakes, take off the heat immediately and let steep 5 min, then strain.
2. Return the dashi to a gentle simmer.
3. Dissolve miso paste in a ladleful of the warm dashi in a separate bowl, whisking until smooth, then stir back into the pot.
4. Once the miso is added, keep the soup at a bare simmer — do not let it boil, which cooks off the aroma and dulls the flavour.
5. Add diced silken tofu and rehydrated wakame, warm through gently, 1-2 min.
6. Adjust with a touch more miso if needed, but do not oversalt with soy on top.
7. Serve immediately in warmed bowls, garnished with sliced spring onion.

**Chef's notes:** boiling after the miso goes in is the one mistake to never make — always finish the soup and dissolve the miso off or at the very edge of a simmer.

name: Gravlax
tagline: Dill-and-juniper cured salmon side, sliced paper-thin.
story: Gravlax turns a whole side of salmon into a week of ready-to-slice protein for almost no active work — no heat, no pan, no last-minute cooking under service pressure. It sits well on both menus: rustic on a bistro board, precise and thin-sliced on the tasting menu. The cure ratio is what separates a clean, firm slice from something soft and oversalted.
method:
1. Pin-bone a skin-on salmon side (about 1.5kg) and pat completely dry.
2. Mix the cure: 200g coarse sea salt, 200g caster sugar, 10g cracked black pepper, 10g crushed juniper berries.
3. Spread half the cure in a non-reactive tray. Lay the salmon skin-down on top. Pack the rest of the cure and 150g chopped dill over the flesh, pressing to adhere.
4. Wrap tightly in cling film, set a tray and a 2kg weight on top, and refrigerate at 2-4°C for 48-72 hours, turning and basting with the released liquid every 12 hours.
5. Unwrap, scrape off the cure and dill, and pat dry. The flesh should feel firm to the touch at its thickest point, not soft — that is the doneness cue, there is no visual one.
6. Slice thin on the bias against the skin with a long flexible knife, cutting to order.
7. Hold whole and wrapped in the fridge up to 7 days. Do not freeze after curing — the texture turns mealy on thaw.

**Chef's notes:** the fault is almost always under-curing the thick end. Press it before you trust it — if it gives like raw fish, rewrap and give it another 12 hours.

name: Cured Sea Bass Crudo
tagline: Citrus-salt-cured sea bass, sliced thin, dressed to order.
story: A short cure firms the flesh just enough to slice cleanly without cooking it, which is the whole point of crudo — it should still taste of raw fish, not of the cure. It is a fast tasting-menu course built entirely at the pass from stock kept ready in the fridge. The cure window is short and easy to overshoot, so it is timed by minutes, not left to instinct.
method:
1. Skin a very fresh sea bass fillet (600g) and remove the bloodline.
2. Mix a dry cure: 15g fine sea salt, 5g caster sugar, 2g lemon zest, 2g lime zest.
3. Lay the fillet on a tray, coat evenly with the cure on both sides, and leave for exactly 12-15 minutes at room temperature — no longer, or the surface turns opaque and rubbery.
4. Rinse quickly under cold water, pat completely dry, and chill for at least 30 minutes before slicing.
5. Slice on a slight bias into thin, even pieces (2-3mm) with a very sharp knife, one clean pull per slice.
6. Fan onto chilled plates just before pass. Dress with 40ml extra virgin olive oil, 20ml lemon juice, and flaky salt to taste at the very last moment — dressing sitting on the fish for more than a minute or two starts to cook it further.
7. Serve immediately; do not hold dressed portions.

**Chef's notes:** the fish must be sashimi-grade and used the day it is cut down — this is not a dish to build a cure-and-hold routine around like gravlax.

ingredients.name: sea bass fillet, skin off, sashimi grade

name: Ceviche Base (Leche de Tigre)
tagline: The citrus-and-fish marinade that cooks ceviche without heat.
story: Leche de tigre is the working base behind any ceviche on the menu — made once, kept cold, and spooned over diced raw white fish or shellfish minutes before it goes out. Blending in a little of the trim fish gives it body and a savoury edge that straight lime juice never has. Made ahead and chilled hard, it also does the job of a sauce for other raw and lightly cured fish plates.
method:
1. Combine 250ml fresh lime juice, 100ml fish stock (or blitzed white fish trim and ice, strained), 10g garlic, 5g ginger, 10g coriander stems, and 20g ají amarillo or mild chilli paste in a blender.
2. Blitz on high for 30 seconds with 50g ice until pale, opaque and fully emulsified — the ice both chills and dilutes it to the right strength.
3. Season to taste with fine salt.
4. Pass through a fine sieve, pressing the solids to extract all the liquid; discard the pulp.
5. Chill hard, ideally over an ice bath, before use — leche de tigre used warm tastes flat and loses its lift.
6. To serve as ceviche, dice raw white fish or shellfish into 1cm pieces, toss with the leche de tigre no more than 2-3 minutes before plating, and serve at once.
7. Store the base (undressed) in a sealed container in the fridge up to 2 days; it separates and dulls beyond that.

**Chef's notes:** the fish only 'cooks' from the acid on contact — dress à la minute, never in advance, or the flesh turns chalky before it hits the table.

ingredients.name: fish stock
ingredients.notes: or blitzed white fish trim and ice, strained

name: Tuna Tataki
tagline: Seared-rare tuna loin, sliced thin over its own dressing.
story: Tataki is a searing technique, not a marinade — the tuna is barely cooked, so quality of the loin and control of the pan are what carry the dish. It plates fast at service, which suits the tasting menu, and the sear-then-ice-bath sequence is the part cooks skip when rushed, which is exactly when the centre overcooks.
method:
1. Bring a sashimi-grade tuna loin (500g) to room temperature and pat completely dry.
2. Season the outside only with fine salt and cracked pepper.
3. Heat a dry pan or plancha until just short of smoking. Sear the loin on all sides, 15-20 seconds per side, until the exterior is opaque grey-brown for about 3mm and the centre is still raw and red.
4. Plunge immediately into an ice bath for 60 seconds to stop the cooking, then pat dry.
5. Wrap tightly and rest in the fridge for at least 20 minutes so it slices cleanly.
6. Slice across the grain into 5mm slices with a sharp knife, one pull per slice.
7. Dress with a mix of 40ml soy sauce, 20ml rice vinegar, 10ml sesame oil, and sliced spring onion; fan the tuna over the dressing rather than pouring it on top.
8. Serve immediately; hold undressed, wrapped, in the fridge up to 24 hours.

**Chef's notes:** the ice-bath step is not optional — skip it and residual heat keeps cooking the tuna after slicing, leaving a grey ring under the sear.

name: Confit Salmon, 42°C
tagline: Salmon portions confit in oil at exactly 42°C — silk, not flake.
story: At 42°C the salmon barely crosses from raw to set — the texture is dense and almost custard-like, closer to a good sashimi than to poached or roasted fish. It needs a probe thermometer and a low, held oil temperature, not a hot pan, and it is unforgiving of guesswork. Once the technique is dialled in it is one of the most consistent things on the tasting menu.
method:
1. Portion a skin-off salmon fillet (1kg) into 6 even pieces and season lightly with fine salt.
2. Fill a deep pot or bath with enough neutral oil (grapeseed or light olive) to fully submerge the portions — about 1.5-2 litres.
3. Heat the oil, monitoring constantly with a probe thermometer, to exactly 42°C. This is well below a visible simmer; there will be no bubbling or movement in the oil.
4. Lower the salmon portions gently into the oil so they are fully submerged. Hold the oil at 42°C (±1°C) for 18-20 minutes.
5. The salmon is done when it yields to light pressure and a probe inserted into the centre reads 40-42°C — it will look barely changed in colour, still translucent pink at the core.
6. Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain briefly on paper, and season with flaky salt.
7. Serve immediately; this dish does not hold or reheat — residual carryover will overcook it past the target texture within minutes.

**Chef's notes:** the failure point is temperature drift — adding cold fish drops the oil temperature, so add portions gradually and give the bath time to recover before checking doneness.

name: Pan-Roasted Hake
tagline: Thick hake loin, skin crisped in the pan and finished in the oven.
story: Hake is delicate and flakes apart if it is pushed around, so the whole method is built to move the fish as little as possible. Crisping the skin properly in a hot pan and then finishing gently in the oven keeps the flesh from drying out before the centre is done. It is a main for both kitchens — simpler and more open on the bistro plate, more precise and composed on the tasting menu.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 180°C. Pat 6 skin-on hake loin portions (about 170g each) completely dry, especially the skin.
2. Score the skin lightly in two or three places and season both sides with fine salt.
3. Heat a thin film of oil in an ovenproof pan over medium-high heat until shimmering.
4. Lay the fish skin-side down and press gently flat with a fish slice for the first 10 seconds to stop it curling. Cook undisturbed for 3-4 minutes until the skin is golden and crisp.
5. Transfer the pan directly to the oven, flesh-side down for the final minute if extra colour is needed, otherwise leave skin-side down throughout, and cook for 4-5 minutes.
6. The fish is done when it just starts to separate into large flakes under light pressure and a probe reads 52-55°C at the thickest point — it will continue cooking off the heat.
7. Rest for 1 minute on a warm plate, skin-side up to keep it crisp, before serving.

**Chef's notes:** never turn the fish more than once. Every extra flip breaks the flakes and dries the surface before the centre catches up.

name: Fish en Papillote
tagline: Fish, vegetables and herbs steamed sealed in paper — opened at the table.
story: The parchment parcel is its own sauce-maker — the fish steams in its own juices with the vegetables and aromatics, so nothing dries out and nothing needs basting. It is a reliable service dish because the timing is exact and hands-off once it is in the oven, and the theatre of opening the parcel table-side does real work on the bistro floor.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 200°C. Cut four large parchment squares (about 40cm) and fold each in half to crease.
2. On one half of each square, lay a bed of thinly sliced fennel, courgette and a few cherry tomato halves (about 100g vegetables per portion).
3. Place a 150g portion of firm white fish (hake, sea bass or similar) skin-off on top of the vegetables.
4. Season with fine salt, a few thyme sprigs, a splash of white wine (15ml) and a drizzle of olive oil (10ml) per portion.
5. Fold the paper over the fish and crimp the edges tightly in small overlapping folds all the way round to seal in the steam.
6. Place on a tray and bake for 12-14 minutes, until the parcel puffs and browns slightly.
7. Serve the sealed parcel directly on the plate and open it at the table — the fish is done when it flakes easily and the vegetables are just tender.

**Chef's notes:** a loose seal is the main failure — steam escapes, the fish dries slightly and the parcel never puffs, which is also the visual cue that it worked.

ingredients.name: white fish fillet (hake or sea bass), skin off, portioned

name: Salt-Baked Fish
tagline: Whole fish baked inside a cracked salt crust, table-side reveal.
story: The salt crust seals the whole fish so it steams in its own moisture and never touches direct heat — the flesh stays seasoned but not salty, since almost none of the salt penetrates the skin. It is a whole-fish centrepiece with genuine theatre: the crust is cracked open at the table, which makes it worth the extra prep for a set-menu moment.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 220°C. Scale and gut a whole fish (sea bass or bream, about 1.2kg), leaving the head and tail on, and pat dry inside and out.
2. Stuff the cavity with lemon slices, thyme and a few fennel fronds.
3. Mix the crust: 1.5kg coarse sea salt with 4 egg whites and 100ml water, until it has the texture of wet sand and just holds together when pressed.
4. Spread a bed of the salt mix on a tray, lay the fish on top, and pack the remaining mix over it in an even 1.5-2cm layer, sealing it completely with no gaps.
5. Bake for 25-30 minutes, until the crust is hard and pale golden.
6. Rest for 5 minutes, then crack the crust open at the table with the back of a spoon and lift it away in pieces.
7. Peel back the skin, which should lift off cleanly, and check doneness: the flesh should be opaque and just flake from the bone.

**Chef's notes:** do not score or slash the skin before crusting — any break lets salt into the flesh and the fish comes out inedibly salty in that spot.

ingredients.name: whole sea bass or bream, scaled and gutted

name: Mussels Marinière
tagline: Mussels steamed open in white wine, shallot and butter, in minutes.
story: Marinière is the base method every other mussel dish on the menu is a variation of — get the wine-to-shellfish ratio and the timing right and the mussels give up their own liquor to build the sauce. It is fast, one pot, and finishes at the table with bread for the broth, which is why it stays a bistro staple.
method:
1. Scrub 1.5kg live mussels under cold water, pulling off any beards, and discard any that are open and do not close when tapped, or that are cracked.
2. Sweat 100g finely chopped shallot and 2 cloves chopped garlic in 30g butter over medium heat until soft but not coloured, 2-3 minutes.
3. Add 200ml dry white wine, bring to a boil, and tip in the mussels. Cover immediately with a tight lid.
4. Cook over high heat, shaking the pot once or twice, for 4-5 minutes until the shells have opened.
5. Lift the mussels out with a slotted spoon into serving bowls, discarding any that have not opened.
6. Whisk 40g cold butter into the cooking liquid off the heat to finish it, add a handful of chopped parsley, and check seasoning.
7. Pour the sauce over the mussels and serve immediately with bread for the broth.

**Chef's notes:** never cook mussels past the point the shells open — 30 seconds too long and they turn rubbery. Pull them the moment the pot is mostly open and let residual heat finish the stragglers.

name: Clams in Salsa Verde
tagline: Clams cooked open in a green parsley-garlic-wine sauce.
story: This is a Basque coastal staple built on a technique, not a long ingredient list — the sauce thickens from the clam liquor and a little flour worked into the garlic oil, then goes green from a heavy hit of parsley at the end. It shares its salsa verde with other dishes on the menu, made in the same batch and split.
method:
1. Purge 1.2kg live clams in cold salted water for 20 minutes, then rinse and discard any that are open and unresponsive or cracked.
2. Heat 60ml olive oil in a wide pan and cook 3 cloves sliced garlic gently until just golden, not browned.
3. Stir in 10g flour and cook for 1 minute to lose the raw taste, without colouring further.
4. Add 150ml dry white wine and 100ml fish stock, whisking to a smooth, loose sauce, and bring to a simmer.
5. Add the clams, cover, and cook over high heat for 4-5 minutes, shaking the pan occasionally, until the shells open.
6. Off the heat, stir in a large handful (about 30g) of finely chopped parsley — added at the end it stays bright green rather than dulling.
7. Discard any clams that have not opened, check seasoning, and serve immediately with bread.

**Chef's notes:** purging is not optional with sandy clams — skip it and the sauce turns gritty no matter how well the dish is otherwise cooked.

name: Octopus, Boiled then Grilled
tagline: Octopus tenderised by a slow simmer, then charred hard on the grill.
story: Octopus needs two completely different kinds of heat: a long gentle simmer to break down the connective tissue, then a fast, hard char to build flavour and texture on the surface. Skipping the first step and grilling from raw gives rubber; skipping the second gives something soft but flavourless. Cooked ahead and held, it is a fast final step at service.
method:
1. Thaw a whole octopus (about 1.2kg raw) if frozen — freezing itself helps tenderise the flesh.
2. Bring a large pot of water to a simmer with a halved onion, a bay leaf and a splash of vinegar. Do not add salt, which toughens the flesh.
3. Holding the octopus by the head, dip the tentacles into the simmering water three times before fully submerging — this helps the tentacles curl evenly.
4. Simmer gently (small bubbles, not a rolling boil) for 55-65 minutes, until a knife slides into the thickest part of a tentacle with no resistance.
5. Turn off the heat and let the octopus cool in its cooking liquid for 15 minutes before removing — this final soak keeps it moist. At this stage it can be cooled fully, portioned into tentacles, and refrigerated up to 3 days or frozen up to 2 months.
6. To finish, pat tentacles dry, toss in olive oil and season, and grill on a very hot plancha or barbecue for 2-3 minutes per side until deeply charred at the edges and warmed through.
7. Rest 2 minutes, slice thick, and serve.

**Chef's notes:** the char has to be aggressive and fast — a long, gentle reheat on the grill dries out flesh that is already fully cooked from the simmer.

name: Squid a la Plancha
tagline: Squid seared fast and hard on a screaming-hot plancha.
story: Squid has exactly one good cooking window — very fast and very hot, or long and slow. This recipe is the fast route: scored and seared in under two minutes so the flesh sets before it has time to seize into rubber. It is quick enough to fire to order for both kitchens, either as a tapa or a tasting-menu bite.
method:
1. Clean 800g squid, separating tubes and tentacles, and peel off the outer membrane from the tubes.
2. Score the inside of each tube in a tight crosshatch, cutting about two-thirds through the flesh — this helps it curl and cook evenly and lets it take on more char.
3. Cut the tubes into flat pieces if large, or leave whole if small. Pat completely dry — any surface moisture will steam the squid instead of searing it.
4. Heat a plancha or heavy pan until visibly smoking hot. Toss the squid in a little olive oil and season just before it hits the pan, not before.
5. Lay the pieces scored-side down first. Sear for 60-90 seconds without moving them, until deeply golden and starting to curl.
6. Flip and sear the other side for 30-45 seconds — total cooking time should be under 2 minutes.
7. Remove immediately, finish with a squeeze of lemon and chopped parsley, and serve at once while still hot from the pan.

**Chef's notes:** every extra 30 seconds past the point it curls tightens the protein further — pull it early rather than late; carryover heat will finish it.

name: Prawn Cleaning
tagline: Peeling, deveining and shell-saving prawns without wasting anything.
story: Every prawn dish on the menu depends on this being done the same way every time — clean flesh, no grit vein, and shells saved rather than binned, since they carry more flavour into stock than the meat does. It is basic mise-en-place, but a rushed devein is the single most common reason a prawn dish comes back.
method:
1. Working over a bowl to catch shells and heads separately from trim, twist the head off each raw prawn and set aside for stock.
2. Peel the shell away from the tail meat, leaving the last tail segment and fin on if the dish calls for a whole-tail presentation, or removing it fully for a clean piece of meat — check the dish spec before deciding.
3. Reserve all shells and heads in a separate container for stock; do not discard them.
4. Run a small paring knife along the back of the peeled prawn, about 2-3mm deep, to expose the dark digestive vein.
5. Lift the vein out with the knife tip or your fingers and discard it — this is the single step that most affects the finished dish, since a left-in vein reads as grit at the table.
6. Rinse cleaned prawns briefly under cold water and pat dry; do not soak, which waterlogs the flesh.
7. Hold cleaned prawns covered in the fridge, used within 24 hours; freeze shells and heads if not making stock the same day, up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** a shallow cut that misses the vein is worse than a deep one — go slightly deeper than feels necessary rather than leaving grit behind.

name: Prawn Stock
tagline: Roasted prawn shells and heads, simmered down to a concentrated stock.
story: This is where the shells and heads saved from every prawn dish on the menu end up — roasted hard before simmering, which is what gives it real depth rather than a thin, boiled-shellfish taste. It underpins bisques, rice dishes and sauces on both menus and freezes well, so it is worth batching whenever enough shells accumulate.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 200°C. Spread 1kg raw prawn shells and heads on a tray and roast for 12-15 minutes, turning once, until deep orange-red and fragrant — do not let them blacken.
2. Heat 30ml oil in a large pot, add 150g roughly chopped onion, carrot and celery, and sweat for 5 minutes.
3. Add the roasted shells and heads, along with 30g tomato paste, and stir over medium heat for 2-3 minutes to cook out the paste.
4. Deglaze with 100ml white wine or brandy, scraping up any browned bits, and let it bubble for a minute.
5. Cover with 1.5 litres cold water, add a bay leaf and a few peppercorns, and bring to a gentle simmer.
6. Simmer uncovered for 35-40 minutes, skimming any foam, until reduced to about 1 litre and tasting clean and concentrated.
7. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing the shells firmly to extract all the liquid, then discard the solids.
8. Cool quickly, and store in the fridge up to 3 days or freeze up to 3 months.

**Chef's notes:** roast the shells properly before simmering — an unroasted stock tastes thin no matter how long it reduces.

name: Crab Picking
tagline: Breaking down a cooked crab into clean white and brown meat.
story: Picking a crab properly is slow, deliberate work with no shortcuts — every piece of shell missed ends up as a complaint at the table. Kept separate, white and brown meat serve different purposes: white meat for dressed crab and salads, brown meat for bisques and enriching sauces. It is a technique every new cook on the section has to be checked on before being trusted with it unsupervised.
method:
1. Start with a whole cooked crab (about 1kg), cooled completely.
2. Twist off both claws and legs at the joints. Crack each claw and leg segment with the back of a knife and pick out the white meat in as large pieces as possible, checking each piece for shell fragments by feel.
3. Turn the crab onto its back, pull off the tail flap ('apron') and discard.
4. Prise the main shell away from the body — the brown meat sits in the shell; scoop it into a separate bowl and set aside.
5. Remove and discard the gills ('dead man's fingers'), the mouth parts, and the stomach sac just behind the eyes.
6. Split the remaining body into two or four sections with a heavy knife and pick out the white meat from the internal channels using a small pick or skewer.
7. Keep white and brown meat in separate covered containers in the fridge, used within 24 hours of picking.

**Chef's notes:** check every piece of white meat by pressing it gently between finger and thumb before it goes in the bowl — shell fragments are far easier to feel than to see.

name: Dressed Crab
tagline: Picked crab meat dressed simply and served back in the shell.
story: Dressed crab lives or dies on the picking, not on what is added to it — the dressing should season the meat, not mask it. Served back in the cleaned shell it needs almost no plating work, which makes it an efficient starter for a busy service once the crab itself is picked ahead.
method:
1. Pick a whole crab following the standard picking method, keeping white and brown meat separate; reserve the cleaned main shell.
2. Season the brown meat with a little mayonnaise (about 20g), a pinch of cayenne, and a squeeze of lemon juice, then spread it in a thin layer around the inside edge of the cleaned shell.
3. Season the white meat lightly with lemon juice, a little extra virgin olive oil, and salt — keep it dressed lightly enough that the crab still tastes of itself.
4. Pile the white meat into the centre of the shell over the brown meat border.
5. Finish with a scatter of finely chopped parsley or chives and a wedge of lemon on the side.
6. Serve chilled with thin brown bread or toast.
7. Hold dressed crab covered in the fridge no more than a few hours before service; it does not improve with time.

**Chef's notes:** taste the white and brown meat separately before dressing — brown meat carries most of the crab's flavour and can easily overpower the white meat if not kept to a thin border.

ingredients.name: cooked crab, picked, white and brown meat separated

name: Oyster Shucking
tagline: Opening a live oyster clean, with all its liquor intact.
story: Shucking is a safety and quality technique before it is anything else — a slipped knife is the most common kitchen injury tied to raw bar work, and a torn adductor muscle or spilled liquor ruins the point of serving oysters raw. Done right, every oyster reaches the table with its own seawater still in the shell, which is most of what anyone is actually paying for.
method:
1. Check each oyster is tightly closed and smells of clean seawater — discard any that are open, cracked, or smell off.
2. Hold the oyster flat-side up in a folded cloth or oyster glove, hinge end pointing toward you, cupped side down so the liquor stays inside.
3. Find the hinge — the pointed end where the two shells meet — and insert the tip of an oyster knife at a slight downward angle.
4. Apply firm, steady pressure and twist the knife, rather than forcing it straight in, until you feel the hinge give and the top shell loosens.
5. Slide the knife along the inside of the top shell to cut the adductor muscle attaching it, then lift the top shell away, keeping the oyster and its liquor in the bottom shell.
6. Run the knife under the oyster to release it from the bottom shell as well, without lifting it out — it should sit loose but whole, still bathed in its own liquor.
7. Check for any grit or shell fragments and wipe the underside of the shell clean before setting it on ice.
8. Shuck to order wherever possible; if holding, keep shucked oysters level and iced, and serve within 20 minutes.

**Chef's notes:** the hinge is the only entry point that works reliably — attacking from the side edge is how knives slip and hands get cut.

name: Oysters on the Half Shell with Mignonette
tagline: Freshly shucked oysters served iced, with mignonette on the side.
story: This is the simplest possible use of two other kitchen preparations — shucked oysters and mignonette — brought together only at the very last moment. The whole job at service is timing and presentation: cold plate, fresh ice, oysters shucked as close to the pass as possible. Nothing here should be cooked, reduced, or made in advance beyond the mignonette itself.
method:
1. Prepare mignonette ahead and keep it chilled.
2. Shuck 12 live oysters to order, following the standard shucking technique, keeping each oyster level in its shell with its liquor intact.
3. Fill a serving plate or platter with crushed ice, mounding it slightly so the shells sit stable and tilted.
4. Nestle the shucked oysters into the ice, cupped side down flat, distributing them evenly around the plate.
5. Spoon a small amount of mignonette onto three or four oysters, and serve the rest of the mignonette in a small dish alongside so guests can dress the others to taste.
6. Add lemon wedges to the plate.
7. Serve immediately — oysters held on ice for service should go out within 15-20 minutes of shucking, no longer.

**Chef's notes:** never let the oysters and their liquor tip out on the ice — a spilled oyster looks and tastes worse than a slightly late one; take the extra few seconds to seat them level.

name: Fish Mousseline
tagline: Airy, emulsified fish and cream base for quenelles and terrines.
story: Mousseline is the fish kitchen's equivalent of a working dough — a light, set emulsion of fish, egg white and cream that holds its shape when poached or baked, used to bind terrines, fill quenelles, or lighten a fish cake mix. Getting a stable emulsion depends entirely on keeping everything cold, which is the one variable that separates a silky mousseline from a grainy, split one.
method:
1. Chill a food processor bowl and blade in the freezer for 15 minutes before starting; keep all ingredients cold throughout.
2. Cube 500g skinless white fish (whiting, hake or pike work well) and blitz in the chilled processor until smooth, about 30 seconds.
3. Add 2 egg whites and 8g fine salt, and blitz again until fully incorporated, another 20 seconds.
4. With the motor running, pour in 250ml very cold double cream in a slow, steady stream, blitzing only until just combined — over-processing at this stage will split the emulsion.
5. Pass the mixture through a fine sieve to remove any sinew or fibre, pressing gently with a spatula.
6. Test the set by poaching a small spoonful in simmering water for 1-2 minutes; it should hold its shape and taste light, not dense or rubbery. Adjust cream slightly if it feels too firm.
7. Use immediately, or cover and refrigerate up to 24 hours — the mixture firms up further on standing, which is normal.

**Chef's notes:** the moment the mixture looks slightly grainy or the cream seems to separate on the sides of the bowl, stop the machine — it has gone as far as it will go, and more blitzing will not fix it.

ingredients.name: white fish fillet, skinless (whiting, hake or pike)

name: Fish Cakes
tagline: Flaked cooked fish and mashed potato, breaded and pan-fried.
story: Fish cakes turn cooked leftover or trim fish into something worth serving on its own, provided the fish-to-potato ratio stays generous — the fault in most versions is too much filler. A firm chill before crumbing is what keeps them holding together in the pan rather than falling apart.
method:
1. Cook 500g potato until tender, then mash dry with no added milk or butter; it needs to be firm, not creamy.
2. Fold in 500g cooked, flaked white fish (poached or steamed), 30g chopped parsley, 10g Dijon mustard, zest of one lemon, and season with salt and pepper.
3. Check the mix holds together when pressed; if it feels wet, add a spoonful of breadcrumbs to firm it, but keep additions minimal.
4. Shape into 8 even cakes, about 120g each, and chill on a tray for at least 30 minutes — this is what stops them breaking apart later.
5. Set up a standard breading line: flour, then 2 beaten eggs, then breadcrumbs. Coat each cake in flour, egg, then breadcrumbs, pressing gently to adhere.
6. Heat a shallow layer of oil in a pan over medium heat. Fry the cakes for 3-4 minutes per side until deep golden brown and heated through.
7. Drain briefly on paper and serve immediately. Uncooked, breaded cakes hold in the fridge up to 24 hours, or can be frozen raw up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** frying straight from the fridge, not at room temperature, is what keeps the cake from collapsing before the crust sets — do not let them warm up on the pass before cooking.

ingredients.name: fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Brandade de Bacalao
tagline: Desalted salt cod worked with potato and olive oil into a soft spread.
story: Brandade takes desalted bacalao and turns it into something closer to a rustic mash than a piece of fish — beaten with warm potato and oil until it just holds together, still with texture from the flaked cod. It sits equally well as a bistro starter with toast or as a smoother tasting-menu spoonful.
method:
1. Start with 500g bacalao that has already been desalted (48 hours, water changed at least three times) and poached until tender, about 10 minutes in barely simmering water.
2. Flake the cod, discarding any skin or bones, and set aside.
3. Boil 400g peeled potato until tender, then mash while still hot, without adding milk or butter.
4. Warm 150ml extra virgin olive oil and 100ml milk separately, but do not let either boil.
5. In a heavy pan over low heat, beat the flaked cod with a wooden spoon or spatula, gradually working in the warm oil in a slow stream, as if making an emulsion, until it loosens and turns pale and slightly fluffy.
6. Beat in the warm milk in the same way, then fold in the mashed potato until the mixture is smooth but still shows flecks of cod.
7. Add a crushed garlic clove and a grind of white pepper; taste before adding any salt, since the cod itself carries some.
8. Serve warm with toasted bread, or chill and serve as a cold spread; hold covered in the fridge up to 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** work the oil in gradually off direct high heat — pour it all in at once and the mixture splits into an oily, grainy mess instead of binding smooth.

name: Bacalao Desalting
tagline: Reducing salt cod's salt to a usable level with a controlled soak.
story: Salt cod is preserved to be almost inedible straight from the packet — this is the fixed process that makes it usable, not something to shortcut under time pressure. Every bacalao dish on the menu, from brandade to a simple stew, depends on this step being done properly and started with enough lead time.
method:
1. Rinse 1kg dried, salted cod under cold running water to remove surface salt crystals.
2. Place in a deep container and cover generously with cold water, at least three times the volume of the fish.
3. Refrigerate and change the water at least every 8 hours, three to four times over 48 hours total — do not leave it at room temperature, which risks spoilage before the salt has left.
4. After 48 hours, taste a small piece: cut a sliver, simmer it briefly, and taste. It should taste pleasantly savoury with only a light salinity, not sharp or unpleasant.
5. If still too salty, continue soaking in fresh cold water for a further 12-24 hours and taste again.
6. Once desalted, the cod is ready to poach, flake or cook according to the specific dish. It should feel plump and rehydrated, no longer stiff and dry.
7. Use desalted cod within 24 hours, or hold submerged in fresh cold water in the fridge up to 2 days, changing the water daily.

**Chef's notes:** always taste-test before cooking a full batch — cod varies in how heavily it was salted, and the same 48-hour rule does not fit every piece equally.

name: Sardines, Butterflied and Grilled
tagline: Sardines opened flat along the backbone, grilled skin-side down.
story: Butterflying a sardine removes the spine and most of the small bones in one motion, leaving a flat fillet that cooks in under two minutes a side and eats far more easily than a whole grilled fish. It is quick, cheap and honest — exactly the register of the bistro menu — provided the fish is scaled and gutted with some care first.
method:
1. Scale each sardine (about 8, 100g each) by scraping firmly from tail to head under running water, then gut through the belly and rinse the cavity clean.
2. Cut off the head just behind the gills. Open the fish flat, skin-side down, and press firmly along the length of the backbone with your thumb to loosen it from the flesh.
3. Turn the fish over and lift out the backbone from the head end, working towards the tail; most of the rib bones should lift away attached to it. Pick out any stray bones by hand.
4. You should now have a flat, butterflied sardine, skin on one side, joined at the tail.
5. Season both sides with fine salt and a little olive oil.
6. Heat a grill or plancha until very hot. Lay the sardines skin-side down and cook for 90 seconds to 2 minutes without moving, until the skin is crisp and releases easily.
7. Flip and cook the flesh side for a further 30-45 seconds, until just opaque throughout.
8. Serve immediately with lemon; sardines do not hold or reheat well once grilled.

**Chef's notes:** press hard enough along the backbone the first time — a light press leaves bones behind that only show up as the guest bites down.

name: Fish Skin Crisps
tagline: Fish skin trim, dried and rendered crisp for garnish.
story: This is the use for the skin trimmed off fish that is otherwise filleted skinless — pressed flat, dried and rendered until it shatters like a cracker, it adds crunch and a concentrated hit of fish flavour on top of plates that are otherwise soft in texture. It is a zero-waste habit worth keeping running in the background rather than a dish made to order.
method:
1. Save clean, scaled skin trimmed from salmon, sea bass or similar fish (about 200g), scraping off any remaining flesh with the back of a knife.
2. Lay the skins flat, flesh-side up, on a tray lined with parchment. Season lightly with fine salt.
3. Cover with a second sheet of parchment and another flat tray on top to weight them down and keep them from curling.
4. Dry in a low oven at 90-100°C for 45-60 minutes, until the skins feel firm and mostly dry but not yet crisp.
5. Remove the weight, raise the oven to 160°C, and bake uncovered for a further 8-12 minutes, watching closely, until the skins are fully crisp and golden, blistering slightly.
6. Cool completely on a rack — they crisp further as they cool, so do not judge doneness while still hot.
7. Break into shards for garnish. Store in an airtight container with a desiccant or silica sachet at room temperature up to 5 days; they turn soft quickly in humid air.

**Chef's notes:** the low-and-slow drying stage is what prevents blistering and burning later — rushing straight to a hot oven scorches the outside before the inside has dried.

ingredients.name: fish skin trim (salmon or sea bass), scaled

name: Scallop Searing
tagline: A hard, fast sear that colours the outside without overcooking the centre.
story: Scallops overcook in seconds, which makes searing them properly one of the more demanding basic techniques on the pass — the whole method exists to get maximum colour in minimum time. It underlies every scallop dish on both menus, and the standard is the same regardless of what sauce or garnish it ends up with.
method:
1. Remove scallops from the fridge and pat completely dry on all sides with paper towel — any surface moisture prevents a proper sear and causes steaming instead.
2. Season lightly with fine salt just before cooking, not in advance, which draws out moisture.
3. Heat a heavy pan over high heat with a thin layer of neutral oil until it is visibly shimmering, close to smoking.
4. Lay the scallops in the pan flat side down, leaving space between each — overcrowding drops the pan temperature and stops a proper sear.
5. Cook without moving them for 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until a deep golden-brown crust forms on the base.
6. Flip once, add a knob of butter to the pan, and cook for a further 30-45 seconds on the second side, basting briefly with the foaming butter.
7. The scallop is done when the sides feel firm but the very centre still yields slightly — pull it from the pan while it still looks a shade underdone; it continues cooking off the heat.
8. Serve immediately; scallops do not hold or rest well once seared.

**Chef's notes:** resist moving the scallop to check the crust — lifting it early breaks the sear before it has fully formed, and it will not recolour in the same spot.

name: Dry-Brined Roast Chicken
tagline: Whole chicken salted a day ahead for crisp skin and seasoned meat.
story: Salting the bird well ahead, uncovered in the fridge, does two things at once: it seasons the meat all the way through, and it dries the skin so it roasts properly crisp instead of steaming under its own moisture. It needs almost no active work, just the discipline to start it the day before, which makes it a dependable centrepiece for the bistro's roast slot.
method:
1. Pat a whole chicken (about 1.6kg) completely dry. Season all over, including under the skin at the breast and inside the cavity, with fine sea salt at roughly 1% of the bird's weight (about 16g).
2. Place uncovered on a rack over a tray and refrigerate for 12-24 hours — the surface will look dry, almost matte, by the next day; this is correct.
3. An hour before cooking, remove from the fridge to come closer to room temperature. Preheat the oven to 220°C.
4. Truss loosely or tuck the wing tips under, and place breast-side up in a roasting tray.
5. Roast at 220°C for 20 minutes to colour the skin, then reduce to 180°C and continue roasting for a further 35-40 minutes.
6. The chicken is done when a probe in the thickest part of the thigh reads 74-75°C and juices run clear, not pink.
7. Rest for 10-15 minutes under loose foil before carving — this redistributes the juices and finishes the cooking gently.
8. Carve and serve; leftover meat holds refrigerated up to 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** do not skip the uncovered rest in the fridge — a bird salted and roasted the same day never gets the same dry, crisp skin, no matter how hot the oven runs.

name: Spatchcock Chicken
tagline: Chicken opened flat along the backbone for fast, even roasting or grilling.
story: Butterflying the chicken flat cuts the cooking time roughly in half and exposes far more skin to direct heat, which is why it works so well over wood or on a grill. It is the faster, more rustic sibling of the whole roast bird, and it suits the wood oven at Bistro Mondo particularly well.
method:
