1. Place a whole chicken (about 1.6kg) breast-side down. Using poultry shears, cut along both sides of the backbone from tail to neck and remove it entirely; reserve for stock.
2. Turn the bird breast-side up and press down firmly on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until you hear it crack and the bird lies flat.
3. Tuck the wing tips under and push a skewer through the thighs and body to hold the flattened shape during cooking.
4. Season both sides generously with fine salt, pepper and a little olive oil, and let sit at room temperature for 20-30 minutes if time allows.
5. Preheat the oven to 220°C, or heat a grill/wood oven to a similarly high, steady heat.
6. Roast skin-side up for 30-35 minutes, until the skin is deeply golden and a probe in the thickest part of the thigh reads 74-75°C.
7. Rest for 8-10 minutes before carving into portions.

**Chef's notes:** cracking the breastbone fully is what lets the bird sit flat and cook evenly — a bird only half-flattened cooks unevenly, with the legs done before the breast.

ingredients.name: fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Chicken Ballotine
tagline: Boned chicken leg, stuffed and rolled into a neat, sliceable cylinder.
story: A ballotine turns an uneven cut like a chicken leg into a clean, even cylinder that slices into perfect medallions — precisely the sort of controlled, composed protein a tasting menu depends on. The boning is the hard part; once that skill is solid, the stuffing and rolling are straightforward.
method:
1. Bone out a whole chicken leg (thigh and drumstick, skin on), keeping the skin intact in one piece and working the meat off the bone with a small knife, following the bone closely.
2. Lay the boned leg skin-side down, flesh-side up, and lightly flatten any thick areas with the flat of a knife so it is an even thickness throughout.
3. Spread a thin, even layer of mousseline or a simple herb-and-butter stuffing (about 80g) over the flesh, leaving a small border.
4. Roll the leg tightly from one edge to the other into a neat cylinder, using the skin to hold the shape, and wrap tightly in cling film, twisting and tying both ends.
5. Bring a pot of water to 65°C and poach the ballotine for 25-30 minutes, until a probe inserted through the film reads 68-70°C at the centre.
6. Remove, unwrap while still warm, and pat dry. Sear in a hot pan with a little oil for 1-2 minutes on all sides to colour and crisp the skin.
7. Rest for 5 minutes, then slice into medallions with a sharp knife.
8. Hold poached and unsliced, wrapped, in the fridge up to 2 days; sear and slice to order.

**Chef's notes:** roll it as tight as the skin allows without tearing — a loosely rolled ballotine leaves air pockets that collapse on slicing and ruin the clean round shape.

ingredients.name: fish or chicken mousseline, or herb butter stuffing
fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Duck Breast, Rendering the Fat
tagline: Duck breast cooked skin-side down first, to render the fat to a crisp shell.
story: The whole technique is about patience on one side of the pan — starting the duck breast skin-side down in a cold pan lets the fat render out slowly, leaving crackling-crisp skin instead of a thick, chewy layer of unrendered fat. The rendered fat itself is not wasted; it is strained and kept for confit and roasting elsewhere in the kitchen.
method:
1. Score the skin of a duck breast (about 200g) in a tight crosshatch, cutting through the fat but not into the flesh, and season with fine salt.
2. Place skin-side down in a cold, dry pan and set over medium-low heat — starting cold is what allows the fat to render gradually rather than seizing and burning the skin.
3. Cook for 8-10 minutes, pouring off the rendered fat into a heatproof container every 2-3 minutes and reserving it, until the skin is deep golden-brown and crisp and most of the fat layer has rendered away.
4. Turn the breast over and cook flesh-side down for 3-4 minutes, until a probe reads 54-56°C for medium-rare.
5. Rest for 5 minutes, skin-side up, on a warm plate before slicing.
6. Slice on the bias into even pieces, keeping the crisp skin intact on each slice.
7. Strain the reserved rendered fat through a fine sieve into a clean container; store refrigerated up to 1 month, used for confit, roast potatoes or searing other meats.

**Chef's notes:** never start duck breast in a hot pan — it looks faster but seizes the skin before the fat underneath has a chance to render, leaving a thick, unpleasant layer of fat under a burnt surface.

name: Pork Tenderloin, Brined
tagline: Lean pork tenderloin brined briefly to stay moist through a hot sear.
story: Tenderloin is the leanest cut on the pig and dries out fast if it is pushed even slightly past medium — a short wet brine buys a margin of moisture that makes the difference between a good result and a dry one. It is a quick, low-effort insurance step rather than a flavouring technique in its own right.
method:
1. Make a brine: dissolve 60g salt and 30g sugar in 1 litre of water, along with a bay leaf and a few peppercorns; cool completely.
2. Submerge a trimmed pork tenderloin (about 600g) fully in the brine and refrigerate for 45-60 minutes — longer risks the meat turning overly firm and slightly hammy.
3. Remove, rinse briefly under cold water, and pat completely dry.
4. Season the outside lightly with pepper (the brine has already salted it).
5. Heat a pan with a little oil over medium-high heat. Sear the tenderloin on all sides, 2-3 minutes per side, until evenly browned.
6. Finish in a 180°C oven for 6-8 minutes, until a probe reads 62-63°C at the centre — pork tenderloin is safe and best at a light pink centre, not cooked through grey.
7. Rest for 5 minutes before slicing on the bias.

**Chef's notes:** do not brine longer than an hour — tenderloin is small and lean enough that an overnight brine, which works for a whole pork loin or chicken, turns this cut unpleasantly dense and salty.

name: Pork Chop
tagline: Bone-in pork chop, seared and butter-basted to a juicy medium.
story: A thick, bone-in chop is more forgiving than a lean tenderloin, but it still overcooks fast once it is past temperature — the searing and basting method here is designed to build a proper crust while giving the centre time to catch up gently rather than racing ahead of it.
method:
1. Bring a bone-in pork chop (about 350g, at least 3cm thick) to room temperature for 20 minutes before cooking.
2. Pat dry and season generously with fine salt and pepper.
3. Heat a heavy pan with a little oil over medium-high heat until shimmering.
4. Sear the chop for 3-4 minutes per side, standing it on its side against the bone briefly as well, until deeply golden all over.
5. Reduce the heat to medium-low, add a knob of butter, a smashed garlic clove and a sprig of thyme, and continue cooking for 4-6 minutes, basting the chop regularly with the foaming butter and tilting the pan.
6. The chop is done when a probe in the thickest part (away from the bone) reads 62-64°C.
7. Rest for 5 minutes on a warm plate before serving; the temperature will climb a few more degrees as it rests.

**Chef's notes:** cooking too close to the bone with the probe gives a false low reading — always check the thickest part of the meat itself, a couple of centimetres away from the bone.

ingredients.name: fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Lamb Rack
tagline: Frenched lamb rack, seared then roasted to a rosy pink.
story: A properly frenched rack looks clean on the plate and lets the bones caramelise separately from the meat, but the technique that actually matters is the sear-then-roast sequence, which builds a crust before the low, gentle oven heat carries the loin up to temperature evenly. It is a reliable centrepiece cut for both menus, more rustic whole on the bistro table, portioned into cutlets for the tasting menu.
method:
1. Trim a lamb rack (about 800g, 8 bones) of excess fat, leaving a thin, even layer, and scrape the bones clean of any remaining membrane and fat (frenching) if not already done.
2. Season generously with fine salt and pepper and let sit at room temperature for 20-30 minutes.
3. Preheat the oven to 180°C. Heat a pan with a little oil over high heat until shimmering.
4. Sear the rack fat-side down first for 2-3 minutes until deep golden, then sear the remaining sides briefly, about 1 minute each.
5. Transfer to a roasting tray, bones curling upward, and roast at 180°C for 12-16 minutes.
6. The rack is done at medium-rare when a probe in the centre of the loin reads 55-57°C.
7. Rest for 8-10 minutes under loose foil before carving between the bones into cutlets.
8. Serve immediately after carving; the rest is essential to keep the juices in the meat rather than on the board.

**Chef's notes:** rest it standing on its bones rather than lying flat where possible — it keeps the seared crust from steaming against the tray and going soft.

ingredients.name: fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Lamb Kofta
tagline: Spiced minced lamb, worked smooth and grilled on skewers.
story: Kofta depends on working the mince properly before it ever sees the grill — kneading it until it turns slightly tacky and homogenous is what lets it hold its shape on a skewer without a binder. The spicing is direct and warm rather than heavy, built to survive a hot, fast char.
method:
1. Combine 800g minced lamb (20% fat) with 100g finely grated onion, squeezed of excess liquid, 15g minced garlic, 10g ground cumin, 5g ground cinnamon, a pinch of chilli flakes, 20g chopped parsley, and 15g fine salt.
2. Knead the mixture firmly by hand for 3-4 minutes, until it turns slightly sticky and homogenous — this developed texture is what holds the kofta together, not egg or breadcrumb.
3. Chill the mixture for at least 30 minutes to firm up before shaping.
4. Divide into 8 portions (about 100g each) and mould each firmly around a flat metal skewer into an elongated sausage shape, pressing to remove air pockets.
5. Heat a grill or plancha to high heat. Brush lightly with oil.
6. Grill the kofta for 3-4 minutes per side, turning once, until well charred outside and a probe reads 68-70°C at the centre.
7. Rest for 2 minutes off the skewer before serving with flatbread and yoghurt.

**Chef's notes:** if the mix will not hold its shape on the skewer, it has not been kneaded enough — chilling alone will not fix underworked mince.

name: Beef Tartare
tagline: Hand-cut raw beef, dressed simply and seasoned to order.
story: Tartare is entirely about the knife work and the quality of the beef — hand-cutting rather than machine-mincing keeps the texture loose and gives it bite instead of a paste-like mouthfeel. It is dressed and seasoned only at the last moment, so it has to be built to order rather than prepped in bulk ahead of service.
method:
1. Trim a well-marbled, very fresh beef fillet or sirloin (500g) of all sinew and fat.
2. Chill the meat and a knife thoroughly before cutting — working cold keeps the beef firm enough to cut cleanly.
3. Cut the beef into thin slices, then into fine strips, then into small, even dice by hand; do not use a mincer or food processor, which crushes the fibres into a paste.
4. Just before service, combine the diced beef with 15g finely diced shallot, 10g capers, 10g Dijon mustard, 5ml Worcestershire sauce, a few drops of Tabasco, and 20ml olive oil per portion; mix gently by hand.
5. Season with salt and black pepper, adjusting the mustard and Worcestershire to taste — the dressing should season the beef without drowning it.
6. Mould into a neat portion on the plate using a ring or two spoons, and make a small well in the top for a raw egg yolk.
7. Serve immediately with toast; do not hold dressed tartare — mix and plate to order only.

**Chef's notes:** dice, don't mince — a food processor turns tartare into something closer to a pâté, losing the bite that defines the dish.

ingredients.name: beef fillet or sirloin, very fresh, trimmed
fine sea salt and black pepper

name: Carpaccio
tagline: Raw beef, pounded paper-thin and dressed with oil and lemon.
story: Carpaccio depends on the beef being sliced and then pounded thin enough to be almost translucent, which is what makes it easy to eat raw and cold. It is one of the simplest dishes on paper and one of the least forgiving in execution — an uneven pound leaves thick, chewy patches in an otherwise delicate dish.
method:
1. Freeze a trimmed beef fillet (400g) for 30-40 minutes, until firm but not fully frozen — this makes it possible to slice very thin without it tearing.
2. Slice the beef across the grain into thin rounds (2-3mm) using a very sharp knife.
3. Lay each slice between two sheets of cling film and pound gently and evenly with a meat mallet or the flat of a heavy pan, working from the centre outward, until almost translucent.
4. Arrange the pounded slices, slightly overlapping, to cover a chilled plate in a single even layer.
5. Dress just before service with a thin drizzle of extra virgin olive oil, a squeeze of lemon juice, flaky salt and cracked black pepper.
6. Finish with shaved Parmesan and a few rocket leaves, or a light mustard dressing, according to the specific menu.
7. Serve immediately, chilled; do not dress and hold, as the acid and salt begin to firm the beef's surface within minutes.

**Chef's notes:** pound from the centre out and check for thickness against the light — any patch you can't see light through needs more pounding, evenly, not just in the middle.

name: Steak Cooking Guide (Temperatures by Cut)
tagline: Target internal temperatures and pan method by cut, for consistent doneness.
story: Different cuts behave differently under heat, and this is the reference every cook on the grill station should be working from rather than guessing by feel alone — fillet, sirloin and rib-eye all reach the same doneness at the same probe temperature, but they get there differently because of fat content and thickness. Written down once, it keeps doneness consistent across cooks and across a busy service.
method:
1. Bring steaks to room temperature for 20-30 minutes before cooking and pat completely dry.
2. Season generously with fine salt just before the pan, and lightly oil the steak rather than the pan for a cleaner sear.
3. Heat a heavy pan or grill until visibly smoking hot.
4. Sear fillet and sirloin (leaner cuts) for 2-3 minutes per side; sear fattier cuts like rib-eye slightly longer, rendering the fat cap if present.
5. Reference internal temperatures with a probe: rare 48-50°C, medium-rare 54-56°C, medium 58-60°C, medium-well 63-65°C, well done 68°C+.
6. For thick cuts (over 3cm), finish in a 180°C oven after searing rather than prolonging pan time, checking temperature every few minutes.
7. Rest every steak for at least half its cooking time before serving — a 6-minute cook needs a 3-minute rest, minimum — to let the juices settle back through the meat.
8. Baste with butter, garlic and thyme in the last minute of the pan for fattier cuts; leaner cuts like fillet benefit most from this since they carry less fat of their own.

**Chef's notes:** always pull steaks a couple of degrees under target — carryover heat during the rest continues raising the internal temperature by 2-4°C after the pan.

name: Reverse-Sear
tagline: Low oven first, hard sear last — for thick cuts cooked evenly edge to edge.
story: The reverse-sear inverts the usual order: a slow, low oven brings a thick steak up to temperature gently and evenly first, then a very short, hard sear at the end builds the crust without pushing the centre past doneness. It solves the classic problem of a thick cut with a grey band under the crust and an underdone middle, and it is far more forgiving on timing than a straight pan cook.
method:
1. Season a thick-cut steak (at least 4cm, such as a rib-eye or sirloin) generously with fine salt and place on a rack over a tray.
2. Cook in a low oven at 90-100°C, checking with a probe every 10 minutes, until the centre reads about 6-8°C below the final target (for medium-rare, pull around 46-48°C).
3. This stage typically takes 35-45 minutes depending on thickness — there is no rush, and the low, even heat is what keeps the whole cross-section uniformly cooked.
4. Rest the steak briefly, 5 minutes, while heating a heavy pan until visibly smoking.
5. Sear the steak hard for 45-60 seconds per side, just enough to build a deep brown crust — this stage is fast because the meat is already almost at temperature.
6. Check the final internal temperature; it should now sit at the target doneness (54-56°C for medium-rare) with almost no grey band visible when sliced.
7. Rest for 2-3 minutes before slicing, far less than a conventionally seared steak needs, since the meat was never shocked with high heat all the way through.

**Chef's notes:** the technique only pays off on thick cuts — under 3cm, the meat is through to temperature before a crust has time to build in the oven stage, and a standard sear is faster and simpler.

name: Sous-Vide Short Rib, 72 Hours
tagline: Bone-in short rib, cooked sous-vide for three days to a sliceable tenderness.
story: Short rib has enough connective tissue that it needs either a long braise or a very long, low sous-vide cook to break down — held at a steady low temperature for 72 hours, it turns tender enough to slice cleanly while staying pink and juicy rather than falling apart like a braise. It is a genuine investment of time, planned days ahead, that pays off as a precise, composed piece for the tasting menu.
method:
1. Season bone-in short rib (1.5kg) generously with fine salt and sear hard on all sides in a very hot pan until deeply browned, about 2 minutes per side — this is purely for flavour, not for cooking.
2. Vacuum-seal the seared short rib with a splash of red wine (30ml) and a sprig of thyme.
3. Set a water bath to exactly 56°C for a rare-to-medium-rare finish (adjust to 60°C for a firmer, more sliceable texture if preferred) and submerge the sealed bag.
4. Cook for 72 hours, checking the water level and temperature daily, topping up water as needed to keep the bag fully submerged.
5. At the end of the cook, the meat should feel tender through the bag when pressed, with no resistance, while still holding its shape.
6. Remove from the bag, reserving the juices for a sauce, and pat dry.
7. Sear again briefly and hard in a very hot pan, 30-45 seconds per side, to rebuild a crust before serving.
8. Rest for 5 minutes, then slice against the grain into thick portions.

**Chef's notes:** 72 hours is a floor, not a target to shorten under time pressure — pulling it early leaves the connective tissue only partly broken down, and the texture reads as tough rather than tender.

name: Meatballs (Polpette)
tagline: Soft, well-bound beef and pork meatballs, browned then simmered.
story: Polpette stay light and moist because of a soaked bread base folded into the mince, rather than relying on fat alone to carry the texture — this is the detail that separates a soft meatball from a dense one. Browned first for flavour and then finished gently in sauce, they are a base component used across pasta dishes and as a bistro main in their own right.
method:
1. Soak 100g stale bread, crusts removed, in 100ml milk until fully softened, then squeeze out excess milk and mash to a paste.
2. Combine the bread paste with 500g minced beef, 300g minced pork, 1 egg, 60g grated Parmesan, 15g chopped parsley, a crushed garlic clove, and 12g fine salt.
3. Mix gently with your hands until just combined — overworking compacts the mixture and makes the meatballs dense.
4. Roll into even balls, about 40g each (roughly 25 balls), and chill for 20 minutes to firm up.
5. Heat a little oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat and brown the meatballs in batches, turning to colour all sides, about 4-5 minutes total per batch — this is for flavour, not to cook them through.
6. Transfer the browned meatballs into a simmering tomato sauce and cook gently for 12-15 minutes, until a probe reads 70°C at the centre.
7. Hold in their sauce; they improve slightly after a rest of 30 minutes to an hour. Refrigerate up to 3 days or freeze up to 2 months, in sauce.

**Chef's notes:** mix by hand and stop the moment it holds together — a mixer or overworking by hand both push moisture out and turn the texture springy rather than soft.

name: Albóndigas en Salsa
tagline: Spiced Spanish meatballs, browned and simmered in almond-thickened sauce.
story: Albóndigas share a base method with polpette but take a distinctly Spanish turn — a little cumin and paprika in the meat, and a sauce thickened with fried bread and almonds rather than reduced tomato alone, giving it more body. It is a comfortable, well-loved bistro dish that holds and reheats better than most protein mains, which makes it useful across a service.
method:
1. Soak 80g stale bread in 80ml milk, squeeze out and mash. Combine with 400g minced pork, 300g minced beef, 1 egg, a crushed garlic clove, 5g ground cumin, 5g smoked paprika, and 12g fine salt; mix gently.
2. Roll into balls of about 30g (roughly 24 balls) and chill for 20 minutes.
3. Brown the meatballs in batches in a little oil over medium-high heat, about 4 minutes total per batch, and set aside.
4. In the same pan, sweat 150g chopped onion until soft, then add 20g flour and cook for 1 minute.
5. Deglaze with 100ml white wine, then add 400ml chicken or beef stock and a pinch of saffron or extra paprika; simmer for 5 minutes.
6. Make a picada by frying a slice of bread and 20g blanched almonds in oil until golden, then grinding with a little of the sauce to a paste; stir this back into the sauce to thicken it.
7. Return the meatballs to the sauce and simmer gently for 15 minutes, until a probe reads 70°C at the centre and the sauce has thickened to coat a spoon.
8. Rest 10 minutes before serving; holds refrigerated up to 3 days.

**Chef's notes:** the picada is what gives the sauce its characteristic body — without it, the dish is just meatballs in a thin stock, missing the point of the Spanish version.

name: Terrine de Campagne
tagline: Coarse country pâté of pork and liver, baked in a water bath and pressed.
story: A country terrine is a way of using pork shoulder, back fat and liver together so nothing goes to waste, bound and seasoned generously since it is served cold, where flavours read quieter than hot food. It needs a long, gentle bake, a proper press while cooling, and a few days' rest before slicing — none of which can be rushed for a service that same week.
method:
1. Dice 800g pork shoulder and 300g pork back fat, and finely chop 200g pork liver. Combine with 100g diced onion sweated soft, 2 crushed garlic cloves, 15g fine salt, black pepper, a pinch of ground allspice and a splash (30ml) of brandy.
2. Mix thoroughly by hand, then pass roughly half the mixture through a mincer on a coarse setting for texture, leaving the rest hand-chopped for bite; combine both together.
3. Line a terrine mould with strips of pork back fat or blanched, overlapping caul fat, leaving enough overhang to fold over the top.
4. Pack the mixture firmly into the mould, pressing down to remove air pockets, and fold the fat over the top to seal.
5. Cover with a lid or foil and place in a deep roasting tray filled with hot water halfway up the sides of the mould (a bain-marie).
6. Bake at 150°C for 75-90 minutes, until a probe inserted into the centre reads 68-70°C.
7. Remove from the water bath, place a weighted board directly on top of the terrine, and cool completely, then refrigerate under the weight overnight.
8. Rest at least 2-3 days in the fridge before slicing — this is essential for the flavour to settle and the texture to firm for clean slices. Holds refrigerated up to 10 days.

**Chef's notes:** do not skip the weighted press while cooling — without it, the terrine holds air pockets and fat separates out as visible pools when sliced.

name: Rillettes
tagline: Pork shoulder, slow-cooked in its own fat until it shreds, then potted.
story: Rillettes come from cooking pork shoulder low and slow, submerged in its own fat, until it falls apart with almost no resistance — then shredding and beating it back together with enough of that fat to bind and seal it. Potted and chilled, it keeps for weeks under a fat seal, which makes it a useful thing to have batched and ready as a bistro starter or bar snack.
method:
1. Cut 1kg pork shoulder (with some fat) into large chunks and season with 20g fine salt, a few thyme sprigs, a bay leaf, and a pinch of ground clove.
2. Place in a heavy pot with 300g pork back fat or lard, enough to mostly submerge the meat once it releases its own fat as it cooks.
3. Cover and cook very gently on the lowest possible heat, or in a 130°C oven, for 3-3.5 hours, until the meat is completely tender and falls apart at the touch of a fork.
4. Strain the meat from the fat, reserving the fat and cooking liquid separately.
5. Shred the warm meat with two forks, or beat briefly in a mixer on low speed, until it reaches a coarse, fibrous, spreadable texture — not a smooth paste.
6. Beat in enough of the reserved fat and juices, a little at a time, to bind it into a moist, spreadable consistency; taste and adjust salt.
7. Pack into jars or ramekins, pressing down to remove air pockets, and pour a thin layer of the reserved fat over the top to seal completely.
8. Chill until set. Stored sealed and refrigerated, rillettes keep up to 3 weeks; once the seal is broken, use within a few days.

**Chef's notes:** shred, don't purée — the point of rillettes is a loose, fibrous texture, and over-processing turns it into something closer to a pâté.

ingredients.name: pork shoulder, with some fat, cubed

name: Pork Crackling
tagline: Pork skin, dried and roasted until it puffs and shatters.
story: Good crackling is mostly about drying the skin properly before it ever sees a hot oven — moisture trapped in the skin steams instead of blistering, leaving a chewy, leathery result instead of a light, crisp shatter. Made in a batch, it works as a garnish on meat and vegetable plates alike across both menus, not just as a pork accompaniment.
method:
1. Score pork skin (about 500g, with a thin layer of fat attached) in a tight grid, cutting through the skin but not deep into the fat.
2. Rub fine salt generously into the scored surface and leave uncovered on a rack in the fridge for at least 12 hours, ideally 24, to dry the skin thoroughly.
3. Preheat the oven to 150°C. Place the skin fat-side down on a rack over a tray and roast for 30-35 minutes to render the fat slowly.
4. Raise the oven to 220°C and continue roasting for a further 15-20 minutes, watching closely, until the skin puffs, blisters and turns deep golden and fully crisp.
5. If any patches remain leathery rather than crisp, return briefly to the hot oven, checking every 2 minutes — it can go from perfect to burnt quickly at this stage.
6. Remove and drain briefly on paper. It should shatter cleanly when snapped, with no chewy layer underneath.
7. Cool completely, then break into shards. Store in an airtight container at room temperature up to 5 days; it softens quickly in humid conditions.

**Chef's notes:** the overnight dry is not skippable — skin that goes into the oven still damp will blister unevenly and stay tough in patches no matter how long it roasts.

ingredients.name: pork skin, with a thin layer of fat

name: Crispy Pig Ear
tagline: Pig ears braised soft, pressed flat, then fried until crackling-crisp.
story: Pig ear is mostly cartilage and skin, which means it needs a long, gentle braise to soften before it can be pressed flat and fried — a snack-sized bar or starter item that gets its appeal entirely from that crisp-outside, tender-inside contrast. It is a good use of an inexpensive cut and rewards being made well ahead of the fry.
method:
1. Rinse pig ears (about 500g, 4-6 ears) under cold water, scraping off any bristle.
2. Place in a pot with enough water to cover, along with a halved onion, a bay leaf, a few peppercorns and 15g salt.
3. Bring to a simmer and cook gently, covered, for 2-2.5 hours, until the ears are completely tender and a knife passes through with no resistance.
4. Remove the ears while still warm and press flat between two trays with a heavy weight on top, then refrigerate under the weight for at least 4 hours or overnight until fully set and flat.
5. Slice the pressed, chilled ears into thin strips.
6. Heat oil to 180°C. Fry the strips in small batches for 2-3 minutes, until deep golden brown and crisp throughout.
7. Drain on paper, season immediately with fine salt while hot, and serve at once.

**Chef's notes:** press the ears flat while still warm from braising — once fully cold they set in whatever shape they were left in, and an uneven press means uneven frying later.

name: Sobrasada Honey Glaze
tagline: Soft Ibizan sobrasada melted with honey into a spreadable glaze.
story: Sobrasada is soft and already close to a paste, so warming it gently with honey is enough to turn it into a glaze that lacquers meat, flatbread or cheese without any further work — it is a genuinely local ingredient on the island, and this is the simplest way to put it to use across several dishes on both menus.
method:
1. Remove the casing from 200g sobrasada and place the paste in a small pan.
2. Add 80g honey and warm gently over low heat, stirring constantly, until fully melted and combined into a smooth, pourable glaze — this takes only 3-4 minutes; do not let it boil, which can make the fat separate.
3. Taste and adjust with a squeeze of lemon juice (about 5ml) if the mixture feels too rich or sweet.
4. Use warm, brushed generously over grilled meats, flatbread or baked cheese in the final minutes of cooking, or as a finishing glaze just before service.
5. Cool any unused glaze and store in the fridge, covered, up to 1 week; gently rewarm before use, as it firms when cold.

**Chef's notes:** keep the heat low throughout — sobrasada is already rendered and fatty, and boiling it hard splits the fat out from the paste, leaving a greasy, broken glaze instead of a smooth one.

name: Chorizo al Vino
tagline: Chorizo sausages simmered and reduced in red wine until glazed.
story: This is a simple tapa that relies on letting the wine reduce fully around the chorizo, so the sausages end up coated in a dark, syrupy glaze rather than sitting in a thin, watery liquid. It cooks quickly and holds well warm, which makes it an easy addition to a shared bistro table.
method:
1. Prick each chorizo sausage (about 500g, cooking chorizo, not the cured slicing kind) a few times with a fork to let fat escape.
2. Place in a pan just large enough to hold them snugly and cover with red wine (about 300ml) — enough to mostly submerge them.
3. Bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook uncovered for 10-12 minutes, turning occasionally, as the wine gradually reduces.
4. Continue simmering until the wine has reduced to a thick, dark, syrupy glaze that coats the sausages, another 3-5 minutes — watch closely in the final few minutes, as it can catch and burn once mostly reduced.
5. The chorizo is done when it feels firm throughout and a probe reads at least 70°C at the centre.
6. Slice into rounds if serving as a shared tapa, or leave whole for a more rustic presentation.
7. Serve warm, spooning any remaining glaze over the top; best served promptly, as the glaze thickens further and can stick as it cools.

**Chef's notes:** resist the urge to rush the reduction with higher heat — a fast, high boil reduces unevenly and risks scorching the sugars in the wine before the sausage is properly cooked through.

name: Croqueta Base (Jamón)
tagline: A very thick jamón béchamel, chilled and piped for frying later.
story: A croqueta is essentially a very stiff béchamel with jamón worked through it, chilled hard enough to hold its shape through breading and frying — the ratio of flour and butter to milk is what makes or breaks it, since a standard sauce-consistency béchamel will never set firm enough to roll. This base is chilled and piped, then held ready to bread and fry to order, kept separate from the saffron version already on the menu.
method:
1. Finely dice 200g jamón (ham trim works well) and sweat gently in 100g butter over low heat for 2-3 minutes, without colouring, to release its fat into the butter.
2. Add 100g flour and cook, stirring constantly, for 3-4 minutes to form a smooth roux and cook out the raw flour taste, keeping the heat low.
3. Gradually whisk in 1 litre warm milk, a ladle at a time, whisking out any lumps before adding more, until fully incorporated.
4. Continue cooking over low heat, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, for 15-18 minutes — much longer than a pouring béchamel — until the mixture is very thick, pulls cleanly away from the sides of the pan, and holds a defined ridge when the spoon is dragged through it.
5. Season with a little nutmeg, salt and white pepper.
6. Spread the hot mixture in a shallow tray lined with parchment, cover the surface directly with cling film to stop a skin forming, and chill completely, at least 4 hours or overnight.
7. Once fully set and cold, pipe or roll into small cylinders (about 30g each) for breading and frying.
8. Hold the set base, well covered, in the fridge up to 3 days, or freeze piped and unbreaded croquetas up to 1 month.

**Chef's notes:** under-cooking the roux stage is the most common fault — if the mixture still looks glossy and loose after 15 minutes, keep stirring over low heat; it will not set properly in the fridge if it hasn't thickened enough on the stove first.

ingredients.name: jamón or ham trim, finely diced

name: Huevos Rotos
tagline: Fried potatoes topped with fried eggs, broken tableside into the crisps.
story: The dish is named for the moment the yolks are broken over the potatoes, so the timing between the fries and the eggs is the whole technique — potatoes need to still be hot and crisp when the eggs land, and the yolks need to be fully liquid so they run through and coat everything underneath. It is straightforward, satisfying bistro food that depends only on good frying, not on a long ingredient list.
method:
1. Cut 500g peeled potato into thick, irregular chunks or matchsticks and dry thoroughly with a cloth.
2. Fry in batches in oil at 160°C for 5-6 minutes, until just tender but pale, then remove and drain.
3. Raise the oil to 190°C and fry the potatoes a second time, in batches, for 2-3 minutes, until deep golden and crisp on the outside.
4. Drain well and season immediately with fine salt while hot; keep warm on a tray.
5. While the potatoes finish, fry 4 eggs in a separate pan in a little olive oil over medium heat, until the whites are just set and the yolks are still fully liquid, about 2-3 minutes.
6. Pile the hot, crisp potatoes onto a plate or board, and lay the fried eggs directly on top.
7. Optionally scatter over torn jamón or cooking chorizo.
8. Break the yolks at the table (or just before serving) with the edge of a spoon or fork, so they run down through the potatoes, and serve immediately.

**Chef's notes:** everything here has to be served the moment it's assembled — the whole appeal is hot, crisp potatoes meeting a still-liquid yolk, and both fade within a minute or two of plating.

name: French Omelette
tagline: Pale, soft-set egg rolled tight with no colour, in under two minutes.
story: A proper French omelette is one of the standard benchmarks a cook is judged on — no colour, no browning, a soft, barely-set curd rolled into a tight, seamless cylinder in well under two minutes. There is nowhere to hide a mistake in it, which is exactly why it is worth keeping in the library as a technique reference, not just a breakfast item.
method:
1. Whisk 3 eggs thoroughly with a small pinch of salt and a splash (10ml) of milk or water until completely homogenous, with no visible streaks of white.
2. Heat a small non-stick pan over medium-high heat and add 15g butter, swirling until it melts and just starts to foam, without browning.
3. Pour in the eggs all at once. Immediately begin stirring rapidly with a fork or spatula, keeping the pan moving over the heat, drawing the curds toward the centre from all sides.
4. Once small curds form and most of the egg is softly set but still glossy and slightly wet on top (this takes about 30-45 seconds), stop stirring.
5. Tilt the pan away from you and, using a spatula or by shaking the pan, fold the near edge of the omelette over on itself, then roll it forward toward the far edge into a tight cylinder.
6. Tip the pan and roll the omelette out onto a warm plate, seam-side down, so it holds its shape.
7. The surface should be pale yellow with no browning at all, and the very centre should still be a touch soft and creamy.
8. Serve immediately; a French omelette does not hold or reheat.

**Chef's notes:** if the pan is too hot the outside browns before the inside sets — the target heat is one that cooks the egg through in under two minutes without ever colouring it.

name: Scrambled Eggs, Restaurant Style
tagline: Low, slow, constantly stirred eggs — soft curds, never dry, never browned.
story: Restaurant scrambled eggs are cooked much lower and slower than most people cook them at home, off and on the heat repeatedly, which is what produces small, glossy, custard-soft curds instead of the larger, drier curds of a hot pan. It is a controlled, patient technique rather than a quick job, and it is worth teaching precisely because most cooks arrive already doing it the fast, wrong way.
method:
1. Whisk 4 eggs with a small pinch of salt until just combined; do not overbeat or add liquid at this stage.
2. Melt 20g butter in a heavy-bottomed pan over low heat.
3. Pour in the eggs and immediately begin stirring continuously and slowly with a spatula, keeping the pan low over the heat.
4. Every 20-30 seconds, lift the pan off the heat entirely for a few seconds while continuing to stir, then return it to the heat — this repeated on-off motion is what keeps the eggs from ever getting hot enough to firm up quickly or brown.
5. Continue this process for 5-7 minutes total, until small, soft, glossy curds form throughout, with no liquid egg remaining but no dry, crumbly texture either.
6. Just before the eggs reach the final consistency, fold in a small spoonful (about 20g) of cold crème fraîche or double cream off the heat — this halts the cooking instantly and adds richness and shine.
7. Season with a final pinch of salt and serve immediately on a warm plate.

**Chef's notes:** if the eggs look done in the pan, they are already slightly overdone on the plate — pull them from the heat while they still look a touch underset; residual heat finishes them in the seconds it takes to serve.

ingredients.name: crème fraîche or double cream, cold

name: Fish Stock
tagline: A quick, clean stock made from white fish bones and trim.
story: Fish stock is deliberately a short simmer, unlike a meat stock — pushed longer, fish bones turn the liquid bitter and cloudy instead of clean. It is the working base for papillote liquids, sauces, court-bouillon and poaching, made from bones and trim that would otherwise be thrown out, and it does not hold as long as a meat stock, so it is best made in modest batches.
method:
1. Rinse 1.5kg white fish bones and heads (sole, hake, sea bass or similar; avoid oily fish, which turns the stock strong and fatty) under cold water, removing any traces of blood or gills, which cause bitterness.
2. Sweat 150g roughly chopped onion, leek and celery in 20g butter over low heat for 5 minutes, without colouring.
3. Add the fish bones and 150ml dry white wine, and cook for 2-3 minutes.
4. Cover with 2 litres cold water, add a bay leaf, a few parsley stalks and white peppercorns, and bring slowly to a gentle simmer.
5. Simmer very gently, small bubbles only, for 20-25 minutes, skimming any foam regularly — do not let it boil hard, and do not go beyond 30 minutes, or the stock turns cloudy and slightly bitter.
6. Strain through a fine sieve or muslin, without pressing the bones, for a clear stock.
7. Cool quickly over an ice bath and refrigerate up to 2 days, or freeze up to 2 months.

**Chef's notes:** a gentle simmer, never a boil, and a short cook time are both non-negotiable — fish stock rewards restraint in a way meat stock does not.

name: Chicken Stock
tagline: Long-simmered stock from roasted bones — the base for most savoury sauces.
story: This is the workhorse stock behind sauces, braises and risottos across both kitchens, built from bones that would otherwise be waste from every chicken butchered on site. Roasting the bones first, simmering low and long, and skimming diligently are the three habits that separate a clean, gelatinous stock from a cloudy, flat one.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 200°C. Roast 2kg chicken bones and carcasses on a tray for 30-40 minutes, turning once, until deeply golden brown.
2. Transfer the bones to a large stockpot. Deglaze the roasting tray with a splash of water, scraping up the browned bits, and add this to the pot.
3. Cover the bones with 3 litres cold water, ensuring they are fully submerged, and bring slowly to a simmer.
4. As it comes up to heat, skim off any foam and fat that rises to the surface — this is what keeps the stock clear.
5. Add 200g roughly chopped onion, carrot and celery, a bay leaf and a few peppercorns once the initial skimming is done.
6. Simmer very gently, uncovered, for 3.5-4 hours, topping up water if it reduces below the level of the bones, and skimming occasionally throughout.
7. Strain through a fine sieve, discarding the solids, and cool quickly over an ice bath.
8. Refrigerate up to 4 days, or freeze up to 3 months. A good stock will set to a light jelly when fully chilled.

**Chef's notes:** never let it boil hard — a rolling boil emulsifies the fat into the liquid and clouds the stock permanently; a bare, gentle simmer is what keeps it clear.

name: Brown Veal Stock
tagline: Deep, dark stock from roasted veal bones, reduced for sauces and jus.
story: This is the foundation for any serious jus or reduced sauce on the tasting menu — heavily roasted bones and vegetables give it colour and depth that no amount of seasoning can substitute for later. It takes most of a day to make properly and is worth batching in volume and freezing, since a full veal stock is too time-consuming to make to order.
method:
1. Preheat the oven to 220°C. Roast 3kg veal bones on a tray for 45-60 minutes, turning occasionally, until very deeply browned, almost mahogany in colour.
2. In the last 15 minutes, add 300g roughly chopped onion, carrot and celery to the tray to roast alongside the bones until well coloured.
3. Transfer the bones and vegetables to a large stockpot. Deglaze the tray with 200ml red wine, scraping up all the browned fond, and add this to the pot along with 60g tomato paste.
4. Cover with 4 litres cold water, bring slowly to a simmer, and skim thoroughly as it comes to heat.
5. Add a bay leaf, thyme and peppercorns, and simmer very gently, uncovered, for 7-8 hours, topping up water as needed to keep the bones submerged and skimming periodically.
6. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing lightly on the solids, and discard them.
7. Return the strained liquid to a clean pot and reduce further by up to half if a more concentrated stock or base for a jus is wanted.
8. Cool over an ice bath and refrigerate up to 5 days, or freeze up to 4 months. It should set to a firm jelly when cold.

**Chef's notes:** the depth of colour comes entirely from how hard the bones and vegetables are roasted at the start — a pale roast can never be fixed later, no matter how long the stock simmers.

name: Sofrito Base
tagline: Onion, pepper and tomato, cooked down slowly to a deep, sweet base.
story: Sofrito underlies stews, rice dishes and braised meat sauces across the Spanish side of the menu, and the whole technique is patience — a long, low cook that caramelises the vegetables and reduces the tomato to a jammy concentration, rather than a quick sauté. Made in a batch and kept on hand, it saves a meaningful amount of time at service on any dish that calls for it.
method:
1. Finely dice 400g onion, 200g red pepper and 100g green pepper.
2. Heat 80ml olive oil in a wide, heavy pan over low-medium heat and add the onion and peppers with a pinch of salt.
3. Cook slowly, stirring occasionally, for 20-25 minutes, until the vegetables are completely soft, sweet and starting to turn a light golden colour — do not rush this stage with higher heat, which browns rather than melts them.
4. Add 20g minced garlic and cook for a further 2 minutes until fragrant.
5. Add 400g grated or finely chopped ripe tomato (or good tinned tomato) and a pinch of smoked paprika, and continue cooking over low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the mixture has reduced to a thick, jammy paste with no excess liquid.
6. Taste and season with salt; the finished sofrito should taste sweet, deep and concentrated, not acidic or raw.
7. Cool and store in the fridge up to 5 days, or freeze in portions up to 3 months.

**Chef's notes:** the sofrito is ready when the oil visibly separates and pools at the edges of the pan — that split is the visual cue that the vegetables have given up all their water and the base is properly concentrated.

ingredients.name: ripe tomato, grated, or tinned tomato

name: Picada
tagline: A ground paste of fried bread, nuts and garlic, stirred in to thicken and finish stews.
story: Picada is a Catalan thickening and finishing technique used to add body and a final layer of flavour to a stew or braise in the last few minutes of cooking, rather than at the start like a roux. It is made fresh each time it is needed rather than held for long, since the point is a bright hit of toasted, garlicky flavour stirred straight into the pot.
method:
1. Fry a slice of stale bread (about 40g), torn into pieces, in 30ml olive oil over medium heat until golden and crisp on both sides; remove and set aside.
2. In the same oil, fry 30g blanched almonds and 15g whole hazelnuts, stirring often, until golden and fragrant, about 2 minutes — watch closely, as nuts burn quickly.
3. Add 2 cloves of garlic, sliced, to the pan for the final 30 seconds, just until fragrant, not browned.
4. Combine the fried bread, nuts, garlic and a small handful of parsley (10g) in a mortar and pestle or small food processor.
5. Grind or pulse to a coarse, textured paste, loosening it with a splash (30-50ml) of the stew or braise it will finish, or a little stock.
6. Stir the picada into the dish it is finishing during the last 5-10 minutes of cooking, allowing it to simmer briefly so it thickens the sauce and releases its flavour.
7. Use freshly made each time; it does not hold well once ground, as the toasted flavour fades within hours.

**Chef's notes:** grind it to a coarse paste, not a smooth one — some texture is what identifies a picada in the finished dish, rather than it dissolving invisibly into the sauce.

name: Garlic Confit
tagline: Whole garlic cloves cooked slow and low in oil until soft and sweet.
story: Confit garlic trades the raw bite of fresh garlic for a soft, sweet, almost spreadable clove, and the flavoured oil left behind is just as useful as the garlic itself. Kept on hand, it saves time across dozens of dishes that would otherwise need raw garlic minced to order, and it holds well under refrigeration.
method:
1. Peel 200g garlic cloves, keeping them whole.
2. Place the cloves in a small, heavy pot and cover completely with 300ml olive oil — enough that they are fully submerged.
3. Set over the lowest possible heat, or in a 100-110°C oven. There should be only the faintest, occasional bubble, never a visible simmer.
4. Cook gently for 35-45 minutes, until the cloves are completely soft all the way through and can be crushed easily with a fork, and pale gold in colour, not browned.
5. If any cloves show colour before the others have softened, the heat is too high — lower it and continue.
6. Remove from the heat and cool the cloves in the oil to room temperature; this final soak continues softening them gently.
7. Transfer cloves and oil together into a clean, sealed container and refrigerate; both the garlic and the infused oil keep well for up to 2 weeks.

**Chef's notes:** any browning at all means the heat is too high — properly confited garlic should stay pale and soft throughout, with all its sweetness intact and none of the bitterness that comes with colour.

name: Brown Butter (Beurre Noisette)
tagline: Butter cooked until the milk solids toast to a nutty brown.
story: Beurre noisette is butter pushed just past melted, until the milk solids toast at the bottom of the pan and turn the whole thing nutty and fragrant — it is used to finish fish, vegetables and some pastry work, and the difference between right and burnt is a matter of seconds, not minutes. Made ahead and strained, it is a fast way to add real depth to a simple dish at the last moment.
method:
1. Place 400g unsalted butter in a light-coloured, heavy-bottomed pan (a pale pan makes it far easier to judge the colour) over medium heat.
2. Melt the butter fully, then continue cooking as it begins to foam vigorously — the water content is boiling off at this stage.
3. Swirl the pan frequently. As the foam subsides, small brown flecks (the milk solids) will begin to appear and settle, and the butter will take on a nutty, toasted aroma.
4. Watch closely from this point — the colour changes from golden to amber to brown within 30-60 seconds.
5. Remove from the heat the moment the butter turns a deep amber-brown and smells distinctly nutty, before it turns dark and acrid.
6. Immediately pour into a cold bowl or strain through a fine sieve to stop the cooking and separate out the toasted solids if a very clean finish is wanted, or leave them in for extra flavour and texture.
7. Use warm to finish fish or vegetables, or cool and store in the fridge up to 1 week, gently rewarming before use.

**Chef's notes:** pull it a shade earlier than looks perfect — residual heat in the pan continues browning the butter for several seconds even off the heat, and it is very easy to go from nutty to burnt in that gap.

ingredients.name: fine sea salt
ingredients.notes: to taste, if using unsalted for a finishing sauce

name: Master Wet Brine
tagline: The standard salt-and-sugar ratio for brining poultry and pork.
story: This is the reference ratio behind every specific wet-brined item on the menu — a consistent baseline of salt and sugar dissolved in water, adjusted in strength and time by the size and leanness of what is being brined. Having one master formula, rather than reinventing it per dish, keeps every brined item seasoned the same way and stops guesswork creeping in.
method:
1. Combine 2 litres of water with 120g salt and 60g sugar (a standard 6% salt, 3% sugar brine by water weight) in a pot.
2. Add aromatics as needed for the dish — typically a bay leaf, a few black peppercorns, and optionally a sprig of thyme or a few garlic cloves.
3. Bring to a simmer just long enough to fully dissolve the salt and sugar, about 3-4 minutes, then remove from the heat.
4. Cool the brine completely, ideally over an ice bath, before use — submerging meat in warm brine begins cooking the surface and encourages bacterial growth.
5. Submerge the item to be brined fully in the cold brine, weighting it down if necessary to keep it under the liquid.
6. Brine times vary by item: 30-60 minutes for a lean cut like tenderloin, 4-8 hours for chicken pieces, 12-24 hours for a whole bird or a larger roast — always refer to the specific recipe for the exact window, since over-brining leaves meat unpleasantly dense and salty.
7. Remove from the brine, rinse briefly under cold water, and pat completely dry before cooking; discard the used brine.

**Chef's notes:** always brine in the refrigerator, never at room temperature, and always cool the brine fully before the meat goes in — food safety and even seasoning both depend on it staying cold throughout.

name: Master Oil-Confit Technique
tagline: The general low-oil-temperature method behind every specific confit dish.
story: Confit is one technique applied at different temperatures and times depending on what is being cooked — fish confited at 40-45°C, garlic at 100-110°C, duck leg confit closer to 90°C — but the underlying principle is always the same: fully submerge the item in oil or fat held at a controlled, gentle temperature. Written down as one master reference, it keeps the logic consistent across every application on the menu.
method:
1. Choose an oil or fat suited to the item and the desired flavour: neutral oil for delicate fish, olive oil for vegetables and garlic, rendered duck or pork fat for meat confit.
2. Prepare the item as the specific dish requires — season it, and for meats, consider a short dry cure or brine first, since confit itself adds little seasoning.
3. Warm the oil or fat in a pot or deep vessel large enough to fully submerge the item, using a probe or thermometer to monitor it continuously; confit temperatures typically range from 40°C (delicate fish) up to 100-110°C (root vegetables, garlic), and rarely above 90-95°C for meat.
4. Lower the item into the oil so it is fully submerged; add it gradually if in multiple pieces, since cold additions will drop the oil temperature and need time to recover.
5. Hold the temperature steady throughout cooking, adjusting the heat source as needed — this is the entire skill of confit, and the one thing that cannot be rushed.
6. Cooking times vary widely by item and target temperature, from 15-20 minutes for delicate fish to several hours for a tough cut of meat; always refer to the specific recipe for timing and doneness cues.
7. Once done, lift the item out gently, drain briefly, and either serve immediately (delicate fish, vegetables) or finish with a hard sear or crisp (meat confit).
8. Strain and reserve the oil or fat after use; it carries flavour from the confit and can often be reused for the same or a similar application.

**Chef's notes:** a thermometer is not optional for confit — a few degrees too hot turns a gentle poach into a fry, and the entire point of the technique is lost.

ingredients.name: oil or fat suited to the item (neutral oil, olive oil, or rendered animal fat)
ingredients.notes: quantity depends on vessel and item

ingredients.name: item to confit (fish, vegetable or meat, per specific recipe)

name: Pommes Purée
tagline: Butter-heavy potato purée, sieved to silk — the bench standard for every plate that needs one.
story: A purée this smooth only happens by ratio and by sieve, not by whisk. Bistro Mondo plates it under braises and roast birds; Taller uses it thinned as a base under fish. Once a cook can make this one correctly, every other root purée on the list is the same method with a different vegetable.
method:
1. Peel 1.5 kg waxy-floury potatoes (ratte or Yukon gold), cut into even 4 cm chunks.
2. Start in cold, well-salted water (salted as sea water). Bring to a simmer, not a rolling boil — a violent boil waterlogs the starch. Cook 20–25 min until a knife meets no resistance.
3. Drain fully, return to the dry pot over low heat for 1 min, shaking, to steam off surface water.
4. Pass hot through a drum sieve or tamis. Do not use a food processor — it shears the starch and turns the purée gluey.
5. Off the heat, beat in 400 g cold, cubed unsalted butter a handful at a time, working it in fully before the next addition.
6. Warm 250–300 g whole milk separately and beat in to loosen to a slow, ribboning consistency. Season with salt.
7. Hold in a bain-marie at 65–70°C, plastic film pressed directly onto the surface, max 2 hours before it dulls.
**Chef's notes:** butter goes in off the heat, cold and cubed — added hot or all at once, the emulsion breaks and the purée turns oily. Do not refrigerate and reheat from cold on the line; make it fresh or hold warm. Keeps 2 days chilled, loses silkiness on reheat — best remade daily.

name: Celeriac Purée
tagline: Celeriac cooked soft in milk, blended clean — the earthy, lighter answer to potato purée.
story: Celeriac takes on milk the way potato takes on butter, and gives a purée with real vegetable character instead of just richness. It sits well under game, duck and firm white fish where a potato purée would be too heavy, and it is the one root purée on the pass that reads as savoury rather than comforting.
method:
1. Peel 1.2 kg celeriac, removing all the knotty skin, and cut into 3 cm dice.
2. Place in a pot, cover with equal parts whole milk and water (roughly 500 g each), add a pinch of salt, and simmer 20–25 min until completely tender — it should collapse under a spoon.
3. Drain, reserving the cooking liquid.
4. Blend the celeriac in a high-speed blender with 150 g soft butter, adding reserved liquid gradually until smooth and just pourable — celeriac holds more water than potato, so add liquid a little at a time rather than all at once.
5. Pass through a fine chinois for full smoothness. Season with salt and a few drops of lemon juice to lift.
6. Hold warm in a bain-marie, film pressed to the surface, up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** over-blending celeriac (unlike potato) is fine — there's no starch to turn gluey, so push it through the blender fully before sieving. Cools and sets firmer than potato purée; loosen with a splash of hot milk when reheating. Keeps 3 days chilled.

name: Parsnip Purée
tagline: Sweet, nutmeg-warmed parsnip purée — the natural pairing for anything from the wood oven.
story: Parsnip has enough natural sugar that it needs almost no help, just cream and a whisper of nutmeg to keep it from tasting like dessert. It is the purée Bistro Mondo reaches for under roast pork and duck through autumn and winter, when parsnips are at their best and the sweetness reads as warmth rather than excess.
method:
1. Peel 1.1 kg parsnips, quarter lengthwise, and cut out any woody core if large.
2. Simmer in salted water 20 min until fully soft.
3. Drain well and return to the dry pot over low heat briefly to drive off excess moisture.
4. Blend with 200 g warm double cream, 80 g butter, and a fine grating of nutmeg until completely smooth.
5. Pass through a sieve for service-grade texture. Season with salt.
6. Hold warm, film to the surface, up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** taste before adding nutmeg — parsnips vary a lot in sweetness by season, and it's easy to tip the purée into pudding territory. If it tastes flat, it needs salt, not more cream. Keeps 3 days chilled; reheat gently with a splash of milk.

name: Carrot-Ginger Purée
tagline: Carrot purée sharpened with fresh ginger — bright enough to cut through oily fish or duck fat.
story: Plain carrot purée reads as one-note sweet; ginger gives it a spine. It's the purée Taller uses under seared scallops or duck breast where the plate needs acidity and heat as well as sweetness, and it holds its colour and punch far better than a purée relying on citrus alone.
method:
1. Peel and slice 1.1 kg carrots into even rounds. Peel and finely grate 25 g fresh ginger.
2. Sweat carrots and ginger gently in 40 g butter for 5 min without colour.
3. Add enough water or vegetable stock to just cover (about 300 g), cover the pot, and simmer 20 min until the carrots are fully tender.
4. Drain, reserving liquid, and blend carrots with 60 g butter, adding reserved cooking liquid until smooth and glossy.
5. Pass through a fine sieve. Season with salt and a squeeze of lemon.
6. Hold warm in a bain-marie up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** grate the ginger rather than mincing it — a grater releases the juice without leaving fibrous strands that survive blending. Older carrots need longer cooking and more sieving to lose fibre; taste for ginger heat before adding more, it builds after blending. Keeps 3 days chilled.

name: Pea Purée
tagline: Fast-blanched pea purée, blended to order — the one purée that must be made close to service.
story: Pea purée is the exception to batch-and-hold: it must be blended hot and used within the hour, or the chlorophyll dulls to khaki. Both kitchens keep frozen peas on hand specifically for this — they're picked and frozen at peak sweetness and give a more reliable green than anything sitting in a delivery crate.
method:
1. Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Have an ice bath ready.
2. Drop 800 g frozen peas in and blanch just 90 seconds from the water returning to the boil — they only need to cook through, not soften.
3. Drain immediately and shock hard in the ice bath to lock the colour, then drain again thoroughly.
4. Blend hot-drained peas (reheat briefly if shocked cold) with 60 g soft butter, a few mint leaves if using, and a splash of the blanching water, blending on high until completely smooth — this takes longer than it looks, 2–3 min.
5. Pass through a fine sieve to remove skins. Season with salt and a touch of sugar if the peas taste starchy rather than sweet.
6. Use within 1 hour of blending; do not hold long in a bain-marie, the colour and flavour both drop off within the hour.
**Chef's notes:** the sieve step is not optional — unsieved pea purée is grainy from the skins no matter how long it blends. Make close to service in small batches rather than one big batch held all night.

name: Jerusalem Artichoke Purée
tagline: Jerusalem artichoke purée, nutty and faintly sweet — Taller's Nordic-leaning root purée.
story: Jerusalem artichoke cooks down to something closer to chestnut than potato, with a natural sweetness that needs only milk and butter to round it out. It fits the Nordic-Mediterranean register of the tasting menu better than potato purée does, and pairs particularly well with anything smoked or with mushroom.
method:
1. Scrub 1 kg Jerusalem artichokes well (no need to peel if scrubbed clean — the skin is thin) and slice into 2 cm rounds.
2. Place in a pot with 300 g milk, 200 g water, and a pinch of salt. Simmer 20–25 min until completely tender.
3. Drain, reserving the liquid.
4. Blend with 100 g butter, adding reserved liquid until smooth and pourable.
5. Pass through a fine sieve — Jerusalem artichoke has more fibre than potato and benefits from a thorough sieve.
6. Season with salt and a touch of lemon juice. Hold warm, film to the surface, up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** Jerusalem artichokes discolour fast once cut — work quickly or hold cut pieces in acidulated water until they go into the pot. The purée thickens noticeably as it cools; loosen with hot milk before plating if it's been holding a while. Keeps 3 days chilled.

name: Sweet Potato Purée
tagline: Roasted, not boiled, sweet potato purée — concentrated flavour with no added water.
story: Boiling sweet potato dilutes it and can leave it watery; roasting whole in the skin concentrates the sugars and keeps the purée dense enough to hold its shape on a plate. It's the purée that goes under game birds and pork at Bistro Mondo, where a touch of orange zest keeps the sweetness from turning cloying.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 190°C. Prick 1.2 kg whole sweet potatoes and roast on a tray 45–55 min until a knife slides in with no resistance and they've collapsed slightly.
2. Halve while hot and scoop the flesh into a bowl, discarding the skins.
3. Pass hot flesh through a sieve or ricer directly.
4. Beat in 80 g soft butter and the finely grated zest of half an orange. Season with salt.
5. If too thick to plate cleanly, loosen with a small amount of warm milk or cream, added a spoonful at a time.
6. Hold warm in a bain-marie, film to the surface, up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** roasting whole and unwrapped concentrates flavour that boiling washes out — don't shortcut to boiling for speed. Orange zest is easy to overdo; start with half a zest and taste. Keeps 3 days chilled.

name: White Bean Purée
tagline: Cannellini beans cooked soft and blended with olive oil — the dairy-free purée for the pass.
story: Every kitchen needs one purée with no milk or butter in it for the dairy-intolerant table, and this is it — smooth, savoury, and rich from olive oil alone rather than cream. It also does double duty as a base for a quick white bean crostini or a component under lamb.
method:
1. Soak 400 g dried cannellini beans in plenty of cold water overnight (at least 8 hours). Drain and rinse.
2. Place in a pot with 1 confit garlic clove or 2 raw cloves, a bay leaf, and enough water to cover by 5 cm. Do not salt yet — salt added early toughens the skins.
3. Simmer gently, uncovered, 60–90 min until completely soft and starting to break apart. Top up water as needed to keep beans submerged.
4. Drain, reserving cooking liquid, and remove the bay leaf.
5. Blend beans with 100 g good olive oil, adding reserved cooking liquid until smooth and glossy.
6. Pass through a sieve for full smoothness. Season with salt and lemon juice now, once beans are cooked.
7. Hold warm, film to the surface, up to 2 hours.
**Chef's notes:** salting the soaking or cooking water early is the most common way this goes wrong — the skins toughen and never fully break down. Season only after the beans are tender. Keeps 4 days chilled, freezes well.

name: Pommes Fondantes
tagline: Potato cylinders braised in butter and stock — crisp top and bottom, molten centre.
story: This is the potato dish that proves technique over ingredients: three humble things, potato, butter, stock, done in the right order, give something no amount of seasoning fakes. It's a Bistro Mondo standby alongside roast meats because it can be built ahead and finished to order in the oven.
method:
1. Peel large potatoes and trim into cylinders roughly 5 cm tall and 5 cm across using a round cutter (12 cylinders from about 1.5 kg potato).
2. Heat 60 g butter and 30 g oil in a heavy ovenproof pan over medium-high heat. Colour the potatoes on both flat faces until deep golden, 4–5 min per side.
3. Add 400 g chicken or vegetable stock, 2–3 thyme sprigs, and a crushed garlic clove — the liquid should come about a third of the way up the potatoes.
4. Transfer to a 180°C oven. Bake 25–30 min, basting once or twice, until a knife meets no resistance and most of the stock has been absorbed or reduced to a glaze.
5. Rest 5 min before plating; spoon over the pan glaze.
**Chef's notes:** the potatoes must brown properly before the stock goes in — that's what gives the crust that holds while the inside turns to a soft purée. Reheat gently in a low oven with a splash of stock; they dry out fast under a hot lamp. Keeps 2 days chilled.

name: Pommes Anna
tagline: Wafer-thin potato discs, layered and pressed in butter, turned out as one crisp cake.
story: Pommes Anna is nothing but potato, butter and heat, arranged with enough discipline that it holds together when sliced. Boris keeps this on the Bistro Mondo menu as the potato dish that plates dramatically with almost no ingredients — a reminder that technique is the flavour here, not additions.
method:
1. Peel 1 kg waxy potatoes and slice paper-thin (1.5–2 mm) on a mandoline. Do not rinse — the surface starch helps the layers bind.
2. Clarify 200 g butter (see Clarified Butter method) and keep warm.
3. Brush a heavy ovenproof blini or cake pan generously with clarified butter. Arrange potato slices in a tight overlapping circle from the centre out, brushing each layer with butter and seasoning lightly with salt.
4. Continue layering to about 4 cm deep, pressing down firmly every few layers to compact.
5. Cook on the stovetop over medium heat 5 min to set and colour the base, then transfer to a 200°C oven with a weight (a smaller pan) on top for the first 20 min to keep it compact.
6. Remove weight, continue baking 20–25 min until the top is tender and the base is deep golden through the pan edge.
7. Rest 10 min, then invert onto a board and slice into wedges.
**Chef's notes:** the mandoline slice thickness is the whole recipe — too thick and it never compacts into a cake, too thin and it dries out. Reheat wedges in a hot pan with butter to re-crisp the surface rather than in the oven alone.

name: Triple-Cooked Chips
tagline: Boiled, dried, and fried twice — the shattering-crust, fluffy-centre chip.
story: Three separate cooks sound like overkill for a chip until the first one comes out of the fryer: a crust that shatters instead of just crisping, over a centre that's still fully fluffy. Taller runs these alongside the bar menu because they hold their crunch far longer under a heat lamp than a single-fried chip ever does.
method:
1. Cut 1.2 kg peeled Maris Piper or other floury potatoes into 1.5 cm batons.
2. Simmer in well-salted water 8–10 min until just cooked through but not falling apart — the edges should be slightly fluffed.
3. Drain very carefully (they're fragile) and spread on a wire rack in a single layer. Chill uncovered in the fridge or a blast chiller at least 1 hour, or overnight, to dry the surface fully — this step cannot be rushed.
4. First fry: fry at 130°C for 5–6 min until a pale, sealed crust forms with no colour. Drain and cool completely (again, chill if time allows).
5. Second fry: fry at 180–190°C for 4–5 min until deep golden and audibly crisp. Drain on paper, season with salt immediately.
**Chef's notes:** the drying step between boil and first fry is what makes this method work — skip it and the chips steam rather than crisp. Once through the first fry and cooled, they hold in the fridge up to 2 days before the final fry, which makes them genuinely batchable for service.

name: Hasselback Potatoes
tagline: Fan-sliced potatoes roasted in butter until every cut edge turns crisp.
story: The Swedish original does with a knife what most roast potato recipes try to fake with fat alone — every slice edge gets direct heat, so the surface area of crisp per potato is far higher than a whole roasted one. It's the potato side Taller uses when the plate wants something visually distinct from a plain roast wedge.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 200°C. Peel or scrub 8 medium waxy-floury potatoes.
2. Place each potato between two wooden spoon handles or chopsticks and cut thin slices (2–3 mm) across, stopping the knife on the spoon handles so the base stays intact.
3. Arrange in a roasting dish, fan the slices slightly by hand.
4. Brush generously with 100 g melted butter, getting butter down into the cuts. Season with salt.
5. Roast 35 min, then baste again with pan butter and roast a further 15–20 min until the outer slices are deep golden and crisp and a knife passes easily through the base.
6. For extra crunch, scatter breadcrumbs or panko into the cuts for the final 10 min of roasting.
**Chef's notes:** cut slowly and check the depth as you go — cutting all the way through defeats the point, the base needs to hold the fan together. Best served straight from the oven; they lose their crisp fan quickly once held.

name: Potato Rösti
tagline: Grated potato, pressed and pan-fried into a single crisp cake per portion.
story: Rösti is a good test of a cook's patience: rush the pressing or the heat and it falls apart in the pan instead of holding as one cake. It's kept on both menus as the potato side that plates as a clean single unit rather than a scoop, useful wherever the dish needs a defined shape on the plate.
method:
1. Peel 1 kg starchy potatoes and grate coarsely. Wrap in a clean cloth and wring out as much liquid as possible — this is the step that determines whether the cake holds together.
2. Season the dried gratings with salt and pepper. Divide into portions (about 150 g each for a single-portion rösti).
3. Heat a film of clarified butter or oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat. Press each portion into a compact disc directly in the pan, about 1.5 cm thick.
4. Cook 5–6 min per side, pressing down occasionally with a spatula, until deep golden and a crust has formed that holds the cake together when flipped.
5. Flip carefully (a plate-flip works better than a spatula for larger rösti) and finish the second side.
**Chef's notes:** unwrung potato is the single cause of a rösti that won't hold — squeeze harder than feels necessary. Cook over medium, not high heat: too hot and the outside burns before the inside sets. Best cooked to order; does not reheat well once fully cooled.

name: Gratin Dauphinois
tagline: Thin-sliced potatoes baked slow in garlic cream — no cheese, no eggs, just potato and cream done right.
story: The real Dauphinois has no cheese in it at all — that's a common shortcut that changes what the dish is. Cooked properly, slow and low, the potato starch alone thickens the cream into something that sets when sliced. It's a Bistro Mondo winter staple precisely because it needs almost nothing else on the plate.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 150°C. Peel 1.2 kg waxy potatoes and slice 2–3 mm thick on a mandoline. Do not rinse.
2. Rub a gratin dish with a cut garlic clove, then butter it generously.
3. Warm 600 g double cream and 200 g whole milk with 1 crushed garlic clove, a bay leaf, and a scrape of nutmeg — do not boil, just bring to a bare simmer to infuse, 5 min, then discard bay leaf and garlic if straining, or leave in for a rustic version.
4. Layer the potato slices in the dish, seasoning lightly with salt between layers. Pour the warm cream mixture over to just cover.
5. Bake 70–80 min at 150°C until the top is golden and a knife slides through all layers with no resistance — check the centre, not just the edges.
6. Rest 15 min before cutting into portions; it needs this time to set enough to hold a clean edge.
**Chef's notes:** low and slow is the whole method — a hot oven browns the top before the centre potatoes cook through. If it looks like it's browning too fast, drop the temperature rather than covering it, which traps steam and stops it setting. Reheats well in a low oven; keeps 3 days chilled.

name: Parisienne Potatoes
tagline: Potato balls scooped with a Parisienne cutter, blanched then butter-sautéed to a nutty gold.
story: These are as much about the shape as the flavour: uniform little spheres that sit neatly around a piece of meat where a wedge or a mash would crowd the plate. Classic garniture, and still one of the fastest ways to make a plate look composed rather than piled.
method:
1. Peel large potatoes and scoop balls with a Parisienne (melon-ball) cutter — aim for 700–800 g of balls from about 1.2 kg potato.
2. Blanch the balls in well-salted boiling water 4–5 min until just tender at the edge but still firm at the centre. Drain and cool slightly on a tray.
3. Heat 50 g clarified butter in a sauté pan over medium-high heat. Add the potato balls and sauté, tossing or turning frequently, 8–10 min until deep golden on all sides and cooked through.
4. Finish with a knob of fresh butter, a scatter of chopped parsley, and season with salt just before serving.
**Chef's notes:** blanch only to just-tender — fully cooking at the blanch stage means they fall apart in the sauté pan. Cook to order in small batches; they don't hold well once sautéed, the crust softens within minutes under a lamp.

name: Patatas a lo Pobre
tagline: Sliced potatoes, peppers and onion, slow-cooked in olive oil until soft and lightly caramelised.
story: "Poor man's potatoes" in name only — cooked properly in enough olive oil, low and slow, this turns into something far more than the sum of its three main ingredients. It's the potato side Taller keeps for anything that wants a Spanish register without competing for attention on the plate.
method:
1. Peel and slice 1 kg potatoes into rounds about 4 mm thick. Slice 2 green bell peppers and 1 large onion similarly.
2. Heat 150 g olive oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium-low heat. Add the potatoes, onion, peppers, and 3 crushed garlic cloves.
3. Cook slowly, uncovered, stirring gently every few minutes to prevent sticking without breaking up the slices, 30–35 min, until the potatoes are fully tender and lightly golden at the edges and the onion and peppers have softened and taken a little colour.
4. Season with salt and a pinch of smoked paprika if using, right at the end.
5. Serve warm, straight from the pan.
**Chef's notes:** the heat must stay low — this is a slow poach-fry in oil, not a sauté, and rushing it at higher heat browns the outside before the inside softens. Reheats well in a pan with a splash more oil; keeps 2 days chilled.

name: Glazed Carrots
tagline: Carrots reduced in butter, sugar and stock to a shining glaze — classic garniture, done right.
story: The glaze is nothing more than a stock reduction that happens to coat the carrots as it thickens, but the timing has to be exact — too far and it catches and turns bitter, too little and it's just wet carrots. It's a Bistro Mondo staple because it turns out the same every time once the ratio is set.
method:
1. Peel 1 kg carrots (baby carrots whole, larger ones cut into batons or on the bias).
2. Place in a wide, shallow pan just large enough to hold them in one layer. Add 300 g chicken or vegetable stock, 50 g butter, 20 g sugar, and a pinch of salt — the liquid should come about halfway up the carrots.
3. Bring to a simmer, uncovered, and cook 15–18 min, shaking the pan occasionally, until the carrots are tender and the liquid has reduced to a syrupy glaze that coats them.
4. If the carrots are tender before the liquid reduces enough, lift them out, reduce the liquid further, then return them to coat.
5. Finish with a few turns of pepper and a scatter of chopped chervil or parsley.
**Chef's notes:** watch the pan closely in the last 2–3 min — the glaze goes from perfect to burnt-sugar bitter fast once the liquid is mostly gone. Best made close to service; reheating tends to break the glaze.

name: Braised Fennel
tagline: Fennel wedges braised soft in stock, wine and butter until they lose their raw bite entirely.
story: Raw fennel is a garnish; braised fennel is a side dish with real body, and the anise note mellows into something closer to sweet celery. It's the vegetable Taller reaches for with fish courses where a crunchy raw element elsewhere on the plate needs a soft, warm counterpart.
method:
1. Trim 3–4 fennel bulbs (about 1 kg), keeping the root end intact, and cut each into 6 wedges through the root so they hold together.
2. Heat 30 g butter and a little oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Colour the fennel wedges lightly on the cut sides, 3–4 min.
3. Add 150 g dry white wine and let it bubble 1 min to cook off the harshest alcohol.
4. Add 250 g vegetable or chicken stock, a couple of thyme sprigs, and season with salt. Cover and simmer gently 20–25 min until a knife passes through the root end with no resistance.
5. Uncover and reduce the remaining liquid to a light glaze, 3–5 min, spooning it over the fennel as it reduces.
**Chef's notes:** cut through the root, not across it — wedges cut the other way fall apart in braising. Keeps 3 days chilled; reheats well in its own braising liquid.

name: Roasted Cauliflower Steak
tagline: Thick cauliflower slabs, seared then roasted until deeply caramelised and tender at the core.
story: Cut through the core, a whole cauliflower yields two or three real steaks with enough surface area to take a hard sear — treated like that, it stops being a side note and becomes something that can carry the centre of a vegetarian plate on its own.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 200°C. Remove outer leaves from 2 large cauliflowers, keeping the core intact, and cut each through the centre into 2 cm thick steaks (the outer pieces that crumble can be roasted separately as florets).
2. Season steaks with salt and brush with olive oil on both sides.
3. Heat a heavy ovenproof pan until hot. Sear the steaks 2–3 min per side until deep golden-brown.
