4. Transfer the pan to the oven and roast 12–15 min until a skewer passes through the thickest part of the core with only slight resistance — it should be tender but not mushy.
5. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and any spice or herb dressing to suit the dish.
**Chef's notes:** don't skip the sear — a cauliflower steak roasted from raw without colour first tastes steamed rather than roasted. Cut steaks from the centre of the head; the outer curved pieces won't hold together as a steak. Best cooked to order.

ingredients.name: cauliflower
ingredients.notes: large, cut into steaks through the core

name: Charred Broccolini
tagline: Broccolini blanched then hit hard on the grill — tender stem, blistered leaf and floret.
story: The blanch-then-char sequence is what keeps the stems from being raw and woody while still getting real char on the leaves and buds. Quick, bright, and one of the few vegetable sides that genuinely wants direct flame rather than an oven — a natural fit for Bistro Mondo's wood-fired setup.
method:
1. Trim woody ends from 600 g broccolini. Bring a pot of well-salted water to a boil and have an ice bath ready.
2. Blanch broccolini 60–90 seconds until just bright green and slightly softened at the stem. Shock in the ice bath, drain well, and pat dry.
3. Toss with a little olive oil and salt.
4. Grill over high, direct heat (wood embers or a hot char-grill) 1–2 min per side, turning once, until the leaves and buds are visibly blistered and charred in spots while the stem stays tender-crisp.
5. Finish with lemon juice, chilli flakes, or a scatter of toasted garlic chips.
**Chef's notes:** dry the broccolini thoroughly after blanching — wet stems steam on the grill instead of charring. Cook close to service; it wilts within minutes once dressed and doesn't hold.

name: Creamed Spinach
tagline: Wilted spinach bound in a light nutmeg cream — the classic steakhouse side, made from scratch.
story: Done properly, this isn't spinach drowned in cream sauce — it's spinach wilted, well drained, and bound in just enough cream to coat, so the vegetable still leads. It's the side Bistro Mondo pairs with anything from the grill that needs a rich but not heavy counterpoint.
method:
1. Wash 1 kg fresh spinach thoroughly and remove any thick stems.
2. Wilt in batches in a hot, dry wide pan (or with a splash of water), turning constantly, 1–2 min per batch until just collapsed. Drain in a colander, pressing gently to remove excess water, then roughly chop.
3. In the same pan, sweat 1 finely diced shallot in 20 g butter until soft, no colour, 2–3 min.
4. Add 150 g double cream and a scrape of nutmeg, bring to a gentle simmer, and reduce slightly, 2–3 min.
5. Fold in the drained spinach and toss to coat evenly in the cream. Season with salt.
**Chef's notes:** press the water out of the wilted spinach properly — skip this and the cream sauce turns thin and watery on the plate. Make close to service; spinach releases more water the longer it sits, even after draining.

name: Ratatouille
tagline: Provençal vegetable stew, each vegetable cooked separately before it comes together — no mush.
story: Ratatouille cooked all in one pot from the start turns to soup; cooked in stages, each vegetable keeps its own texture and the dish holds structure on the plate as well as in a jar. Bistro Mondo runs it as a component under grilled fish and lamb through the summer glut of courgette, aubergine and pepper.
method:
1. Cut 400 g aubergine, 400 g courgette, 2 red peppers, and 1 large onion into even 2 cm dice, kept separate.
2. Sweat the onion in 40 g olive oil until soft, no colour, 5 min. Remove and set aside.
3. In the same pan with more oil as needed, sauté the peppers until starting to soften and colour lightly, 5–6 min. Remove and set aside.
4. Sauté the courgette similarly, 4–5 min, until just softened with light colour. Remove and set aside.
5. Sauté the aubergine last, with more oil (it absorbs the most), until tender and golden, 6–8 min.
6. Return all vegetables to the pan with 400 g crushed ripe tomatoes, 3 crushed garlic cloves, a sprig each of thyme and a bay leaf. Simmer gently, uncovered, 15–20 min until it comes together into a loose stew but each vegetable is still distinct.
7. Finish with torn basil, and season with salt.
**Chef's notes:** the separate sautéing is what keeps this from becoming baby food — resist the shortcut of throwing everything in together. Keeps 4 days chilled, improves by the next day.

name: Caponata
tagline: Sicilian sweet-sour aubergine, celery, capers and olives — served at room temperature.
story: Caponata's agrodolce base sets it apart from every other Mediterranean vegetable stew on this list: it's built to be sweet and sour at once, and it's meant to be served cool or at room temperature rather than hot. Kept in the fridge as a ready component for antipasti boards and to sit alongside grilled fish.
method:
1. Cut 600 g aubergine into 2 cm cubes, salt lightly, and leave to drain in a colander 20 min, then pat dry.
2. Fry the aubergine in batches in olive oil until deep golden, 5–6 min per batch. Drain on paper and set aside.
3. In the same pan, sauté 150 g diced celery and 1 diced onion until softened, 5 min.
4. Add 300 g crushed tomatoes, 40 g pitted green olives (halved), 30 g capers, and 20 g raisins if using. Simmer 10 min.
5. In a small pan, dissolve 30 g sugar in 40 g white wine vinegar over low heat and let it reduce slightly to a light agrodolce syrup. Add to the pan.
6. Return the fried aubergine to the pan, stir to combine, and simmer a further 5 min so the flavours meld. Season with salt.
7. Cool to room temperature before serving; finish with toasted pine nuts if using.
**Chef's notes:** salting and draining the aubergine before frying stops it soaking up excessive oil — don't skip it even under time pressure. Improves after a day in the fridge; keeps 5 days chilled.

name: Pisto
tagline: Spanish stewed vegetables — courgette, pepper, tomato and onion, cooked down slow and soft.
story: Pisto is closer in spirit to a well-reduced sauce than a stir-fried vegetable dish — everything goes soft and melds together over slow heat rather than staying distinct. It's the base Taller keeps on hand for a simple fried egg on top, or spooned under white fish.
method:
1. Dice 1 large onion, 2 green peppers, and 2 red peppers evenly.
2. Sweat the onion in 60 g olive oil over medium-low heat until translucent, 5 min. Add the peppers and cook, stirring occasionally, 10 min until softened.
3. Add 500 g diced courgette and 3 crushed garlic cloves. Cook a further 10 min, stirring occasionally, until the courgette softens.
4. Add 400 g crushed ripe tomatoes and simmer, uncovered, 15–20 min, stirring occasionally, until the mixture has cooked down to a thick, jammy stew with no watery liquid left.
5. Season with salt and a pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are sharp.
**Chef's notes:** the long simmer at the end is what turns this from a vegetable sauté into pisto — keep reducing until a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a clear trail. Keeps 4 days chilled, freezes well.

name: Escalivada
tagline: Whole aubergine, pepper and onion roasted until collapsed, then peeled and dressed simply.
story: Catalan in origin — vegetables roasted whole and slow until the skins blacken and the flesh inside turns to soft smoke-scented pulp, then peeled by hand. No dicing before cooking, which is what gives it a texture and depth that pre-cut roasted vegetables never quite reach.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 200°C. Place 2 whole aubergines, 3 whole red peppers, and 2 whole onions (skin on) directly on a tray, no oil needed.
2. Roast 40–50 min, turning once or twice, until the skins are fully blistered and blackened in places and the vegetables have visibly collapsed and softened all the way through.
3. Transfer to a bowl, cover with cling film or a lid, and let steam and cool for 20 min — this loosens the skins for peeling.
4. Peel off the skins, remove pepper seeds and aubergine stem, and discard onion papery layers. Tear the flesh into strips by hand rather than cutting.
5. Arrange, dress with good olive oil, a little sherry vinegar, and salt. Serve at room temperature.
**Chef's notes:** resist rinsing the vegetables to remove char or seeds — a quick rinse washes out the smoky flavour that's the point of the dish; pick seeds out by hand instead. Keeps 3 days chilled, best brought back to room temperature before serving.

name: Peperonata
tagline: Sweet peppers stewed soft with onion and a touch of vinegar — bright, glossy, and versatile.
story: Simpler than caponata and without the aubergine, peperonata is mostly about cooking peppers slowly enough that their sweetness fully develops, then sharpening it with a little vinegar at the end. A quick, dependable component for bruschetta, alongside grilled meat, or folded through pasta.
method:
1. Slice 4 mixed red and yellow peppers into strips and 1 onion into half-moons.
2. Sweat the onion in 40 g olive oil over medium-low heat until soft, 5 min.
3. Add the peppers and 2 crushed garlic cloves. Cook, stirring occasionally, 15–18 min until the peppers have fully softened and released their liquid, then reduced back down to a glossy, jammy consistency.
4. Add 20 g red wine vinegar and a pinch of sugar in the last 2 min, stirring to deglaze the pan and balance the sweetness.
5. Season with salt. Serve warm or at room temperature.
**Chef's notes:** don't rush the initial cooking — undercooked peperonata still tastes like raw pepper with vinegar on it rather than a cooked-down stew. Keeps 5 days chilled.

name: Braised Lentils du Puy
tagline: Puy lentils braised with mirepoix and thyme until tender but whole — never mushy.
story: Puy lentils hold their shape through cooking in a way most other lentils don't, which is exactly why they're kept as the house lentil for a warm bed under duck, salmon or sausages. Cooked in stock with a classic mirepoix rather than just water, they carry real depth on their own.
method:
1. Rinse 300 g Puy lentils; no soaking needed.
2. Finely dice 1 small carrot, 1 celery stick, and half an onion (a fine mirepoix). Sweat in 20 g butter over medium heat until softened, 4–5 min, no colour.
3. Add the lentils, 700 g vegetable or chicken stock, a bay leaf and a thyme sprig. Do not salt yet.
4. Bring to a simmer and cook, uncovered, 22–28 min, checking from 20 min, until the lentils are tender but still hold their shape and most of the liquid has been absorbed.
5. Remove bay leaf and thyme. Season with salt and pepper now that they're cooked. Finish with a knob of butter or a drizzle of good olive oil.
**Chef's notes:** salting the lentils before they're cooked toughens the skins, the same rule as dried beans — season only at the end. Keeps 4 days chilled; loosen with a splash of stock when reheating.

name: Confit Shallots
tagline: Whole shallots cooked slow and low in oil until jammy-soft and deeply sweet.
story: Confit turns a sharp raw shallot into something soft enough to spread and sweet enough to sit under a piece of grilled meat without any added sugar. Kept on hand as a ready garnish and as a background flavour builder — folded into a vinaigrette, it replaces raw shallot with none of the bite.
method:
1. Peel 400 g small shallots, leaving them whole (halve any larger ones).
2. Place in a small, heavy pot and cover completely with olive oil (roughly 400–500 g), adding a few thyme sprigs and a bay leaf.
3. Bring to the barest simmer over low heat — bubbles should just break the surface occasionally, not roll — and cook 40–50 min until the shallots are completely soft all the way through and lightly golden.
4. Cool in the oil. Store submerged in the cooking oil, refrigerated.
5. Season with salt only at the point of use, not during cooking.
**Chef's notes:** if the oil is bubbling steadily rather than barely simmering, the shallots will brown and turn bitter on the outside before the centre softens — turn the heat down. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated, submerged in oil; the flavoured oil itself is worth keeping for dressings.

ingredients.name: salt
ingredients.notes: to taste, at point of use

name: Roasted Beetroot
tagline: Whole beetroot, salt-roasted in foil until tender, then peeled while warm.
story: Roasting whole in a foil parcel with salt keeps beetroot's flavour concentrated instead of leaching into boiling water, and the skins slip off with a thumb once cooked rather than needing a peeler. A Taller staple for the Nordic register of the tasting menu, served warm, cold, or pickled from this base.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 190°C. Scrub 1 kg beetroot (mixed sizes trimmed of leaves, root left on).
2. Place on a large sheet of foil, scatter with coarse salt and a splash of water or vinegar, and wrap tightly into a sealed parcel.
3. Roast 50–70 min depending on size, until a skewer slides through the largest beet with no resistance.
4. Open the parcel carefully (hot steam) and let the beets cool just enough to handle.
5. While still warm, rub the skins off with a clean cloth or gloved hands — they should slip away easily. Trim the root and stem ends.
6. Cut or leave whole depending on use. Dress with oil or hold plain, refrigerated.
**Chef's notes:** peel while still warm — once fully cooled the skins grip much harder and need a knife, tearing the flesh. Wear gloves or expect stained hands. Keeps 5 days chilled, peeled or not.

name: Crispy Shallots
tagline: Thin-sliced shallots fried slow to a shattering, deep-gold crumb topping.
story: A jar of these on the pass turns any soup, purée or braise into something with textural contrast at zero extra thought — every kitchen needs a batch made and ready rather than fried to order under pressure. The trick is entirely about temperature control, not the shallot itself.
method:
1. Peel 300 g shallots and slice as thinly and evenly as possible on a mandoline (2 mm).
2. Toss lightly with 15 g flour or cornflour to help crisping (optional but recommended), shaking off excess.
3. Place shallots in a pan with 400 g neutral oil while it's still cold — starting cold and heating together is what gives an even, non-bitter crisp.
4. Heat over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the shallots start to turn golden, about 8–10 min, then reduce heat to medium-low for the final stage, stirring more frequently to prevent burning.
5. As soon as they turn a deep gold (they darken further off the heat), strain immediately through a fine sieve and spread on paper towel to drain and crisp fully.
6. Season lightly with salt while still warm.
**Chef's notes:** they carry over and darken for a good 30 seconds after straining — pull them a shade lighter than you want the final colour. Store airtight at room temperature up to 1 week; they go soft, not stale, so re-crisp briefly in a low oven if needed.

name: Fried Capers
tagline: Capers dried and flash-fried until they bloom open and turn crisp.
story: Fried, capers lose their briny pop and gain a completely different texture — crisp shells that shatter, with concentrated saltiness instead of vinegar sharpness. A fast garnish for fish and anything that wants a salty crunch rather than a fresh herb note.
method:
1. Drain 100 g capers thoroughly and pat very dry on paper towel — excess moisture causes violent spitting in the oil.
2. Heat 150 g neutral oil in a small pan to 180°C.
3. Fry the capers in a single batch, standing back — they will spit and pop as the moisture releases, 60–90 seconds until they visibly open up like small flowers and turn crisp.
4. Remove immediately with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towel.
**Chef's notes:** dry the capers properly before frying — undried capers spit oil aggressively and cook unevenly. They crisp further as they cool; do not over-fry waiting for a crunch that develops off the heat. Use within a few hours for best crunch; they soften if stored.

name: Herb Salad
tagline: Loosely dressed soft herbs, picked whole and tossed just before the plate leaves the pass.
story: This is the garnish that must be built à la minute — dressed even a few minutes early and the leaves wilt and darken. Kept as a standard mix (parsley, chervil, dill, tarragon in whatever ratio suits the dish) so any cook on the pass can build it the same way under pressure.
method:
1. Pick 100 g mixed soft herb leaves whole from their stems — a mix of flat-leaf parsley, chervil, dill and tarragon works across most dishes; adjust ratio to what the plate needs.
2. Wash gently in cold water if needed, spin dry thoroughly, and hold on damp paper towel in the fridge until service, uncovered so they don't sweat.
3. Just before plating, toss the leaves very lightly with a few drops of good olive oil, a squeeze of lemon juice, and a pinch of flaky salt — use your hands, not a whisk, so the leaves don't bruise.
4. Place on the plate loosely, without pressing down, so the salad keeps volume and air.
**Chef's notes:** dress at the very last moment — even 5 minutes ahead of time, the acid and salt wilt the leaves and the salad loses its lift on the plate. Never hold dressed herb salad; build to order only.

ingredients.name: mixed soft herbs (parsley, chervil, dill, tarragon)

name: Microgreen Mix Handling
tagline: How microgreens are received, stored and dressed so they last the service without wilting or slime.
story: Microgreens are the most fragile thing that comes through the walk-in and the easiest to waste through bad handling — a batch stored wet or sealed airtight can turn to slime within a day. This is the standard the kitchen follows on delivery, not a recipe with a finished dish at the end of it.
method:
1. On delivery, check the punnet for any wet, dark or slimy patches and remove them immediately — one bad patch spreads through the whole box overnight.
2. Do not wash microgreens unless visibly dirty; washing shortens their life dramatically. If washing is necessary, do it in ice water, and dry immediately and thoroughly in a salad spinner on the lowest setting.
3. Line a shallow container with dry paper towel, lay the microgreens loosely on top (do not pack down), and cover loosely — not airtight — with a lid or cling film with holes, or a barely damp cloth.
4. Store at 2–4°C, away from the coldest part of the fridge (frost damages them), and check daily, removing any greens that have started to wilt or discolour.
5. At service, pick or cut only what's needed with clean scissors or fingers; dress with the lightest touch of oil and acid immediately before plating, the same way as herb salad.
**Chef's notes:** airtight storage is the single biggest cause of loss — trapped moisture with no airflow turns microgreens to mush within 24–48 hours. Properly stored, most varieties hold 4–5 days; check them every service.

name: Dehydrated Olive Crumb
tagline: Black olives dried low and slow, then ground to a savoury, umami-rich powder.
story: Drying concentrates the olive down to almost pure savoury intensity, with none of the oiliness or brine sharpness of the fresh fruit — a pinch does the work a whole olive would. Taller keeps a jar of this on hand as a finishing dust for anything Mediterranean on the tasting menu that needs a last note of salt and depth without added liquid.
method:
1. Pit 300 g good-quality black olives (oil-cured work especially well for depth) and pat dry.
2. Spread in a single layer on a dehydrator tray, or on a wire rack over a baking tray in an oven set to its lowest temperature (around 60–70°C) with the door propped slightly ajar.
3. Dry for 6–8 hours (dehydrator) or check from 4 hours in the oven, until the olives are fully hard and brittle all the way through with no give when pressed — break one open to check the centre.
4. Cool completely, then blitz in a spice grinder to a fine, dark crumb.
5. Store in an airtight container.
**Chef's notes:** the olives are not done until they're brittle right through the centre — any residual moisture and the crumb will clump instead of staying a fine powder, and it will mould in storage. Keeps 1 month airtight at room temperature.

name: Parmesan Crisp
tagline: Grated parmesan baked to a lace-thin, self-supporting crisp — no batter, just cheese.
story: Nothing but parmesan and heat: the cheese melts, spreads, and as it cools re-sets into a genuinely crisp wafer with a distinct, nutty toasted edge. A reliable textural garnish for salads and soups that needs no more than an oven and a template.
method:
1. Preheat oven to 180°C. Line a baking tray with a silicone mat or parchment.
2. Using a small ring cutter as a template, spread finely grated parmesan (about 15 g per crisp) in thin, even rounds on the tray, spaced apart.
3. Bake 5–7 min, watching closely, until the cheese has fully melted, spread, and turned golden at the edges — pull it just as the centre stops looking wet, before it browns too far and turns bitter.
4. Let cool fully on the tray for 1–2 min until firm enough to lift — they are floppy straight from the oven and will crisp as they cool.
5. Once cool, transfer carefully; they can be draped over a rolling pin while still warm and pliable for a curved shape if wanted.
**Chef's notes:** pull them a shade paler than you think — parmesan goes from golden to burnt within seconds once it starts to darken, and burnt parmesan turns bitter, not just dark. Store airtight with silica or in a very low, dry environment; they pick up moisture and soften within hours in a humid kitchen.

ingredients.name: black pepper
ingredients.notes: to taste, optional, mixed in before baking

name: Garlic Chips
tagline: Garlic sliced paper-thin, blanched to soften its bite, then fried to a crisp golden chip.
story: Raw-fried garlic slices burn before they crisp and taste bitter; a quick blanch first draws out some of the sulphur compounds and lets the frying stage crisp them evenly without scorching. A finishing garnish that adds crunch and roasted garlic flavour without raw heat.
method:
1. Peel 8–10 garlic cloves and slice as thinly and evenly as possible on a mandoline.
2. Blanch the slices in simmering water for 30 seconds, drain, and pat completely dry on paper towel.
3. Place in a pan with 200 g neutral oil while cold — start cold, as with crispy shallots.
4. Heat over medium-low heat, stirring frequently, 5–7 min until the slices turn light golden. They colour quickly once they start, so watch closely from the first sign of colour.
5. Strain immediately through a fine sieve and spread on paper towel; season lightly with salt while warm.
**Chef's notes:** dry the slices completely after blanching — any water left on them causes spitting and uneven frying. Like shallots, they carry over and darken after straining, so pull a shade light. Keeps 3–4 days airtight at room temperature before losing crunch.

name: Pangrattato
tagline: Stale bread crumbs toasted crisp in olive oil and garlic — Italy's poor man's parmesan.
story: A way to use bread past its best that turns into a genuinely useful finishing crumb — crisp, garlicky, and able to carry lemon zest or chilli depending on the dish. Bistro Mondo, running on 100% sourdough, always has stale ends on hand for exactly this.
method:
1. Tear or blitz 200 g stale sourdough (crust included) into coarse, uneven crumbs — texture should vary, not be uniform like store-bought breadcrumbs.
2. Heat 60 g olive oil in a wide pan with 1 crushed garlic clove over medium heat until fragrant, about 1 min, then remove the garlic (or leave it in, finely minced, for a stronger flavour).
3. Add the breadcrumbs and toast, stirring constantly, 5–7 min until deep golden and audibly crisp throughout — they will look done before the centre pieces are fully crisp, so keep tossing.
4. Season with salt off the heat. Optionally toss through lemon zest, chopped parsley or chilli flakes once cooled.
**Chef's notes:** stir constantly — pangrattato goes from golden to burnt fast because the crumbs are uneven in size and the small ones catch first. Add any fresh herbs or zest only after cooling, or the residual heat cooks off their flavour. Keeps 1 week airtight; re-crisp in a dry pan if it softens.

ingredients.name: stale sourdough bread
ingredients.notes: torn or blitzed to coarse crumbs

name: Toasted Seeds Mix
tagline: Pumpkin, sunflower and sesame seeds, dry-toasted and lightly salted for crunch and nuttiness.
story: A standing pantry item rather than a made-to-order garnish — one batch covers salads, purées and grain dishes across a week of service. Dry-toasting rather than oil-toasting keeps the seeds crisp for longer without going rancid as fast.
method:
1. Combine 80 g pumpkin seeds, 80 g sunflower seeds, and 40 g sesame seeds in a wide, dry pan.
2. Toast over medium-low heat, tossing or stirring constantly, 4–6 min until the pumpkin seeds start to pop lightly and everything turns golden and fragrant — sesame seeds colour fastest, so watch them as the marker for doneness.
3. Remove from the heat immediately (they continue cooking in the residual pan heat) and tip onto a tray to cool and stop the cooking.
4. Toss with a small pinch of salt while still warm so it sticks.
**Chef's notes:** dry-toasting needs constant movement — seeds left still in the pan for even 10 seconds too long scorch, especially the sesame. Store airtight at room temperature up to 2 weeks; the natural oils turn rancid past that.

name: Candied Nuts
tagline: Walnuts or pecans coated in caramelised sugar to a glossy, crackable shell.
story: Sugar-coated nuts add sweetness and crunch to a savoury salad or cheese course without needing a separate dressing to do it — the caramel shell is the whole flavour delivery system. A pantry-stable garnish both kitchens keep made ahead in batches.
method:
1. Toast 200 g walnut or pecan halves in a dry pan or 160°C oven for 5 min until fragrant, then set aside.
2. In a clean pan, combine 100 g sugar with 30 g water. Cook over medium heat without stirring (swirl the pan if needed) until it turns to a light amber caramel, 5–7 min.
3. Working quickly, add the toasted nuts to the caramel and stir with a wooden spoon or heatproof spatula to coat every piece evenly.
4. Tip immediately onto a silicone mat or oiled parchment, spreading the nuts apart with two forks so they don't clump into one mass.
5. Sprinkle with a pinch of flaky salt while still warm and tacky. Let cool completely and harden before breaking apart.
**Chef's notes:** the caramel sets hard and fast — have the nuts toasted and ready before starting the sugar, and work fast once it colours, there's no time to pause partway through. Store airtight with a desiccant; sugar coating draws moisture from the air and turns sticky in a humid kitchen. Keeps 2 weeks well-sealed.

name: Fried Sage
tagline: Whole sage leaves fried briefly in butter or oil until crisp and translucent.
story: A few seconds in hot fat turns sage from a strong, slightly musty herb into something crisp, aromatic and much milder — a classic finish for brown butter dishes and squash or pumpkin preparations through autumn at Bistro Mondo.
method:
1. Pick 20 whole sage leaves, washed and thoroughly dried — any water on the leaves causes violent spitting.
2. Heat 60 g clarified butter or neutral oil in a small pan until shimmering but not smoking, around 160–170°C.
3. Fry the leaves a few at a time, 10–15 seconds per side, until they turn translucent and crisp and stop bubbling audibly.
4. Remove immediately with a slotted spoon or tongs and drain on paper towel. Season with a pinch of salt while warm.
**Chef's notes:** they crisp fast and burn just as fast — pull them the moment the bubbling around the leaf edges quiets down, don't wait for visible colour change, which happens seconds later. Best used the same day; they go limp if stored more than a few hours.

name: Croutons
tagline: Sourdough cubes toasted in butter and garlic until crisp through, not just on the surface.
story: The difference between a good crouton and a bag-of-stale-bread crouton is toasting evenly through the cube rather than just browning the outside while the centre stays soft — worth the extra attention for a garnish that appears on soups and salads across both kitchens daily.
method:
1. Cut 300 g day-old sourdough into even 1.5 cm cubes.
2. Melt 50 g butter with 20 g olive oil in a wide pan over medium heat with 1 crushed garlic clove until fragrant.
3. Add the bread cubes and toss to coat evenly. Spread in a single layer (use two pans if crowded) and cook over medium heat, tossing every minute or two, 8–10 min until golden and crisp on all sides, not just the top.
4. Alternatively, toss coated cubes onto a tray and bake at 180°C for 10–12 min, shaking the tray halfway, for a more even, hands-off result at volume.
5. Season with salt while warm.
**Chef's notes:** crowding the pan is the most common fault — cubes that touch steam each other rather than crisping evenly, so use a tray in the oven for anything beyond a small batch. Keeps 3–4 days airtight; re-crisp in a low oven before use.

name: Tomato Water
tagline: Ripe tomatoes blitzed and strained overnight, unforced, into a clear, intensely flavoured essence.
story: Gravity and time, not a squeeze, are what keep tomato water clear — forcing it through the cloth clouds it with pulp. The result tastes purely of tomato with none of the acidity or texture, and Taller uses it as a base for a clean gazpacho-style consommé or a delicate dressing.
method:
1. Roughly chop 1.5 kg very ripe tomatoes (no need to peel or seed) and blitz to a rough pulp in a blender with a pinch of salt.
2. Line a fine sieve or colander with a double layer of muslin or a clean j-cloth set over a deep container, leaving plenty of clearance underneath.
3. Pour the pulp into the cloth, gather loosely, and let it drip through under its own weight, refrigerated, for 8–12 hours or overnight.
4. Do not squeeze or press the cloth at any point — this is what keeps the liquid clear rather than cloudy.
5. Discard the pulp (or keep for another use, such as a base for a sauce). Season the clear tomato water lightly with salt if needed.
**Chef's notes:** any pressure on the cloth pushes pulp through and ruins the clarity — set it up and walk away. Keeps 3 days refrigerated; freezes well in small portions.

name: Clarified Butter
tagline: Butter melted slow to separate the milk solids — pure butterfat for high-heat cooking.
story: Removing the milk solids raises butter's smoke point dramatically and stops it burning in a hot pan, which is why it's the fat of choice for searing and for building Pommes Anna and rösti. A basic every kitchen keeps on hand rather than reaching for whole butter under high heat.
method:
1. Melt 500 g unsalted butter in a heavy pan over low heat, without stirring.
2. As it melts, a white foam of milk solids will rise to the top — skim this off gently with a spoon and discard, continuing gently over low heat.
3. Continue heating gently until the butter is fully melted and a clear golden layer sits on top with the remaining milky solids visible settled at the bottom of the pan — do not let it colour or brown.
4. Carefully pour or ladle off the clear golden butterfat, leaving the milky solids behind in the pan. Discard the solids.
5. Store the clarified butter in a sealed container.
**Chef's notes:** keep the heat low throughout — clarified butter that browns has become brown butter (beurre noisette), a different thing with a nutty flavour that isn't neutral for this purpose. Keeps 1 month refrigerated, longer than whole butter, since the milk solids that spoil first have been removed.

ingredients.name: water
ingredients.notes: optional splash, helps separate the solids cleanly

name: Ghee
tagline: Butter cooked past clarified, until the milk solids toast to a nutty gold before straining.
story: One step further than clarified butter: the milk solids are allowed to toast in the fat rather than being skimmed off raw, which gives ghee its distinct nutty, almost caramel aroma. Kept as a separate pantry item from clarified butter because it brings its own flavour rather than being neutral.
method:
1. Melt 500 g unsalted butter in a heavy pan over low-medium heat.
2. As it melts, it will foam; let the foam rise and partially subside without skimming it off — unlike clarified butter, the solids are meant to stay in and toast.
3. Continue cooking gently, swirling the pan occasionally, 20–25 min. The milk solids will sink and begin to toast, turning golden-brown, and the butter itself will turn a deeper gold with a distinct nutty aroma.
4. Watch closely once the aroma turns nutty — remove from heat as soon as the toasted solids are golden-brown, not black, which would taste burnt.
5. Strain through a fine sieve lined with muslin into a clean container, leaving the toasted solids behind.
**Chef's notes:** the difference between perfect ghee and burnt ghee is a matter of under a minute once the solids start toasting — stay at the pan for the last 5 minutes rather than stepping away. Keeps well over a month at room temperature in a sealed jar; it doesn't need refrigeration once fully clarified.

name: Beurre Manié
tagline: Equal parts soft butter and flour, kneaded to a paste — the last-minute sauce thickener.
story: Where a roux is cooked into a sauce from the start, beurre manié is whisked in at the end, raw, to thicken a sauce or braising liquid quickly without further cooking time. Kept ready in the fridge as insurance for any sauce that comes out thinner than it should on the pass.
method:
1. Bring 100 g unsalted butter to room temperature until fully soft.
2. Combine with 100 g plain flour in a bowl.
3. Work together with a fork or by hand until fully combined into a smooth, uniform paste with no dry flour visible.
4. Roll into a log or press flat, wrap, and refrigerate.
5. To use: whisk small pieces into a simmering (not boiling) sauce or liquid a little at a time, allowing each addition to fully incorporate and the sauce to come back to a simmer for a minute before adding more, until the desired thickness is reached.
**Chef's notes:** the sauce must return to a simmer after each addition — beurre manié needs a minute of gentle heat to lose its raw flour taste, added off the boil it will taste pasty. Keeps 2 weeks refrigerated, or freeze in small pieces for longer storage.

name: Roux
tagline: Butter and flour cooked to white, blond or brown stage — the base thickener behind most sauces.
story: The same two ingredients in the same ratio give three completely different tools depending on how long they cook: white roux for béchamel, blond for a velouté, brown for a gumbo-style depth with much less thickening power. Knowing all three stages by sight, not by the clock, is one of the first things a cook has to learn cold.
method:
1. Melt 150 g unsalted butter in a heavy-bottomed pan over medium-low heat.
2. Add 150 g plain flour all at once and whisk continuously to combine into a thick paste.
3. **White roux:** cook 2–3 min, whisking constantly, just until the raw flour smell disappears and the mixture is pale and foaming, with no colour change. Use for béchamel and other pale sauces.
4. **Blond roux:** continue cooking 5–7 min total, whisking constantly, until it turns a light golden, biscuit colour and smells lightly toasted. Use for velouté-style sauces.
5. **Brown roux:** continue cooking 15–20 min total over medium-low heat, whisking constantly and watching closely as it darkens, until it reaches a deep peanut-butter to chestnut brown and smells distinctly nutty and toasted. Brown roux thickens much less than white per gram, so use proportionally more for the same body.
6. Cool before storing, or use immediately, whisking into hot liquid gradually to avoid lumps.
**Chef's notes:** whisk continuously at every stage, especially brown roux — it can go from perfect to burnt in under a minute once past blond, and burnt roux tastes bitter and cannot be salvaged by cooking further liquid into it. Keeps 1 week refrigerated; whisk cold roux into hot (not cold) liquid to avoid lumps.

name: Liaison
tagline: Egg yolk and cream, tempered into a hot sauce or soup for a final silken enrichment.
story: A liaison is the finishing move on a sauce that's already made, adding gloss and body without more cooking — but it has to be handled with real care, since a liaison added carelessly scrambles into a hot sauce and ruins it instantly. Worth knowing cold rather than improvising under pressure.
method:
1. Whisk together 3 egg yolks and 100 g double cream in a bowl until smooth and fully combined.
2. Ladle a small amount (about 50 g) of the hot sauce or soup into the yolk-cream mixture, whisking constantly, to gradually raise its temperature — this is the tempering step and it cannot be skipped.
3. Repeat with another ladle of hot liquid, whisking, until the mixture in the bowl is warm to the touch.
4. Whisk the warmed liaison back into the main pot of sauce or soup, off the heat or over the lowest possible heat.
5. Return briefly to very gentle heat, stirring constantly, just until the sauce thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon — do not let it approach a simmer, or the egg will scramble and the sauce will curdle and separate.
**Chef's notes:** once the liaison is in, the sauce can never boil again — hold below 80°C for the rest of service. This is the point where careless heat ruins an otherwise finished sauce; work over the lowest heat you have. Use the same day; a liaison-finished sauce does not reheat safely from cold without risk of splitting.

name: Egg Wash
tagline: Beaten egg and milk, brushed onto pastry and dough for shine and even browning in the oven.
story: A basic every station needs on hand rather than mixing fresh for every batch — the ratio of egg to milk changes the finish from deep glossy brown (more yolk) to pale even colour (more white or milk), so it's worth having both versions ready depending on what's going in the oven.
method:
1. Whisk 2 whole eggs with 30 g whole milk (or water for a lighter, less glossy finish) until fully combined and no streaks of white remain.
2. Pass through a fine sieve to remove any chalazae (the stringy egg white bits) for a perfectly smooth brush application.
3. Brush a thin, even coat onto pastry or dough with a soft pastry brush just before baking, avoiding pooling in creases or at the base, which can glue the layers together or burn.
4. For extra shine, apply a second thin coat halfway through baking on longer bakes.
**Chef's notes:** don't apply it too thickly or let it pool — excess egg wash can seal pastry edges shut (stopping lamination from puffing) or drip and burn on the tray. Keeps 2 days refrigerated in a sealed container; whisk again before use as it separates slightly on standing.

name: Brine (General 5%)
tagline: A standard 5% salt brine for poultry, pork and fish — measured by weight, not guesswork.
story: A brine at a known percentage means the result is repeatable across chickens, pork chops or fish fillets rather than relying on how salty the water tastes by mouth — and it's the difference between consistently juicy roasted or grilled protein and a coin-flip result depending on who made it that day.
method:
1. Weigh 2000 g cold water into a container large enough to submerge the protein.
2. Weigh 100 g fine salt (5% of the water weight) and dissolve fully in the water, stirring until no grains remain — warming a portion of the water gently can speed dissolving, then cool the whole batch back down before use.
3. Add aromatics as suited to the protein — a few bay leaves, peppercorns, a smashed garlic clove, a spoon of sugar to balance — these are optional and don't change the ratio.
4. Submerge the protein fully in the cold brine, weighting it down if it floats. Refrigerate.
5. Brine times vary by protein and size: about 30–45 min for fish fillets, 1–2 hours for chicken pieces, 4–8 hours for a whole chicken, up to 12 hours for a larger pork joint. Do not exceed recommended times — over-brining pushes the protein past seasoned into cured and rubbery.
6. Remove, rinse briefly under cold water, and pat completely dry before cooking.
**Chef's notes:** always weigh water and salt rather than measuring by volume — a 5% brine by weight is a genuinely different (and correct) concentration from a rough cup-of-salt-per-litre guess. Discard the brine after use; do not reuse on a second batch of raw protein.

name: Dry Cure (Fish)
tagline: Salt and sugar cure for firm fish fillets — a gravlax-style base, dill and citrus optional.
story: A dry cure draws moisture out of the fish and firms the texture while seasoning it right through, and it's the starting point for anything gravlax-adjacent on the Nordic side of Taller's menu. The ratio and timing matter more than any flavouring added on top.
method:
1. Combine 100 g fine salt with 80 g sugar (a roughly 55:45 salt-to-sugar ratio) as the base cure mix. Adjust total quantity to fully coat the fish.
2. Pat a 500 g skin-on fillet (salmon, trout or similar firm fish) completely dry. Check carefully for pin bones and remove with tweezers.
3. Spread a thin, even layer of the cure mix on a tray, place the fillet skin-side down on top, then pack the remaining cure evenly over the flesh side, covering completely. Add fresh dill and citrus zest on top of the cure if flavouring.
4. Wrap tightly in cling film and place on a tray, weighted lightly (a second tray with a small weight) in the refrigerator.
5. Cure 8–24 hours depending on fillet thickness and desired firmness — check at 8 hours for a thinner fillet, up to 24 for a thick one; the flesh should feel noticeably firmer and slightly translucent at the surface when ready.
6. Rinse the cure off thoroughly under cold water, pat completely dry, and slice thinly on an angle to serve, or hold whole, wrapped, refrigerated.
**Chef's notes:** always weigh the cure ingredients rather than eyeballing — too little salt under-cures and leaves a food safety risk, too much draws out too much moisture and turns the fish leathery. Cured fish keeps 4–5 days refrigerated after curing and rinsing.

name: Sous-Vide Egg 63°C
tagline: Whole eggs cooked in the shell at a precise 63°C — a custard-set white and a fully runny yolk.
story: No other method holds this exact texture — white just barely set, yolk still liquid but noticeably thickened — because a pan or a pot of boiling water can't hold a temperature that precise. Once the bath is dialled in, it's the most reliable egg on the pass, unaffected by egg size or how busy the line is.
method:
1. Set an immersion circulator in a water bath to exactly 63°C.
2. Lower whole eggs, straight from the fridge, gently into the bath using a spoon or basket (do not drop them in, they can crack).
3. Cook for 45–60 min — 45 min gives a slightly looser white, 60 min a fully set, custard-like white with the yolk still fluid; test and adjust to house preference.
4. Remove and either use immediately or shock briefly in ice water if holding, then keep the eggs in their shells in the water bath or a warm holding unit at serving temperature until needed.
5. To serve, crack gently into a small bowl or directly onto the dish — the white should hold together as a soft custard and the yolk should flow but not run thin like a raw egg.
**Chef's notes:** the bath temperature is the entire method — even 65°C sets the white too firm and starts to thicken the yolk more than intended, and 60°C leaves the white too loose to hold shape when cracked. Cook to order or hold in the bath at temperature for service, but don't hold longer than about 1 hour past the target time or the texture keeps developing.

name: Poached Egg Batch
tagline: Eggs poached ahead in barely simmering vinegar water, shocked and held for reheat-to-order service.
story: Poaching to order for every ticket doesn't scale on a busy brunch service — poaching a batch ahead, trimmed and held in iced water, means a 30-second reheat in hot water gets a perfect egg out the door on demand, with none of the swirling-water guesswork happening mid-service.
method:
1. Bring a wide, deep pan of water to a bare simmer (not a boil) and add 40 g white vinegar per 2 litres of water — the acid helps the white set quickly and hold together.
2. Crack each egg into a small cup or ramekin first, not directly into the pan.
3. Create a gentle whirlpool in the water with a spoon and slide the egg in from the cup, close to the water's surface. Poach 2.5–3 min until the white is fully set and the yolk is still soft to the touch.
4. Lift out with a slotted spoon and transfer immediately to a bowl of ice water to stop the cooking. Repeat in batches, not overcrowding the pan.
5. Once cold, trim any straggly white with scissors if a neat shape is wanted. Store the poached eggs submerged in fresh cold water, refrigerated, changing the water daily.
6. To serve, drop into a pan of hot (not boiling) water for 45–60 seconds to reheat through, then drain on a cloth.
**Chef's notes:** the vinegar water and the whirlpool both matter for getting a tight, non-stringy white — skip either and the whites trail badly. Batch-poached eggs keep, submerged in water and refrigerated, up to 2 days.

name: Soft-Boiled Egg 6:30
tagline: Eggs boiled exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds from a full boil — a set white, a jammy, half-set yolk.
story: Timed to the second rather than by feel, this is the exact point between a runny and a fully set yolk — jammy enough to hold its shape sliced in half but still glossy and soft through the centre. Kept as a house standard time so every cook on the section gets the same result.
method:
1. Bring a pot of water to a full rolling boil.
2. Lower fridge-cold whole eggs gently into the water with a spoon (a small pin-prick in the rounded end beforehand can help prevent cracking, though it's optional).
3. Start timing the moment the eggs go in and the water returns to a boil. Cook at a steady boil for exactly 6 minutes 30 seconds.
4. Remove immediately and plunge into an ice bath for at least 2 minutes to stop the cooking and make peeling easier.
5. Peel carefully once cool enough to handle, tapping and rolling gently under a thin film of water to help the shell release without tearing the white.
**Chef's notes:** the exact time depends slightly on egg size and altitude — 6:30 is calibrated for a standard large egg at sea level; test and adjust by 15–30 seconds if the yolk consistently comes out too firm or too loose for house standard. Peel and serve promptly; a soft-boiled egg held too long after peeling loses its neat shape and starts to weep from the yolk.

name: Sugar Syrup 1:1
tagline: Equal parts sugar and water, dissolved to a clear simple syrup for bar and pastry use.
story: A basic that both the bar and the pastry section keep stocked separately from any flavoured syrup — it sweetens without adding water-diluting risk the way granulated sugar does when stirred cold into a drink, and it's the base every flavoured or spiced syrup on the list starts from.
method:
1. Combine 250 g granulated sugar and 250 g water in a small pot.
2. Heat gently, stirring, until the sugar has fully dissolved — the mixture should look completely clear with no visible grains, which happens well before it comes to a boil.
3. Bring just to a simmer, then remove from the heat immediately; there's no need to boil it or reduce it further.
4. Cool completely before bottling to avoid trapping steam and diluting the syrup with condensation.
5. Store in a sealed, sterilised bottle, refrigerated.
**Chef's notes:** don't over-boil it — reducing the syrup concentrates it past 1:1 and throws off any recipe measured assuming the standard ratio. Keeps 1 month refrigerated in a sterilised, sealed container; discard if it looks cloudy or shows any sign of mould.

name: Gastrique
tagline: Caramelised sugar deglazed with vinegar — a sharp, glossy sweet-sour reduction for rich meats.
story: A gastrique cuts through fat the way nothing else quite does — the caramel gives body and colour, and the vinegar keeps it from ever tasting like straight sugar. Bistro Mondo keeps it as the go-to finishing sauce for duck, pork belly and other fattier dishes across the menu.
method:
1. Place 100 g sugar in a heavy pan with a splash of water just to moisten it evenly. Heat over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan occasionally, until it turns to a deep amber caramel, 6–8 min. Watch closely near the end — it darkens fast.
2. Remove from the heat and carefully add 100 g red or white wine vinegar in a slow stream, standing back — it will bubble and spit violently as the cold liquid hits the hot caramel.
3. Return to low heat and stir until any hardened caramel has fully redissolved into the vinegar.
4. Simmer gently 3–5 min to reduce slightly to a syrupy, glossy consistency that coats the back of a spoon.
5. Optionally finish with a splash of stock or a knob of butter for body, depending on the dish it's supporting.
**Chef's notes:** add the vinegar off the heat and slowly — pouring cold liquid into hot caramel too fast causes a dangerous, aggressive spatter. Keeps 1 week refrigerated; reheat gently and thin with a splash of water or stock if it's set too firm.

name: Beurre Monté
tagline: Whole butter emulsified into simmering water — a stable, pourable butter sauce for poaching and finishing.
story: Whisked into water rather than melted alone, butter stays emulsified and stable at a much wider range of temperatures than melted butter on its own, without breaking — which is what makes it usable to poach delicate fish or hold as a finishing sauce that won't split under a heat lamp.
method:
1. Bring 50 g water to a gentle simmer in a wide pan.
2. Reduce heat to low. Add 500 g cold, cubed unsalted butter a few cubes at a time, whisking constantly, waiting for each addition to emulsify into the water before adding more.
3. Keep the heat low throughout — the mixture should stay warm enough to keep whisking in butter (around 65–70°C) but never approach a simmer or boil, which would break the emulsion.
4. Once all the butter is incorporated, the beurre monté should look like a smooth, opaque, pourable sauce, holding together rather than looking oily or separated.
5. Use immediately as a poaching medium for fish or shellfish, or as a finishing sauce, keeping it at a steady low warmth (a thermos or a very low bain-marie) throughout service.
**Chef's notes:** if it looks like it's about to split (oily and separating), whisk in a splash of cold water immediately off the heat to bring it back together — don't keep adding butter to a breaking emulsion. It does not hold well once fully cooled and re-melted from solid; make fresh for service rather than trying to save leftovers as a new batch.
